Monday — Designing data products
Monday’s plan
Monday starts with a consumer and a decision. Your team works out who needs the product and what
decision it supports, where the data comes from and what you’re promising. You also write down what
you don’t know yet. The rest of the week builds on that design. On Tuesday Catalyst drafts from it, on
Wednesday some of your transformation rules become dbt models and tests, and on Thursday Airflow
runs them in order. On Friday you build and present a CG product-information data product.
The Policy Team joins us at 09:00–09:30. They’ll talk about how the course fits the wider data creator
initiative, and which parts of a training example are real organisational requirements. If they can’t answer
a question on the day, put it in your team’s assumption register with the role that can answer it.

• Wednesday–Thursday: implement mappings as dbt models and tests, then schedule and inspect

Business and technical participants work together throughout. Experienced engineers can help with
implementation while practising interviews and design; less technical participants learn enough to assess
the models, tests and execution evidence.
The aim is to review and validate a product with the supported tools. Five days cannot cover every
product or platform integration. Use current Confluence guidance and EDO support for policies, access
and follow-on enablement.
One chain runs through the week: a contract clause becomes a model and test, the test runs in a DAG,
and a failure requires diagnosis, recovery and communication. Tool choices involve trade-offs: a stricter
schema is easier to enforce and harder to change; a finer-grained DAG is easier to inspect and costs more
to operate.

that the training brief cannot answer. Instructor demonstrations use prepared examples; screenshots

Introduce your product context
OUTPUTS A named business product, consumer decision and two pain points

Introduce your role and expectations. Choose a data product your team creates or consumes and explain the

Case study: Common product responsibilities
Cases: product and service pain points
Personal-trading, legal and ESG data can require entitlement decisions, consistent formats, ownership and an
assessment of downstream impact. Decision: identify the owner and authorised consumers before interpreting
a formatting fix as a complete solution. Reasoning: a usable file can still be inaccessible or expose information
to the wrong audience. Lesson: treat access and accountability as product promises.
Exposure data represents portfolio risk at a date, often with proportions between zero and one across geography
or style.

Decision: agree the unit, grain, definition and expected arrival, then test the output against them. Reasoning:
technical completeness alone cannot resolve two different meanings of “exposure”. Lesson: the glossary and
source commitment belong beside the model.
Investment-team reference data describes managers, covered funds and experience, sometimes combining
HR-derived information with other sources. Global-results consumers may receive the same underlying source
through files or APIs with different service expectations.

Decision: record delivery formats and service

commitments for each consumer class. Reasoning: one producer can support several products, and different
delivery paths can fail differently. Lesson: distinguish a shared source from the promises made by each

Climate, transactions, analytics and investment-operations data can cross privacy, compliance and vendorcontract boundaries. Decision: classify fields and intended uses before joining the sources. Reasoning: a
useful combined analysis may still require restricted access or a permitted-use decision. Lesson: a platform
such as Caspian hosts multiple data domains; naming the platform does not define a product or authorise
every combination.

Case study: Integration problems and design responses
Cases: boundaries, timing and identifiers
A missed SLA may expose a pipeline problem or a mismatch between producer and consumer deadlines.
Decision: record the end-to-end dependencies, arrival times and checks rather than assuming an identical
dbt pipeline removes every discrepancy. Reasoning: sources can still have different commitments. Lesson:
measure the consumer’s required outcome.
A positions-and-transactions mapping question may cross domain and engineering boundaries. A support
ticket or unanswered shared inbox provides little value without someone who can route the business question.
Decision: name a liaison and document meanings beyond the basic asset, position, return and fund vocabulary.
Reasoning: source teams own transformations while consumers need an explanation of the resulting product.
Lesson: an accountable contact and domain knowledge can be as necessary as correct SQL.
Different aggregations can produce different position values; different identifier-generation rules can create
a portfolio UID collision, or leave CUSIP/ISIN-like security identifiers unmatched. Decision: agree a canonical
identity, mapping rules and reconciliation checks. Reasoning: joining plausible keys can silently associate the
wrong records. Lesson: cross-system unique identity must be specified and tested, even when names appear
consistent.
Vendor products can change arrival times, restate values and restrict permitted use.

API or warehouse

connections also carry cost. Decision: record the licence, correction behaviour, procurement cost and approved
delivery route before building a bespoke report. Reasoning: a technical connection does not settle rights to
redistribute or repurpose data. Lesson: include vendor dependencies in feasibility and viability.
A creator translating between camelCase and underscore schemas can repeatedly absorb work from both
producer and consumer.

Decision: declare a stable interface, mapping and change policy.

Reasoning:

uncontrolled translations create discrepancies and support work. Lesson: make the boundary and responsibility
visible rather than becoming an unbounded intermediary.

Knowledge check: Map the responsibility
For your example, who produces the source, owns its meaning, transforms it, approves access and uses the
result? Which role would answer a question about an unexplained position or return? Identify a contact role

The CG product-information case
A fictional internal Product Information Analyst supports sales and relationship colleagues answering financialprofessional enquiries.

The analyst needs traceable product identities, published fund expenses and

THIS SESSION ANSWERS

• E1: What does the snapshot say about CGGR’s vehicle and net expense ratio, and where did the answer

• E2: Which scoped fund offerings have published net expenses no greater than 50 bps, and which have

• E3: Which three-year annualized NAV returns reported at September 30, 2026 meet the declared

Knowledge check: Reading the CG product brief
Who is the direct internal consumer, which enquiry are you answering, and which source limitation affects the
answer?

Use three roles. The consumer explains the enquiry and their current research process. The producer
explains the frozen public representations, dates and extracted fields. The creator connects those facts
to a reviewed output. A fourth person can challenge quality assumptions. The role and enquiries are
fictional classroom scenarios, rather than statements about an actual CG department.
Choose product lookup and one contrasting enquiry, such as the expense shortlist or performance
evidence. Work backwards from each consumer need to its output, source selection, transformation
and independent check. Keep the rules in plain English: select the declared representation, preserve the
product ID and source link, and convert percentage points to basis points by multiplying by 100.

The scope is 25 ETFs, 65 Class F-3 mutual-fund identifiers and 19 SMA strategy IDs. These are 109
offerings, rather than 109 underlying portfolios. All selected ETF fee reporting dates are unknown; SMA
returns cover only 12 strategies. Do not replace missing costs or dates with zero or retrieval time. SMA

For an empathy map, separate what the consumer said from your interpretation. A request for a traceable
source link is evidence; an invented refresh commitment is an assumption. Record what would resolve
each uncertainty before turning it into a product promise.

How to use today’s examples
The motivations later today (power, control, competence, trust, esteem) help you ask better questions
about what someone needs. When a consumer objects to a change, look at the objection itself first. It’s
often a real problem with the product. And someone with no formal influence can still know things you
need.
Source-aligned, domain-aligned and consumer-aligned describe who the data serves. The CG product
combines selected public representations, reusable offering/cost definitions and enquiry-specific outputs.
Name the consumer and explain what each intermediate table is for.
Use CG product-information for today’s required interview and design canvas. The other business cases
illustrate design choices in different domains; use them to test your reasoning or choose an optional
follow-up.
Today you frame the need, interview consumers, decide whether to reuse an existing product or build one,
and agree its promises in a design brief. That brief is the first draft of the contract. Later in the week you
connect the contract to tests, an execution graph and a reviewed handoff. Operational examples show
where alerting, support ownership and a runbook fit.

What is a data product?
Different teams may use different definitions of a data product. Establish a working definition, then test it
through an interview about a consumer’s decision.
THIS SESSION ANSWERS

• What is a data product, and how is it different from a data set?
• Should we create a data product?
• What data product should we create?
• How do you find out what a consumer actually needs?

Knowledge check: Product or data source?
What promise turns a table into a useful product for your consumer? Can the same output be a product for
one team and a source for another?

Consider several candidate properties: consumable, discoverable, trustworthy, accessible, observable
and aligned with enterprise standards. Useful metadata names a business purpose, owner and lifecycle:
planning, design, creation, governance and observation. A “single source of truth” is a claim to examine
against the intended decision and source limitations.
Two teaching points follow:
• Wrong answers are welcome. Part of learning is unlearning what we’ve misunderstood.
• A data product is more than a data set, or a data set plus a view (a dashboard or report). It’s that
plus something, such as discoverability, quality properties and above all trust. “A data set we can
trust” is a fair first pass.
There are three views of what a data product is. They are not equivalent, but they describe the same
thing from different angles.

1. The promises view
The simplest formulation is that a data product is a data set plus a set of promises.
You could think of the promises as SLAs, but it is broader than SLAs:
data set + SLAs + ownership + governance + quality + …

All of these reduce to someone promising something about the data. A data product is not a data set,
and not a property of a data set. It consists principally in the promises. When we ship a data product,
we are releasing something with a set of promises attached: it will have a certain quality, it will arrive at
a certain time, it has an owner who will manage it, respond to emails, and so on. Otherwise it’s just a
dump of data, and no one cares about that.
A promise creates an obligation to a consumer. State who is responsible, what will be delivered and how
a failure will be handled. A dataset without those commitments leaves the consumer to discover its
limitations.

2. The asset view
A data product is code + infrastructure + data:
• the code that produces the data,
• the infrastructure the code runs in,
• and the data itself (plus metadata).

18

+44 (0)20 3583 0972 | info@decoded.com | decoded.com

DECODED

Monday — Designing data products

Code automates the promises: building and serving the data, enforcing constraints, testing quality,
monitoring delivery and recording failures. The infrastructure supplies the resources and interfaces that
let that code run.

3. The alignment view
Alignment describes whose needs shape the vocabulary, structure and meaning of an output. A source
is arranged for its producer; a product adapts that information for a consumer’s decision.
A data product transforms data from a source-aligned state to a consumer-aligned state.
• Source-aligned means aligned with the interests of the outside party that produced it, some person
or organisation that isn’t us, who structured the data for their own purposes.
• Consumer-aligned means aligned with the interests of our consumer.
• The data product creator sits in the middle and does the realignment.
For an illustrative vendor-feed case, suppose a source supplies equity observations and a consumer
needs fund-level exposure. Confirm the supplier’s actual fields, identifiers, permitted use and provenance
before designing that output. A provider name such as Morningstar does not establish fund ownership,
manager assignments or an official book of record. The creator realigns verified source information to
the agreed consumer question. These are relative terms: a consumer product for one team can become
a source for another.
A second example: an Apple Watch could give you a thousand heart-rate readings a second. That’s
aligned to the sensor. The consumer wants to know whether their heart rate is healthy, whether they’re
improving, whether the exercise is working.
The heart of designing a data product, beneath the data, code, infrastructure and properties like trust,
is taking something the consumer doesn’t want (a data source) and transforming it into something they
do want. The transformation from an uninteresting source to a useful product is the product. Alignment
covers more than schema, values and rows. It includes why the vocabulary is the way it is, what a column
name means.

Domain-aligned, and why these are relative terms
A third label is sometimes used. Domain-aligned data has been transformed away from the source into
something reflecting a business or subject area, but not yet aligned to a particular consumer. In practice,
if you merge multiple sources (an Apple Watch, a room thermostat and others) into “health data”, the
intermediate result reflects what the data is about rather than anyone’s goals. Even more practically,
there’s an input folder, an output folder, and intermediate folders of transformed stuff in the middle. The
middle ones are the “domain” ones.
These labels are relative to the product boundary. A consumer-ready output for one team can become
source data for another.
• There is no such thing as “a data source” in the world. Your product is someone else’s source.
Labelling something a data source really says “this was produced by someone who isn’t me, aligned
to their interests”; consumer-aligned says “aligned to my interests” (or to the people we care about).
• In this course, the creator is accountable for a defined product boundary and its consumer
requirements. That consumer may be another data team: a reusable domain-aligned product can
be a legitimate deliverable. Alignment does not impose a universal CG restriction on which products
a creator can build. Confirm the actual owner, consumers and responsibilities for the assigned
product.
One possible interpretation is a ladder: source-aligned = data (raw temperatures per second), consumeraligned = information (the trend), domain-aligned = insight (multiple data points combined).

That

interpretation is not a fixed definition; the ladder projects your goals onto the steps.

To the factory making the sensor (testing a resistor), temperature per second is the insight. That’s their
consumer-aligned product. Go a level below and another team dealing in voltages and resistors thinks
that is the insight. From different positions in the chain, the three labels rotate. The labels change with
the producer and consumer boundary.

Alignment, and whose needs the data serves
A source-aligned table reflects its producer. A domain-aligned table defines reusable offering identity
or expense meaning; a consumer-aligned output answers the analyst’s lookup, shortlist or comparison
enquiry.

Figure 1: Alignment: whose needs the data serves

Reconciling the three views
• Most promises are automated by code. If you promise delivery at a certain time, code delivers on
that promise. That connects the promises view to the asset view.
• Alignment is a specific, not-fully-specified kind of promise: a promise that the product will meet
your needs. That connects the alignment view to the promises view.

Worked example: ESG data
• Source: MSCI provides environmental and social data, e.g. CO₂ data per company, plus lists of
properties.
• Consumer product: an exposure or risk report, e.g. exposure to EU carbon taxes, perhaps 0.01 of
risk per million tonnes of CO₂ produced by held companies.
• Promises we make to the customer: the report will be available at a given time (and if the promise
itself says “95% of the time”, then hitting 95% is keeping the promise, because the promise sets the
expectation); there is a clear internal data owner who handles governance (who has access), quality
validation, and so on.

Why do data products fail?
Consider both engineering and organisational failure conditions.
Engineering answers: lack of governance; quality; security/access control; non-functional requirements
failing (performance, access, formats, where “non-functional” means requirements not associated with
the operational functioning of the system).

Repeated departures from a documented process can become accepted practice. Record exceptions and
their consequences so a workaround does not silently replace the agreed quality or change policy.
Human answers (the part engineers miss, issues that arise between people): the product is not needed,
misaligned requirements, lack of adoption, loss of trust, lack of training or onboarding, and poor
communication.
How do we solve those problems?
• Profile the consumer. Understand customer needs before building.
• Communication.
• Data lineage. Understand the source of the data and the events in its lifetime.
• Improve the technology stack (with the caveat that “improve” often just means “update”).
• Ownership and accountability. A defined owner, and responsibility.
• Documentation.

Note the link to trust.

Accurate documentation records the thought process,

requirements and decisions behind the product. Even if consumers only ever feed it into an AI
model for a summary, having a sense of why decisions were made improves trust. Unexplained gaps
can lead consumers to make incorrect assumptions about the data.
• Transparency, organisational as well as documentary. Be open with downstream consumers about
what you’re doing, release information early, bring people into meetings, offer access. It makes them
feel secure.

Borderline questions
For this course, distinguish recording an event from transforming existing records for a consumer. An
order-entry application creates transaction records; a reporting product reshapes those records under
an agreed meaning and service promise. A larger system can contain both responsibilities.
Is the data product just the data asset, or the whole pipeline? It’s the whole thing (code, infrastructure,
data assets, promises), but the emphasis depends on your role. For data creators the emphasis is the data
asset and the promises. Code and infrastructure are instrumental, the means of fulfilling the promises.
Software engineers see it the other way around: code and infrastructure are their product, the data and
promises are for other people.
So the smallest data product is an Excel file plus a promise to email it every day, and the largest is the
lakehouse and everything in it.
Isn’t ETL the same as what a data creator does? This is a real tension in the course. The person who
does the consumer interview and the person who assembles lakehouse infrastructure have very different
skill sets. So everyone creating data products should know something about the whole process, with
role-dependent emphasis. Engineers benefit from understanding the design motivation so they can push
back intelligently. Non-technical designers benefit from first-hand exposure to the systems so they can
hold their own in engineering meetings.

1. Should we create a data product?
2. What data product should we create?

Canvases. The general industry term for a grid of questions and prompts that helps you design something

• a design canvas, which answers the should question (covered later today, after the interviews)
• a product canvas, which answers the what question

The scoping questions
Workflow
The “should we build it?” decision can be framed as eight scoping questions:
1. Who needs it?
2. What’s the value / ROI?
3. Can we build it (feasibility)?
4. Does it already exist?
5. How would it be adopted?
6. Marketplace and discoverability. How will consumers find it?
7. What SLAs would it carry?
8. Legal and compliance?
Question 4 has three possible outcomes: subscribe to an exact match, compose from an extendable partial
match, or build when no suitable product exists.

You can also group the same questions into four themes. Is it desirable (what does the consumer need)?

Which questions need other roles? Separate the questions you can estimate from those that need

• Hardest for the data creator to answer alone: desirability (who needs it, what value?), because we
are not the consumer. Once we know who they are and what they want, we can estimate much of
the rest.
• Easiest to answer ourselves: feasibility and delivery, meaning how we actually build and ship it.
• Most likely to be misunderstood: who needs it (requires business context) and metrics for success.
• Design implication: desirability and viability are the two ends with a human-behaviour element,
hence hardest to predict; the central columns (feasibility, delivery) can largely be managed with

Four assessment themes on the design canvas
Desirable means the consumer needs it. Feasible means the data and the technology can produce it.
Viable means it’s worth what it costs, and deliverable means this organisation can build it and keep it
running. A query that works can still fail on deliverability if nobody owns the data or you can’t get access
to it.

Figure 2: Six questions for assessing a product design

Finding out what data product to create
As the data creator, we are neither the consumer nor the source. We do the translation, so we don’t
automatically know what to build. Ways to find out from the consumer:
• Ask for a problem statement
• Survey them (email forms, questionnaires)
• Interview them (calls, meetings)
• Observe them (sit with the team, watch what they actually do)
• Research existing documentation
• Ask about pain points. What do you do now? what are the workarounds?

Turning ambiguous accounts into requirements
A consumer’s description may leave gaps, reflect competing priorities or omit steps that have become
routine. A statement and an observed action can differ because of the environment, available tools,
incentives or the person’s understanding. Use multiple forms of evidence before concluding what should
change.
A requirement that another organisation has solved still needs interpretation for this team: the available
sources, decision rights and vocabulary may differ. Making a vague need precise is part of the creator’s
work. Like diagnosing a technical fault, start with the reported issue and investigate its cause. Check the
resulting explanation with the consumer, then record the requirement and remaining uncertainty.
For difficult adoption or workflow concerns, Managing stakeholders expands evidence, observation and
empathy methods. Continue with the core interview before the design canvas.

Interviewing producers and consumers
Interview the consumer about the decision and the producer about the source. Record what each person
actually says, distinguish evidence from assumptions, and check your interpretation with them. A product
can be technically correct and still miss the consumer’s working deadline or meaning of a field.
Knowledge check: Before the interview
What would you ask a consumer who requests a dashboard? Which answers require a producer or a data
owner? What observation would show whether the current workaround is meeting the need?

Preparing for an interview
Prepare an evidence-led interview
DURATION 10 minutes within the interview session
OUTPUTS Role briefs, questions and an assumption register

1. Use the CG product-information brief, or a business product introduced in your opening discussion. Name
the consumer, the decision and the producer. If roles overlap, identify which responsibility the person is
answering for.
2. Write down what the brief already establishes: source tables, proposed row grain, output, working
deadline and any quality or access constraints. Leave unspecified values as open questions.
3. Choose an interviewer/data creator, consumer and producer. The consumer prepares a description of a
decision and current workaround; the producer prepares source meanings, availability and constraints.
Role holders can add plausible training assumptions, labelled as assumptions.
4. Prepare open questions and follow-up probes. Start with a recent concrete example before asking for an
ideal future state. Ask permission to inspect an example of the existing output or workflow.
5. Prepare a notes table with columns for statement, evidence/example, implication, unresolved question
and owner. Record tensions between consumer needs and source constraints rather than resolving them
silently.
Check: each role can explain their responsibility; the questions address the decision as well as data fields;
assumptions have owners. No empathy-map output is required.

Interview for the CG product brief
DURATION 60 minutes (10:30 to 11:30)
OUTPUTS Interview notes, a requirements handoff and an uncertainty register

Work in threes using the CG product brief. The consumer asks E1, E2 or E3; the producer explains frozen
products, fees and returns; the creator translates between them. Use the brief as authority and label added
training assumptions.
1. Prepare role notes and select questions (10 minutes). The consumer describes how the result will be
used; the producer explains what the source can provide. The creator initially sees only the shared brief.
2. Interview the consumer (15 minutes), asking for a concrete decision and current workaround. Probe timing,
definitions, quality and failure impact. Read back two important requirements in the consumer’s words.
3. Interview the producer (15 minutes). Check row grain, keys, join coverage, update and correction behaviour,
access and upstream commitments. Ask how each consumer requirement maps to an available source
or an unresolved gap.
4. Write a handoff (10 minutes): named consumer and decision; output grain and fields; glossary and
proposed transformations; measurable promises; access assumptions; fallback; unresolved questions
with responsible roles. Mark each statement as confirmed, proposed or unverified.
5. Review together against the original brief (10 minutes).

misinterpretation or missing condition. Revise the handoff and give the next decision an owner. A
requirement that cannot yet be supported remains a question or risk.

recording the missing producer validation explicitly.

Case study: Global results for Singapore: identifying the consumer
Global results for Singapore: identifying the consumer
FactSet data passes through global-results processing and a creator before reaching an investment team. The
immediate customer and end decision-maker are different roles.
Decision: Define the interface and promises at the creator’s own boundary, while obtaining enough upstream
and downstream context to validate the end decision.
Reasoning: One downstream consumer may justify a tailored interface; many consumers require a stable
standard so accommodating one team does not silently acquire every downstream commitment. Available
access and time limit how far the creator can inspect the chain.
Lesson: Keep the end decision visible, record upstream dependencies and ask the accountable owner to settle
responsibility boundaries. Local product ownership can help; it does not remove the need for explicit promises.

Case study: ESG risk results: connecting value to prioritisation
ESG risk results: connecting value to prioritisation
Third-party data flags issuers with material ESG risks for analysts and investors, while the creator may sit
several steps away from their decision.
Decision: Interview an end consumer and describe the benefit over the product lifetime before claiming a
prioritisation advantage.
Reasoning: The value materialises downstream; a local pipeline improvement is a means to that value and may
not establish the business case on its own.
Lesson: Record both the causal explanation and any available measurement. An unquantified benefit is an
assumption to investigate, not a fabricated return.

Case study: Morningstar exposures: counting recurring cost
Morningstar exposures: counting recurring cost
An exposure-ingestion product serves analysts, product managers and portfolio managers within CSG; other
teams also want its output.
Decision: Declare the consumer population and interface, then include maintenance, troubleshooting and
communication in the lifetime cost.
Reasoning: An illustrative estimate of four development sprints and about 20 support hours per week makes
recurring effort visible. These are case assumptions, not forecasts for CG product-information.
Lesson: Support is part of viability. Transaction costs between teams remain real inside a large organisation
and belong beside compute and procurement costs.

Case study: Investment research: designing for an AI consumer
Investment research: designing for an AI consumer
Research published in a portal is requested by an AI-agent workflow. A schema designed for a web application
may not be the most useful representation for that consumer.
Decision: Compare authorised plain-text or Markdown extracts with other supported representations on a
defined retrieval and interpretation task.
Reasoning: Text removes many presentation details, but tables, layout and richer media can still carry meaning.
Compare outputs rather than assuming one format always preserves everything.
Lesson: Treat the agent as a consumer with explicit access, meaning and validation requirements. Structure
and representation need evidence; retain provenance and review the result. Additional logging or observability
is a later design consideration, not production work assigned here.

Case study: External counsel invoices: transparency and sensitivity
External counsel invoices: transparency and sensitivity
Invoice detail supports budgeting, authorisation and optimisation of external-counsel spend, but source matter
details and named parties may be sensitive.
Decision: Design a permitted output that exposes the cost information needed for the decision and limits
inappropriate disclosure.
Reasoning: Useful transparency does not require every source detail to be available to every consumer.
Lesson: Record classification, access and any disclosure or evidence-preservation questions for the authorised
owner to resolve before committing to delivery.

Case study: Client engagement analytics: explaining the benefit
Client engagement analytics: explaining the benefit
Marketing, communications and related teams use engagement information to choose content and assess
interest.
Decision: State how better behaviour information changes a content decision, then identify a way to evaluate
that change.
Reasoning: “Improves marketing” is too broad to test without a decision, comparison and expected outcome;
early discovery may not yet establish numerical benefit.
Lesson: Keep uncertain lifetime value visible and owned. The canvas should reveal the next evidence to collect.

Case study: Retirement client data: procurement and user experience
Retirement client data: procurement and user experience
External recordkeepers charge for large feeds and API calls. Investors need a usable portfolio experience, and
an existing product must be replaced or migrated.
Decision: Assess procurement and recurring call costs alongside delivery needs, and plan how to compare the
new experience with the old.
Reasoning: Cost and user experience have different measures. Retention, task completion or interaction
patterns may provide evidence, but a monetary value is not automatic.
Lesson: Separate known costs from benefit assumptions and migration risk. When competitors offer similar
core services, usability may still matter; validate its effect rather than attributing every improvement to the
data product.

Case study: Fund data: serving several consumer classes
Fund data: serving several consumer classes
A fund-data product may serve internal applications and external recipients, including a vendor, with different
delivery expectations.
Decision: Specify the consumer classes and supported formats, such as a file, API or approved database

Reasoning: One output shape may not fit every consumer, and each additional interface creates access, support

Lesson: Delivery and adoption are linked. Offer a supported boundary with accountable promises rather than

Data mesh and product ownership
Knowledge check: Ownership and shared platforms
Which responsibilities should stay close to the domain, and which standards or services can be shared?

Data mesh, briefly
A working definition (the term was coined around 2019 by Zhamak Dehghani). Data mesh is decentralised
or localised data-product development, where “local” means in the team most relevant to creating the
data product, as opposed to a centralised IT or engineering department building everything. There are
two broad organisational models: one central team does everything, or teams self-serve. Data mesh is
really about self-service with shared standards. You have access to Databricks, to the platform tools, to
Catalyst, and Catalyst can support that pattern. Give everyone a tool that can create data products, and
let them create their own.
The team closest to the data knows the data best, knows the SLA promises required, knows the
customers. So local knowledge can reduce communication barriers, but ownership and downstream
promises still need explicit agreements.
This isn’t wholly new. The 90s had data marts and marketplaces with limited self-service, but mesh
is more radical, because you do the development yourself. Local development can coexist with shared
storage and platform services. A folder split alone does not establish domain ownership or product
accountability.
The deeper point is that the hard part of a large business is making communication work across large
numbers of people. As organisations grow, explicit ownership and communication become necessary.
Data mesh is, in a sense, a self-organising management system.
For the relationship between domain ownership, shared storage and platform services, see Wednesday’s
data-mesh architecture explanation. Confirm current Capital Group responsibilities with the accountable
platform or product owner.

Knowledge check: A use case with a consumer
Which decision would a combined dataset support, and who would use it? What permission or grain mismatch

Optional use-case discovery
DURATION 15 minutes within canvas/application time if the core brief is complete
OUTPUTS A list of use cases, row grains and named consumers

In new mixed teams, introduce each other:
• Your team and what you work on; your data sets, pipelines and processes
• What SLAs (if any) are relevant to you, your team, your data
• What data pipelines, processes and source-to-target mappings are relevant
• Explore: if you combined data across the team’s sources, what insights might that reveal? (There may be
no useful or permitted combination; record that conclusion.)
Review two more questions: What is a row in one of your data sets, and who are your consumers?

Case study: Discovery across product boundaries
Cases: grains, joins and consumers
Advisor meetings, fund reference and equity-trading records can support an investment lifecycle view. Meetings
may be weekly, fund reference monthly and trading daily. A trade authorisation, broker order and settlement
are distinct row grains; an advisor/buying-unit meeting record and a fund record are different again. Decision:
trace portfolio construction through authorisation, execution and settlement before joining it to advisor notes.
Reasoning: the same proposed purchase may be constrained by a position limit or compliance rule. Lesson: a
useful combined decision needs explicit keys, timing and ownership across the lifecycle.
An expense pipeline ingests bank spend and derives employee-expense metrics. A client view may combine
CDM client data, TACO territory, transactions/redemptions, product reference and digital interactions. Decision:
identify whether the consumer wants expense analysis, client/AUM coverage or fund-performance comparisons
before combining them. Reasoning: a broad “single truth” label does not identify the decision or join grain.
Lesson: comparisons of funds, managers, benchmarks or compensation need agreed definitions and authorised
use.
An advisor-education platform produces progress records; an investment-data product transforms an external
source into dashboards with a working delivery time and backup generations.

Decision:

distinguish

producer responsibilities from downstream analytical promises, then map how advisor activity and investment
information might support a business outcome. Reasoning: data can cross several teams and systems before
a consumer sees it. Lesson: record lineage and source dependencies alongside proposed insight.
Advisor profiles, territory, fund transactions and web engagement can already form an advisor view. A profile
row, a transaction and a page-visit event are different grains. Decision: aggregate and join deliberately for
an analyst’s opportunity assessment or a marketing journey. Reasoning: engagement does not itself establish
intent or authorise use of every profile detail. Lesson: explain who acts on the result, through what channel,
and under which access and purpose constraints.
Advisor–client interaction records, portfolio market values and end-of-day asset prices from vendors or the
investment-operations ecosystem could support an analysis of interaction outcomes. Decision: define the
outcome, valuation date and permitted links before claiming a return on an interaction. Reasoning: a possible
join does not establish causation or consistent observation periods. Lesson: treat the combined insight as a
hypothesis until consumer, source and measurement checks support it.

On this course, every contract makes freshness, completeness and accuracy commitments. Add validity,
uniqueness and consistency rules when the data and the consumer need them. Completeness itself
splits three ways. Row completeness means all expected records arrive, column completeness means
required fields have no unexpected nulls, and referential completeness means every foreign key points
at a valid reference.
Pair each technical commitment with a business measure. A fund product can hit every freshness and
accuracy target while someone still spends 20 hours a week on manual reconciliation, or consumers carry
on using their spreadsheet. A business measure, such as reconciliation hours or the number of people
still on the spreadsheet, will show you that.

The data contract: where it all lands
In the supplied course template, the design decisions are recorded in a human-readable data contract
with eight sections. This template does not establish the current enterprise-wide CG standard; confirm
the applicable version and approvals for a live product:
1. Identity — of the product, stakeholders, etc.
2. Schema — one row per column: type, whether PII is involved, etc. It can also hold the glossary,
meaning what the columns mean.
3. Service Level Agreements
4. Data quality
5. Access (entitlements)
6. Change (change management) — a removed column breaks consumers that select it; narrowing
DECIMAL(10,6) to DECIMAL(10,2) breaks precision; changing a return from TWR to MWR breaks

meaning even though CI sees the same name and type. Semantic versioning gives breaking changes
a major bump, additive changes a minor bump, and description or corrective changes a patch.

7. Team involvement / consumer registry — record one row for each consumer and its use case. Use
a durable contact role such as Consumer Representative — Portfolio Management, because an
individual’s name may go stale. Derive the row’s access level from the decision already recorded in
§5.
8. Approvals
Together these sections are everything you can say about the product at the design stage. Dependencies
(e.g. “we expect a certain amount of data coming in to be able to meet our SLA”) ground the SLA section.
You’ll find a worked §6 change table, versioning policy and §7 registry in Appendix B.
The phrase “data contract” unhelpfully refers to two different things:
1. A human-readable Markdown document with the eight sections above. It’s the contract between
you and whoever uses the product. It is really a data product design document (a service definition,
if you prefer); calling it “the data contract” is the supplied course’s terminology. Confirm the current
internal vocabulary and authoritative format for the assigned product.
2. Automatic code enforcement of schemas, quality rules, and so on, in actual code. Wednesday’s dbt
tests are this sense: schema and data-content tests together check that the schema is correct and
the values obey the rules. In other words, they’re part of the data contract, enforced.
Schema and data checks are different
For a prepared or curated model, contract: {enforced: true} in its YAML makes dbt compare the declared
columns and types with the model’s SELECT; an added, removed, renamed or retyped column then fails the
build before the table is written. Tests check the data values, and the enforced model contract checks the
schema. A contract/ directory with no dbt block can stay the same while the SQL drifts, so update both
column lists in the same pull request.

So in conversation, someone designing a data product who says “we need to produce a data contract”
almost certainly means the document. An engineer who says “I’ve just written a data contract” almost
certainly means code.

SLAs, SLIs, SLOs and RAID
Knowledge check: Service levels and failure
What would you measure to know whether a promised working deadline was met? What upstream dependency
could cause it to fail?

SLAs, SLIs and SLOs
• SLI — service-level indicator: the measured service behaviour, such as the proportion of deliveries
received by a deadline.
• SLO — service-level objective: the target or range for that indicator over a stated window.
• SLA — service-level agreement:

the promise to the consumer, including the response or

consequence when a target is missed.
For example, measure the share of business-day deliveries available by 07:00. An SLO might require at
least 95% over a quarter. The SLA adds who is notified after a miss, when the next update is due and any
agreed remedy. A target need not mean perfect service. Google’s SRE explanation distinguishes these
terms.

The nines: a rule of thumb
90% is “one nine”, 99% two nines, 99.9% three nines, 99.99% four nines, and there is a five-nines. Applied
to a year, roughly how much downtime does each allow?
Availability

Downtime in a 365-day year

90% (one nine)

36.50 days

99% (two nines)

3.65 days

99.9% (three nines)

8.76 hours

99.99% (four nines)

52.56 minutes

99.999% (five nines)

5.26 minutes

Calculate permitted downtime as (1 − availability) × measurement period. For four nines over a
365-day year, (1 − 0.9999) × 365 × 24 = 0.876 hours. A real agreement also states the measurement
window, exclusions and response to a breach.

Four components and an error budget
Check an SLA for four components: an Indicator we can measure, an Objective with a threshold and
measurement window, a Budget for the failures the objective permits, and a Consequence that says what
happens when the budget or target is breached. If any of the four is missing, go back to the consumer
and agree it before you call the statement an SLA.
Work out the error budget like this.
Error budget = total measured events × (1 − reliability target), rounded down

Take a 95% freshness objective across 63 business days. The calculation gives 63 × (1 − 0.95) = 3.
15, rounded down to 3 missed days. Rounding up would allow a fourth miss that the objective did not

permit. Keep the direction of the comparison straight as well. 28 successful refreshes out of 30 is about
93%, which misses a 95% objective.
The count says how much budget has gone; the burn rate says how quickly it is going. A three-miss budget
spread over a 13-week quarter expects roughly 0.23 misses per week, so an early cluster of misses needs
action before the budget is gone.

Error budgets at CG
Error budgets and burn rates are site reliability engineering (SRE) practice. In SRE, a spent budget usually means
holding back risky changes while the team works on reliability. For a CG product, agree the consequence with
the DPM and the consumers and write it into the contract.

What do we make agreements about? Timeliness (daily, weekly, 8 AM, monthly, or batch completion, such
as “the batch must complete before 10 AM every day”), schema / data contract (fields, values, typing,
metrics on the data), quality, uptime, recovery time (if data is deleted or a system goes down, how many
hours until it is available again), support. And importantly, not everything in an SLA is neatly measurable.
There are qualitative agreements about what happens when a promise is broken, such as a duty to notify
(messaging, emailing, updating people), a responsible person acting, a duty to explain (if uptime is missed,
you at least get an email explaining why) and a duty to provide a root-cause analysis. (Duty to fix may
belong to a broader business agreement rather than the data product’s SLA.)
The duty to explain, with an example: during the pandemic, oil futures went negative, which had never
happened in recorded history. An oil futures contract obliges you to take delivery; if you can’t, you sell
it on; if nobody is buying, you pay someone to take delivery, otherwise you bear the enormous expense
yourself. A trader looking at a report with oil futures in the portfolio wants to know why is this number
negative? It could equally be a data-quality issue, or something seriously broken. It’s Tuesday’s distinction
between a data error and a real tail event, turning up in production. Part of support can be that a person
exists whose duty is to explain such patterns, without waiting for an incident.

RAID
• Risks — possible future consequences.
• Assumptions — bets you’re making; things you hope will be true.
• Issues — current and past risks (already materialised).
• Dependencies — upstream and downstream reliance.
Applied to a data product plan, assumptions exist at every layer. There are assumptions that enable the
product to exist, assumptions behind the mapping and behind the glossary, and above all the assumptions
that ground the SLAs (we only promise to meet our SLAs if upstream providers meet theirs). Dependencies
follow directly, because upstream systems have their own SLAs we depend on. Issues are present-day
problems with the things we’re proposing. What problems exist now, and how are we looking to solve
them? This profiling belongs in the proposal.
To score a risk, multiply probability (1–5) by impact (1–5), taking the higher of the delivery-delay and
consumer-harm impact scores. A score of 16 or above needs immediate mitigation, and 4 or below can
be monitored. The full scale is in Appendix C.

From contract package to backlog
Workflow
A complete contract package contains the data product contract, SLA definitions, non-functional requirements,
a prioritised backlog and a feasibility review.
The builder rates feasibility Green, Amber or Red across source availability, schema implementability, quality,
SLAs and operational sustainability. Every Amber names the required modification, and every Red names the
blocker.
Derive the backlog from the contract sections: schema creates build and constraint work, quality rules create
tests, SLAs create monitoring, access creates permissions, and consumers create onboarding. Then apply
MoSCoW with Must work at no more than 60% of estimated effort, leaving room for delivery variation and
Should work. The full worked package is in Appendix B.

Prioritising promises: RAID, RICE and MoSCoW
Sometimes you can’t keep every promise a product makes. This afternoon you rank them, then work out who
has to back the product before anyone will use it.
THIS SESSION ANSWERS

• How do you decide which promise to break when you can’t keep them all?

Knowledge check: Ranking commitments
If two promises cannot both be delivered this iteration, what evidence would let you rank them? Which
uncertainty belongs in RAID?

The promises you rank here are the service levels from the previous session.

RAID
Risks, Assumptions, Issues, Dependencies — assessing the degree to which you can keep your promises.
Applied to a data product plan:
• Risks — of violating the promises.
• Assumptions exist at every layer.

There are assumptions that enable the product to exist,

assumptions behind the mapping, behind the glossary, and above all the assumptions that ground
the SLAs (we only promise to meet our SLAs if upstream providers meet theirs).
• Issues are present-day problems with the things we’re proposing. What problems exist now, and
how are we looking to solve them? This profiling belongs in the proposal.
• Dependencies follow directly: upstream systems have their own SLAs we depend on, and note who
depends on us.
In practice: assess RAID before starting a PI, reassess at leadership sync-ups as new risks occur, escalate
blockers to leadership, and roll residual risks into the next PI at the end; other teams use it at quarterly
planning.

MoSCoW
Must, Should, Could, Won’t (Would) sorts things into what we must do, what we should do but don’t
have to, what we could do and what we’d like to do. Applied to SLIs, it asks which measures must
hold, and what redress follows when a must fails. Generally speaking, SLAs live at the level of should,
37

+44 (0)20 3583 0972 | info@decoded.com | decoded.com

DECODED

Monday — Designing data products

which is why MoSCoW alone can’t rank them. Most SLAs sit at the same MoSCoW level, so it gives no
discrimination. You need an impact-based system like RICE. The frameworks can operate at different
granularities: MoSCoW may support planning, while RAID is updated as risks and issues change.

RICE
When several SLAs are of similar importance and one has to give:
(Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effort

• Reach — the blast radius of the breakage: five systems, five million pounds, five clients, five anything.
• Impact — what each affected thing is worth (e.g. revenue per system, dollars per client).
• Confidence — how likely that impact is to be realised across those things (e.g. 20%).
• Effort — divide by what it will cost you to honour or fix the obligation.
Worked example: three SLAs covering timing (deliver by 7:30), duty to explain, and quality. If breaking
the timing SLA by ten minutes lets you deliver the explanation, RICE gives you a way to choose that you
can justify afterwards (“here’s the audit of my decision-making: reach × impact × confidence over effort
said it was better to be ten minutes late with the explanation”).
Practical guidance on scales and units:
• Design each factor to land on a 0–100 scale, then define a simple mapping from the real world onto
the scale (e.g. effort: 10 = a day, 20 = a week; impact: each unit = $1M). A 0–100 result can be
reported to different stakeholders as a percentage, a probability, a score.
• Alternatively, stay in raw units. Leave confidence between 0 and 1 and keep the rest in units, so the
result reads as, say, “client-dollars per week”. Either works. These formulas are comparative, and
all that matters is that they rank the SLAs correctly.
• For reach, pick a granularity at which you can define impact. If you can’t define impact per person,
define it per team (“this team is delayed by this amount”); reach then becomes a number of teams.
Ideally find common units across your SLAs so they’re comparable. If you can’t, that’s the argument
for normalising everything to 0–100.

Edge cases in promises
General promises run into edge cases:
• The two-phase refresh. A 7:30 AM delivery SLA covering three years of monthly plus one year of daily
data was physically impossible to refresh in time. The fix was to ask the consumer what they care
about most, which was yesterday’s data. So refresh in two phases: yesterday’s data (5–10 minutes
of work) lands by 7:30, and the full history refreshes in the background during the day. It isn’t the
original promise, but it works. You’ve refined a general, universal SLA into a more specific one built
around the customer’s priorities.
• Force majeure. SLAs implicitly assume things like people being alive and available (deaths, holidays).
Here you don’t modify the SLA down. You accept that promises get broken when they can’t be met;
you just need a good reason.
• Breach handling. Agreements should specify what happens when a promise fails: breach codes,
actions to take, notification.

What these acronym frameworks are actually for
Use a framework when the trade-off is difficult enough to need explicit reasoning. An obvious priority
does not need a score, but the decision still needs a record of its impact and owner.

The real value is accountability and transparency. In a large organisation (especially in finance) you must
be able to account to others for the decisions you made, with meeting minutes, audit trails, an email
or PDF recording the impact assessment. Transparency builds trust, and “why did you decide that?” is
much harder to answer well on the spot than the decision was to make. Do MoSCoW first; if everything
is a must (it usually is), drop down to RICE to decide what breaks, and keep the notes.

Data product adoption
Knowledge check: Adoption and responsibility
A product meets its technical tests but consumers keep using a spreadsheet. What would you investigate
before proposing more training?

We’ve covered designing data products (the scoping questions: should we create it, what would it be,
cost and value). Now suppose we have a data product in mind. There are two situations:
1. First release, when we’re concerned about achieving adoption.
2. Already released, when adoption is poor.

Barriers to adoption
• A rival or legacy alternative already in place (possibly the system being replaced)
• Discovery — people don’t know it exists
• Effort to adopt
• Wrong design — doesn’t meet business objectives; not properly consumer-aligned, or aligned to the
wrong consumer
• Data issues — consistency, quality, freshness (or lack thereof)
• Competing initiatives — organisational competition for attention
• Timing — downstream isn’t ready to consume (dependencies on other systems)
• Lack of training
• Documentation and trust — missing glossaries (what the columns and values mean), and trust
deficits
Note that most of the ones that matter are not technical. And distinguish barriers to adoption from
barriers to creation, which stop a product getting off the ground at all. These include sourcing (including
the permitted-use and redistribution terms for each vendor product), ownership (who is the data owner?),
compliance, gatekeeping, cost, operational support and resourcing. The technical issues (writing docs,
odd values) have relatively obvious answers; the institutional ones don’t.

Leadership, management and innovation
Distinguish three things:
• Management — given a policy, align and organise the business to it. Execution: “how do we carry
this out?”
• Leadership — set the policy and the mission, and show people how to follow it. Leadership is a
quality anyone can exercise (it isn’t C-level; it can be within your team, often leadership by example).
• Innovation is different again. The innovator is out ahead of everyone: self-motivated, principled
(sometimes wrongly, often stubbornly), holding themselves and the business to a high standard,
inducting practices that drive the business forward. That’s often because they have information
others don’t, or they’re the first adopters of a system and know how good it is. (Catalyst, produced
by the EDO, is an innovation in this sense.)

39

+44 (0)20 3583 0972 | info@decoded.com | decoded.com

DECODED

Monday — Designing data products

The catch with innovators is that they scare everyone else. They want change and they question the status
quo. Their practices are unusual and so far ahead they’re confusing. They act from information other
people don’t have, which creates friction (“isn’t this obvious?” It’s obvious only inside the ecosystem the
innovator lives in). And they’re often poor communicators. Change makes others feel unsafe.
The reason to draw these distinctions is that innovation and management don’t solve adoption problems.
“I’ll lead by example” from an innovator just means demonstrating practices miles from where people
are. That scares people more than it moves them. Management just tells people what to do. Leadership
stays close to where people actually are, understands them, knows where things need to go, and actively,
empathetically bridges the gap.
Often the real job of a leader is to pick an innovator they trust and say: the business’s job is to follow
that path. Then they bring people along it by selecting a credible direction and making the transition
understandable.

Things a leader does for adoption
• Mandates and quotas (a management tool, but available)
• Champions, delegating to other leaders embedded in teams
• Selling the vision and getting buy-in, for alignment, via meetings and roadshows
• Pilot launches to demonstrate efficacy
• Training, run with your rollout. Publicly credit the early adopters and celebrate the people who
do well in it, and the resistant start wanting the same credit. Recognition should reflect a real
contribution and accompany useful support.
Using the paved-path tools during the course lets you assess their purpose and responsibilities through
practice. Training, pilot evidence and a clear support route help a consumer adopt a product; they do
not replace its quality or access commitments.
The product owner coordinates stakeholder communication and decisions. As creator, record who owns
each unresolved requirement, who can approve it and who needs to review the result. For detailed roles,
influence mapping, transition planning and cases, use Managing stakeholders, including why adoption
needs explicit attention.

On screen: Data Marketplace
The Data Marketplace is where you look for an existing product before you build one. The overview tells
you what the product is for and who owns it. The data details show where the tables live, the preview
shows a few sample rows, and the schema and data dictionary give you the types and what each field
means. Some products have current and historical tables, and those answer different questions.
Knowledge check: Inspect a candidate product
What do you need to know about an existing dataset before reusing it? Which questions can a preview answer,
and which need a contract or owner?

Look at the data dictionary. It is marked “Not Validated”, so those definitions need checking. For the CG
design, compare grain, units, reporting dates, source provenance and ownership with the analyst’s need.
A preview cannot establish complete key coverage.

Learning Review
Without looking back, explain the consumer decision, the source-to-consumer realignment and the promises in
your product. Apply one quality dimension and one SLA measure to your own brief. Check that the requirement
handoff, canvas and proposed contract agree; name an unresolved assumption and the role who can decide

Worked example: Morningstar exposures
Here’s a short RFD for one choice from the week’s Morningstar scenario.
RFD 0042: Publish fund exposures as a prepared star
Context. The product receives Morningstar exposures and fund reference data from separate sources.
Consumers filter by fund, security classification and as-of date, and the contract grain is one row per
fund, per security, per date. Client identifiers and other PII must not be copied into the exposure fact.
The team already maintains dbt staging and integration models on the paved path.
Decision.

We will publish fact_fund_exposure at the stated grain with foreign keys to dim_fund,

dim_security and dim_date. Staging will retain each source’s shape, integration will join and validate

the sources, and the prepared model will expose the star. We will not publish the integration join as one
wide consumer table.
Consequences. Consumer queries use stable dimensions and the same fund definition. The fact remains
free of PII and can keep the reporting history required by its contract. The team must manage dimension
keys and late-arriving security classifications; until a classification arrives, the contract’s quarantine
or agreed placeholder action applies. Adding a new dimension requires a contract and lineage review
because existing consumers may depend on the present grain.
If a Consequences section lists only benefits, send it back. The author names what the team gives up,
what may fail and which mitigation makes that cost acceptable. Without that, a later reader can’t tell a
weighed decision from a favourite option written up after the fact.

How can a creator participate earlier in design decisions?
Explain the decision you need to inform and the consequence of missing source or implementation
knowledge. Ask which role represents that knowledge at the relevant meeting and when the creator
should join. A concise question about a concrete dependency is easier to act on than a general request
to attend every discussion.
If a request remains unresolved, follow the team’s escalation route with the impact and earlier question
visible.

Match the technical detail to the decision: a budget discussion, consumer interview and

implementation review need different levels of explanation. Build working relationships with product,
business and engineering roles; ask for a delegate or documented decision when attendance is not
useful or possible.
An approved AI assistant can help draft a clear memo, but the creator must check facts, recipients and
wording. Discuss roles and decision rights directly rather than assuming exclusion is caused by personality
or motives. The stakeholder map helps identify who can settle a stuck decision.

Annotated contract and stakeholder map
For the CG product brief, the internal analyst needs traceable offering information. Declare product_id as
the offering key, the selected source representation, expense ratios in bps and the meaning of unknown
values. Separate performance basis, period, return kind and reporting date. A contract must also state
ownership, proposed freshness, allowed uses and exception handling.

From a business need to a reviewed Catalyst draft
Use Monday’s CG product interview handoff to produce a contract draft. The business decision determines
the required data; a Catalyst skill provides the document structure; you verify the result against consumer and
producer evidence before handing it to the next creator.
THIS SESSION ANSWERS

• Which evidence does the skill need?
• What does the draft say that the brief does not support?
• Which checks establish correctness, and which decisions still require a person?

Knowledge check: Before generating the contract
Name the consumer decision, proposed output grain and one unresolved source constraint in your Monday
brief. Which of those could an agent infer incorrectly? What would you inspect to test its interpretation?

Classifying and generating
A discriminative task assigns a label to existing content; a generative task produces new content.
Catalyst’s document skills use generation to turn source information into a draft. A well-formed table or
fluent explanation is evidence that text was produced, while the facts and promises still need review.

Prompt, completion and model
A language model generates tokens from the context supplied to it. Tokens are pieces of text, rather than
necessarily whole words. The prompt supplies instructions and evidence; the completion is generated
output. Model weights encode patterns learned during training. A useful simplified description is P(next
token | supplied context; weights). This description helps explain why a plausible continuation can

include an unsupported detail; it does not provide a test of correctness.1

Evidence and the context window
The context window limits what a model can use in a request. It may contain your conversation, skill
instructions, retrieved excerpts and tool results, as well as generation capacity under the model’s own
limits. Keep the relevant consumer brief, producer schema, glossary, mapping and unresolved questions
in durable files. A conversation summary can omit a condition, so ask the agent to reread the authoritative
files when continuing work.

Context capacity and understanding
A larger window can hold more useful information and more irrelevant material. Give a focused evidence
packet and ask a narrow review question. In research on particular long-context tasks, the location of
relevant information affected performance; do not treat the window size as proof that every fact will be
used.2
1

Training and post-training approaches differ between models. The GPT-3 and InstructGPT research examples distinguish
autoregressive generation from instruction and preference training; they do not establish the internal process of every model
in your editor. See AI reference for the supplied explanation and research boundaries.
2
Lost in the Middle evaluates sensitivity to the position of relevant information in the tested models and tasks. It supports
checking context use empirically rather than assuming a universal position rule. Extended discussion is in Appendix G.

What Catalyst provides
Catalyst 1.13.0 is a supplied collection of Capital Group skills, templates, standards and supporting client
code. A skill’s SKILL.md describes a task, its required context, instructions and output. Copilot is the
editor/harness that makes model responses usable as file operations or tool calls. The model supplies
generation. Keep the model, harness, skill and observed action distinct: asking for a document is different
from reading the file that was written, and writing an approval table is different from obtaining an approval.
A document skill can provide a consistent structure and remind you of missing information. A phase
orchestrator can call several other skills, including capabilities that contact services or write outside the
current draft. Read the installed skill and its dependencies before invoking it. For the course, request a
local draft and explicitly retain unresolved decisions; classroom text does not satisfy a live DPLC gate.

The body requires numbered sections, schema fields, SLA measurement and breach response, quality actions,
change policy, registry and approval status. A missing source fact remains an owned decision in the training
draft; it cannot be made concrete by inventing it. The draft is incomplete for live use until the required facts
and approvals exist.

A model, a skill and an observed action
A model’s assertion that a generated contract is correct is another generated statement. Open the file,
compare the columns with the source, and calculate an expected example independently. For the CG
product brief, independently select an ETF’s net expense ratio and convert percentage points to bps
before comparing it with the output. Consumer agreement requires an actual consumer decision, while
a written approval row remains text until that decision exists.

The human role when working with AI agents
The creator remains responsible for the output, the evidence used to validate it and the decision to
proceed. You can use Catalyst to write, critique and revise a document, while consumer agreement,
source meaning and authorised access require evidence from the accountable roles. Open the actual
output and trace its claims to that evidence.

Why this course exists
Understanding product design, dbt, orchestration and the platform enables you to review what an agent
produces. You do not need to learn every implementation detail before drafting, but you need enough
knowledge to identify a wrong grain, unsupported field, missing dependency or unapproved promise. The
course builds that review capability through a connected product example.

Specialisation, purpose and domain evidence
You know why the product exists, how people use it, which terms have local meanings and who can answer
an unresolved question. Put that knowledge into the evidence packet rather than expecting the model to
possess it. Learning from use develops your ability to review the next output; a conversation does not by
itself change the distributed Catalyst skill files. Improvements to those files require a maintained source
change and review.

Judgment and taste in a product review
Judgment is an evaluative decision supported by reasons: remove an unsupported risk-score column,
reject a currency conversion without an FX source, or leave a delivery target proposed until the producer
confirms it. Record the evidence and consequence so another reviewer can assess the decision.
Taste concerns consistent choices where several acceptable forms exist: choose a clear vocabulary,
a coherent document structure and the approved project conventions.

Local experience helps you

notice phrasing that a consumer may misunderstand. Apply that preference consistently while keeping it
separate from a factual or contractual requirement. Both forms of review appear in the worked contract
review; neither transfers accountability to the model.

Uneven capability and review evidence
Expert
Model performance can be uneven across superficially similar tasks. A correct SQL pattern or completelooking contract does not establish correctness for a new source, grain or business rule. The model’s account
of its own work also needs checking: inspect the files, review the changed sections and compare results with
independent expectations. Evaluate the actual task with representative cases.

Longer commentary on training analogies, specialist failure risks and the economics of AI is in AI reference.

Validate facts, meaning and actions
A useful draft can still be wrong in a consequential detail. Validate the source facts, the interpretation of
the business requirement and the action the agent performed. An error in one category is not repaired
by a successful check in another.

Unsupported generated claims
“Hallucination” commonly describes generated content that is unsupported or incorrect.

Treat the

practical problem directly: require a source for a column, value, owner, approval or result.

If the

source does not establish it, remove it or record an owned question. Plausibility and confidence are not
substitutes for evidence.

Variation across runs
Outputs may vary with generation settings, model versions, context and tool results. Run-to-run variation
means a previously good draft is not proof that the next one is correct. Keep a review procedure that
survives different wording and organisation. Save the approved source artefacts and correction log so
future work can use them.

When to add scrutiny
Add scrutiny when a long conversation may have lost context, a novel source or business rule is involved,
or the agent reports a completed check without its result. Ask it to identify the evidence used, then read
that evidence yourself. A second model or self-critique can surface gaps, but agreement can preserve
a shared mistake. The independent CG product-information test rows and expected totals matter more
than another assertion that the model is correct.

Review before continuing
Generated output often becomes input to later steps. Before a contract feeds a mapping or model,
verify the facts that the next step will depend on.

Choose deliberate review points: at minimum,

check the specification before implementation, the model against independent expected rows, and the
orchestration against the agreed dependencies. Preserve evidence for each checkpoint and correct the
source document as well as downstream artefacts.

Before you rely on Catalyst
Ask what the output will be used for, who will own it and what evidence will establish that it is usable.
Limit the request to the next reviewable artefact. If the draft is too broad to review, split it into meaningful
sections rather than treating volume as progress. In this course the handoff remains a reviewed training
draft; live approval, deployment and production responsibilities require their own authorised process.

Choosing the harness settings for the task
Read the installed tools’ settings before starting an agent workflow. The names and available controls
depend on the product and version. Evaluate the choices against the task you need to review rather than
a vendor reputation.
Knowledge check: Text, tool call or completed action?
How would you tell whether the agent proposed a command, ran it, or checked its result? Which operation in
a contract-generation task could change an external system?

The harness
A harness supplies context to a model, interprets structured tool requests, executes permitted operations
and returns their results. Copilot provides this surrounding workflow in the course. A plan or proposal is
a generated artefact; it is not evidence that a tool ran.
Review the available planning, execution and approval settings in your installed environment. Keep the
course request bounded to local draft artefacts and use the organisation’s supported settings. A stored
project-facts file helps the agent find names and constraints but does not authorise an action. Do not
include credentials in such a file. Treat unfamiliar retrieved content as evidence to inspect rather than
new authority over the task.

Effort levels
An available reasoning-effort setting changes the model’s allocation for a response. More effort is not a
guarantee of a better result. Compare settings on a small representative task using the same evidence and
review criteria, including correctness, completeness and the time needed to inspect the output. Record
the setting used when comparing drafts.

Vendors and models
Use the models available and approved in your environment. Compare them empirically on your own
contract or mapping task. A model may follow one template well and perform differently on an openended requirement or a source-specific rule. Model size, branding and apparent fluency do not establish
suitability. Extended model-selection considerations are retained with their source boundaries in AI
reference.

Deliberate prompting and review
Give Catalyst the business objective, authoritative evidence, required artefact and limits on the current
action. Then plan, inspect and revise. A skill reduces the need to invent a structure; your task-specific
context and review still determine whether the output is useful.
Knowledge check: A prompt you can assess
What would you add to “write a contract” so the draft stays faithful to the CG product-information brief? How
would you distinguish missing evidence from a writing preference?

1. Use critique to find questions
Ask the model to critique a draft against named criteria, or compare it with another model’s review. This
can produce useful questions and omissions to inspect. It does not establish an independent proof: read
the actual artefact, trace each proposed correction to evidence and keep tests that were not copied from
the generated implementation.

2. Plan the next artefact
Workflow
1. State the next output and how it will be used.
2. Ask for a plan based on the supplied brief, schema and unresolved questions.
3. Check that the plan respects the product grain, current scope and dependencies.
4. Generate or revise the local artefact, then open the file and inspect the diff.
5. Check the result against the acceptance criteria and record the remaining decisions.

Planning the plan can help when the task is poorly understood, but more planning layers are not
automatically better. Use them to reveal uncertainty and choose a concrete next step.

3. Choose terms and evidence carefully
Define domain terms and distinguish requirements from examples. A word such as “equity” or “real time”
can have several meanings; give the meaning from the product glossary and a concrete business event.
Ask the agent to flag conflicting interpretations. Removing unrelated history can help more than adding
another instruction to a confused conversation.

4. State the later use
Explain the next consumer of the artefact while keeping the current task bounded: “Draft the contract
for later dbt model review; do not generate or deploy a model now.” That gives the model context for the
necessary precision without authorising the next action.

5. Ask what may be missing
Ask for a review checklist or questions a specialist would investigate. Use the answer as a starting point:
check it with source documentation and the relevant domain role. A question about keys, corrections,
backfills or timing can reveal a missing condition even when the model cannot answer it.

6. Start fresh from durable evidence
If a conversation accumulates conflicting assumptions, save the confirmed decisions in the brief and
start a focused request from those files. Keep a correction log. Do not depend on a summary to preserve
every schema detail or unresolved question.

7. Capture a review aloud
A spoken or typed review can capture findings while you read the document. Record section, issue,
supporting evidence, proposed change and confidence. Ask Catalyst to turn those notes into an action
list, then check the list before revising the file. Use an approved transcription route for the data involved
and reread the resulting transcript for errors. Voice notes can help capture a review; durable written
decisions preserve what the next creator needs.

Check that the approved Catalyst plugin is available in your editor using the supplied onboarding
instructions. Record the installed version and inspect the intended skill before selecting it.

Which plugin version is installed, and can you open a relevant SKILL.md and its template? Which operation

Prepare the inputs
Give the skill the smallest set of inputs that still explains the product: Monday’s consumer brief, the
producer list, the agreed glossary, the mini-STTM, the quality questions and a list of what you still don’t
know. Label each one. For example, the internal analyst needs a 50-bps shortlist, the source has multiple
representations and expense components, and missing reporting dates must remain unknown.
