want it approved, posted to Confluence or listed in the marketplace. Some skills call other skills that
can do those things, so check what the skill depends on before you run it.
Here’s an example prompt. Swap in your team’s own filenames, and check which version of the skill you
have first:
Use the supplied data-contract template to draft a CG product-information contract.

in this workspace. Produce a local Markdown draft only.
Keep observed facts, proposed commitments and unresolved decisions distinguishable.
Do not invent table columns, owner names, entitlements, approval dates or measured
quality results. If a mandatory field cannot be supported, describe the unresolved
decision and the responsible classroom role. Do not call external services or
publish an artifact. List the source evidence for every proposed quality rule.

The data-contract template has the eight sections you saw earlier, plus a revision history. The template
asks for specific values in every field. If you don’t have the value, the draft should say so and name who
can supply it, instead of Catalyst making up a person, a threshold or an approval.

Fix one kind of mistake at a time, then reread the file. If Catalyst says it removed a field, check the
schema, the glossary, the acceptance criteria and any later model request, because agents often fix the
one place you pointed at and leave the rest. Keep a short correction log: the source fact, the sections

Then look hard at the SLA table. “Available by 07:30” needs a timezone, which days count, what “available”
means, where you measure it and what happens on a breach. “Ninety-nine percent complete” needs a
denominator. Ninety-nine percent of which offerings, from which registry? You can draft how each target
will be measured today, and mark the targets themselves as proposed.

Separate the four artifact purposes
Catalyst produces four documents that overlap:
• The PRD explains the problem, the consumers, the requirements and how you’ll know it worked. It
starts in Discovery and gets updated in later phases.
• The contract is the agreement between producer and consumer, with its promises on quality,
freshness and change.
• The transformation specification maps out the models and how you’ll build and backfill them.
• The quality-controls plan says which controls you’ll enforce and why, from the business
requirements and the data profiling.
Because they overlap, a contradiction between two of them is easy to spot, and it usually means somebody
hasn’t made a decision yet.
The transformation-spec template puts the detailed logic in the dbt SQL and the quality rules in the
contract. It has no separate section for test definitions. You still want the mini-STTM, because it explains
the business rule the model implements and how you’ll check it. When Catalyst generates a project, line
the mapping up with where the current template puts things. Older templates had different headings.

The quality-controls template asks for scope, profiling results, proposed controls, business requirements,
open questions, handover and approval. It treats the action (block, warn, quarantine) separately from the
severity and wants a reason for each. A duplicate product key breaks the grain, so stopping publication
is reasonable. A snapshot that’s late but still usable can get a warning, but only if the contract says the
consumer accepts that. “Warn, because stopping is a nuisance” is a bad reason.
The plan mentions Capital Group’s internal rule patterns and quality system. You won’t configure that
platform in class. Use the business meaning to review each proposed rule and practise enforcing it in
dbt.
Requirements that can be checked

FROM CATALYST SKILLS

SOURCE skills/requirements-acceptance-criteria/SKILL.md @ Catalyst 1.13.0

The supplied source says:
## Quality Checks
Before finalizing the document, verify:
- [ ] No placeholder text remains (no `[TBD]`, `[fill in]`, `[Name]` etc.)
- [ ] Each requirement has a unique ID and is categorized (functional / non-functional)
- [ ] Every requirement has at least one testable acceptance criterion
- [ ] Acceptance criteria use measurable language ("at least 99.5%") not vague ("high")
- [ ] Priority is assigned to each requirement (Must / Should / Could / Won't)
- [ ] Tables have data rows, not just headers

Turn the CG product-information decision into an identified requirement and measurable acceptance criterion
before asking for code. A metric needs a denominator, source and business meaning; a template number is
not an agreed target.

A corrected local handoff
The corrected draft now says what we know:
• The consumer is the internal Product Information Analyst.
• The catalogue grain is one row per scoped offering, keyed by product_id.
• Source representation and expense component selection are explicit.
• Duplicate product keys fail the quality check.
• Expense units, unknown reporting dates and return comparison dimensions are stated.
• Open service and access decisions are listed, each with someone to answer it.
It has no approval. An engineer can now tell which assumptions they can build on and which need a
decision first.

Case study: A complete-looking PRD still needs source review
Cases: requirements and definitions
Mutual-fund monthly returns. A draft includes a summary, consumers, solution and data requirements, with
a separate mapping. Decision: validate calculation meanings and source-to-target rules before accepting the
mapping. Reasoning: an accurate schema does not establish the business rule or consumer goal. Lesson:
cross-cutting rules such as refresh, referential integrity and allowed columns must be grounded, even when
the document structure is complete.
Client analytics. A requirement mentions outliers without defining the comparison or calculation. Decision: ask
the consumer which behaviour should be identified, then agree a model, baseline and threshold with evidence.
Reasoning: “outlier” is relative to a method and population; a familiar numerical rule is not automatically
appropriate. Lesson: a field name is not a requirement definition.
Internal monthly returns. A draft invents a current-state account instead of asking for missing facts. Decision:
instruct the skill to name unsupported decisions and their owners, then verify the source used for each
statement. Reasoning: a targeted template can reveal the missing section while the model still fills it incorrectly.
Lesson: adapt the prompt and review method without treating a better-looking model response as proof.

Webinar attendance. An earlier contract feeds the PRD, which still needs review of each variable and rule,
especially across several systems. Decision: trace the requirements through the source and use a written or
spoken correction log section by section. Reasoning: fluent reuse of a previous document can preserve its

ESG data. A draft identifies sources, columns and proposed types. Decision: confirm those against source
evidence and the desired consumer rule. Reasoning: a reviewer finding no obvious issue is bounded by the
checks they performed. Lesson: useful drafting removes typing effort while the creator retains validation
responsibility.
Case: listing reference migration
An existing listing-reference consumption moves from LASR to Caspian. Documentation provides column
descriptions, a proposed mapping and possible risks, but the actual data has not been queried. Decision:
treat document-derived risks as hypotheses, then validate the authorised source and affected consumer
examples. Reasoning: a thorough documentation search can still miss value distributions, nulls, keys or
correction behaviour. Lesson: record what was observed and what remains inferred before accepting the
migration design.

The stage names vary. The lifecycle screen says Define, Deliver and Sustain. Some skill descriptions
say Design, Build and Ship, and the skill IDs are dplc-design-stage, dplc-build-stage and dplc-shipstage. They’re the same three stages. RFD 0002 is the published standard, and it defines nine phases,

numbered 0 to 8.
In class you draft documents on your laptop and review them. Nothing gets registered in the Demand
Tracker, published to the catalogue or sent to an approver. A Markdown file in your repo doesn’t meet
the Phase 0 requirement for a real Demand Tracker entry, and an approval table that Catalyst wrote is
just text.

The DPLC and the Concierge
Catalyst is built on a spine of nine phases, numbered 0 to 8, of designing and creating a data product.
That’s the DPLC, the data product lifecycle, the lifecycle represented by the supplied Catalyst version.
Validate its current organisational scope and gates with the responsible product owner before live use.
There is a skill called the DPLC Concierge (dplc-concierge) which runs through all nine phases end to
end. It works out which phase you’re at, asks for what it needs and guides you step by step. It can walk
through several artefacts and capabilities; inspect the current phase and next action rather than starting
an unrestricted end-to-end workflow for a local drafting task.
Here’s the lifecycle on one page:
• Define: 0 Pre-requisite, 1 Triage, 2 Discovery, 3 Design.
• Deliver: 4 Build, 5 Validate, 6 Publish.
• Sustain: 7 Operate, 8 Evolve.
• Phase 0 hard gate: a real Demand Tracker entry and assigned Data Owner, DPM and Creator.
• Phase 1 to 2 hard gate: the Data Owner approves sensitivity, criticality and domain classification.
There are four roles you’ll hear about all week: Data Owner, Data Product Manager, Data Steward and
Data Product Creator. The Data Owner approves classification at the Phase 1 to 2 gate, so they decide
whether the demand can go into Discovery. The Data Steward checks completeness in Discovery and
signs off UAT in Validate.
In Phase 1, marketplace-search looks at the top search_rank. Above 0.5 means STOP, because a strong
match already exists. Between 0.1 and 0.5 means INVESTIGATE, and 0.1 or below means PROCEED.

Late arrival

Critical

Duplicate records

If portfolio_id + as_of_date + exposure_type repeats, block delivery.

Critical

Out-of-range values

If an exposure falls outside 0 to 1, quarantine that row for review.

Workflow
• Block delivery stops the batch when publishing any part of it would break the contract, as with a missing
required field or schema violation.
• Flag and deliver publishes usable data with a status and notification when consumers can work safely
with a known limitation, such as a late source.
• Quarantine row publishes the unaffected rows and holds suspect values for review when the fault may
be local to one record.

Why quarantine an out-of-range value? Because a range check can’t tell a data error from a real but
extreme market move. Quarantine keeps the row so a person can decide. The full quarantine discussion
is in Appendix B.
The contract file itself follows the Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS), and Capital Group adds its SLAs
under customProperties.capitalGroupSla[].

The four roles at phase 0

From a reviewed specification to a generated model
Today is just a preview. You do the technical review on Wednesday, after the SQL and dbt sessions. writedbt-source and write-dbt-model work from your project and source details, so give them the real table

names. Don’t let them guess a table from a familiar-sounding name. setup-dbt-project gives you a
project skeleton, and you still have to check you can reach the warehouse. dbt-unit-test generates
made-up test cases and a report, running on pandas by default or on PySpark. It’s one kind of test among
several in dbt.
Knowledge check: From specification to model checks
What expected example would reveal a wrong join, missing key or duplicate advisor? Which requirement
establishes the expected result independently of the generated SQL?

A generated test report should say which SQL it tested, with what inputs, what it expected and which
backend it ran on. So which test tells you what? A pandas test checks the logic of your transformation.
A query on the warehouse checks the Spark setup and your Unity Catalog permissions. Neither one tests
an edge case unless somebody wrote that case in. Keep the test cases and compare them with the
reasons in the quality-controls plan.
For an advisor roll-up, a good set of edge cases is two portfolios with the same advisor, an advisor with no
eligible portfolios, and a portfolio whose advisor key doesn’t match anyone. Those check the sum, what
happens when there are no rows, and referential integrity. Add a duplicate advisor key to see whether
rows multiply. If the generated tests just rerun the model’s own aggregation on its own output, ask for
the expected result worked out separately from the test rows.

A data product is three folders
Strip the mystique before the tool tour. Fundamentally a data product is about three folders (sometimes
four). Call them raw, transformed and report-ready. A file (say data.csv) moves through stages until
it’s report.csv, source-aligned in and consumer-aligned out. These are relative terms. Your final folder
is somebody else’s raw folder, because alignment is always alignment to people. (Industry and CG layer
names, such as bronze, silver and gold or landing, ingest and curate, are part of the data-systems glossary
covered on day 3.)

Git and GitHub
Git is version control, with three families of capability. There’s versioning code (multiple versions of the
entire piece of software existing in parallel, managed by one tool), code history and sharing.
GitHub is not Git. GitHub is a platform built on Git, a single source of truth, a book of record for code.
The main thing GitHub adds for releasing software at CG is the pull request (PR), a request to take
71

DECODED

Tuesday — AI, Catalyst and the platform

one version of the code and integrate it into or replace another, usually the live version. A PR requests
code integration. Environment promotion separately selects a reviewed revision, target environment and
required approvals.
At Capital Group, PRs are part of the permission structure. The pull request is often where acceptance
for a release actually happens, which makes GitHub, a vendor holding the book of record for code, a key
part of the permissions process. (More on why tomorrow.)

Docker
The problem Docker solves is portable software. The code on GitHub is not a full specification of the
software, because code has dependencies. There are libraries, other code and an operating system.
A container is a bundling of the software with all of its dependencies (even, more or less, the operating
system, with a caveat covered below). Think of it as a mini PC that runs standalone. Press play on
a container and inside could be Airflow code, dbt code, SQL, all working together to produce your
application. A runtime is the programme that runs a container. (Docker in depth after the dev-container
setup.)

dbt
dbt is the data build tool. It does the data transformations, and it’s basically SQL plus templates plus
tests. This is the tool that performs the source-to-consumer alignment.
At the most basic level, dbt is a SQL templating engine. SQL is normally one query per statement, and
dbt lets you turn a query into a template (string interpolation, placeholders) and run it across scenarios.
Think of it as an SQL generator. The salesy framing is that it “brings software-engineering practices to
SQL”: versioning of queries, modularity, code generating SQL.
One distinctive feature is that it wraps your SELECT queries in CREATE TABLE statements automatically.
A data analyst who only knows SELECT inside-out can write plain queries, and dbt treats them as
instructions to create intermediate tables, handling persistence in the background. (And increasingly
you don’t hand-type the SQL anyway. You ask Catalyst, and it writes the dbt.)
What’s a dbt test? A test of the expected output of a query, very often phrased so that the expected
output is no rows. Example: prices should never be negative, so query for negative prices; the test passes
when the query returns nothing. A core part of dbt testing is writing queries that should never produce
data. (More kinds of test tomorrow.)

Airflow
Everyone says “orchestration”, so what is orchestration? Think of a conductor. While the orchestra plays,
the conductor is timing, cueing and coordinating. Violins in, drums in, timpani in. Airflow times, cues
and coordinates tasks, where a task is just a programme that runs on a machine. (Scheduling is one
part of Airflow; its dependency graph, execution records and retry/recovery behaviour provide additional
coordination.)
So Airflow lets you schedule tasks daily, weekly or at a set time, chain them (task 1, then 2, then 3),
branch conditionally (this task if it fails, that task if it succeeds) and monitor the whole pipeline.
A simple local sequence may need little coordination. Airflow is useful when dependencies, scheduling,
execution state and recovery need an explicit managed workflow, whether the tasks execute locally or
remotely.
The main task type we’ll orchestrate is dbt transformation programmes. If Airflow is the conductor, dbt
jobs are the orchestra, with the source section, domain section and consumer section cued in order.
In the paved-path picture, Databricks is where the data lives and dbt is the transformation piece, the
SQL that does the mapping. Airflow is the trigger. It supports scheduled execution and evidence about
72

runs; meeting the consumer SLA also depends on upstream data, correct transformations and the agreed
failure response.

Astronomer
Two answers to “what is Astronomer?”:
1. Managed Airflow, an orchestrator run for us in the cloud. We rent the conductor. (Just as Databricks
vends Spark, Astronomer vends Airflow.)
2. Just as valuable for the paved path, Astronomer packages Airflow in a Docker container. That gives
you a cross-platform bundle that runs locally (Windows, Linux, Mac), and the cloud side runs those
same bundles remotely. Astronomer is basically a bundling-up of Airflow. (Hands-on tomorrow and
Thursday.)
An independently managed Airflow deployment can let a team plan changes at its own boundary while
still coordinating shared dependencies. Astro also provides a local project runtime for development and
tests. Independence does not remove cross-team compatibility, access or upgrade checks. Astronomer
documents the local testing workflow.

Databricks
The problem Databricks set out to solve (~2014) was that querying large volumes of data was hard. Their
solution was to put the data in files and folders in the cloud and run queries over them in parallel. It’s
like keeping your data in a giant Google Drive, with Spark as the query system over it (the people who
founded Databricks are the people who made Spark; earlier systems worked similarly, Spark was faster).
But files and folders don’t really work well on their own. What people actually want is a transactional
database, where data isn’t lost and operations succeed or fail atomically. Those are ACID guarantees, and
they’re very hard to maintain with data scattered across parallel files. Hence the lakehouse, a system of
query and data management that keeps the files and folders but gives you the promises of a traditional
database. It presents managed tables with transaction semantics. ACID refers to atomicity, consistency,
isolation and durability; the exact behaviour depends on the table format and operation. Wednesday
develops those distinctions. More on that tomorrow.
Here’s a more careful breakdown, useful in meetings. In the paved path, Databricks is the compute layer
(it runs queries over your data), plus discoverability and governance (Unity Catalog, the Marketplace).
Those last two are really the same thing, metadata management around your data.
It is not the storage. S3 is the storage, cloud files and folders. The supplied architecture places externally
stored data in S3 and uses Databricks for SQL compute and table governance. This is an example
architecture, not a claim about the proportion of enterprise storage or every vendor delivery route. When
someone names a “data platform”, ask which storage, compute, governance and serving responsibilities
they mean.
What lives in S3 is often parquet files, which are column-oriented storage. You write data a row at a
time but read and analyse it a column at a time, so columnar layout is much faster for analytics. Delta
format is parquet plus metadata, meaning version history, governance metadata and, most importantly,
transaction support (you can DELETE FROM a Delta table, which you cannot do against a bare parquet file
without rewriting it). Databricks then presents a “pretend table”, which is metadata over the S3-backed
files.
This course uses the lakehouse for analytical products. Evaluate transactional latency, write patterns and
application requirements separately rather than assuming an analytical design fits every workload.
Platform selection has technical and institutional dimensions. Compute capability is one consideration;
supported vendor delivery, integration, access, contracts and the team’s operating knowledge are others.
In the supplied example, sources deliver files into agreed storage locations and Databricks executes the

downstream analytical transformations. The delivery convention still needs an accountable source, a

So what does Databricks do on the paved path? It runs our dbt. dbt holds the transformation rules;
Databricks executes them over the files and folders (which live on Amazon S3).
Since the word will keep coming up, Spark is the parallel query engine underneath Databricks, the
machinery that splits a query across many machines and reassembles the answer. PySpark is Spark’s
Python interface. Because PySpark sat on the paved path until recently, plenty of teams still work in it,
so expect to hear the word from colleagues on older products. On the paved path a data creator writes
dbt instead. The SQL still executes on Spark underneath, you just never drive the engine directly.
Why dbt for this transformation practice? dbt supplies SQL model, dependency, test and documentation
conventions.

It connects to supported data platforms through adapters, so supported targets and

behaviour depend on the selected adapter and version. The training route uses its specified Databricks
configuration; it is not an instruction to run dbt against any file or database. dbt documents its supportedplatform/adapter relationship.
PySpark exposes Spark through Python and can support transformations with different requirements.
Here SQL-based models keep the business mappings and tests explicit for the assigned product. Choose
a supported tool according to the actual requirement and platform convention rather than assuming one
interface is universally simpler.
Doesn’t Databricks have its own job scheduler? Why Airflow? Yes, it does, and there’s overlap. The
course uses Airflow to express the wider dependency and scheduling workflow, with Cosmos connecting
the assigned dbt project. Databricks jobs can also schedule work; the existence of overlapping capabilities
does not change the offered course route.
Keep the interfaces and dependencies visible when considering portability. Open-source components,
managed services, storage formats and organisation-specific conventions each have their own
compatibility and operating boundaries.

Harness
Harness provides the demonstrated build/release pipeline context, including controlled infrastructure
steps where configured. Airflow schedules and coordinates the data workflow. A successful release
means the relevant code or configuration step completed; it does not establish that a later data run has

Local ownership and the shared service
Giving each team its own Airflow is one way to localise ownership, as we saw with Astro. Your team
controls its own schedules, but another team may still own the ingestion product upstream of you, and
you still depend on it. So write down four things: what the upstream team promises, how fresh your
consumer needs the data, how you’ll know the upstream data has arrived, and who to call when it hasn’t.
Your scheduler only runs your jobs.

Search the marketplace before you decide to build, both in Triage and whenever someone asks whether

Readiness across your environments
There are four places your work runs. Your laptop runs the editor and Docker. The dev container holds
the repository’s tools. Astro starts a separate local Airflow with its own services. Databricks does the
remote compute and controls access to the data. Getting the dev container open only tells you the first
two work. You still have to check you can reach the warehouse and run a DAG.
The dev container is built from .devcontainer/Dockerfile. The Dockerfile at the root of the repo is
the Astro runtime image for Airflow. If something is wrong with your dev container, edit the one in .
devcontainer. Anything you save inside the mounted repository folder survives when the container is

Known issues
• If startup fails, read the setup/build log before changing resources. Check the supplied environment
requirements, available host memory, registry/network access and the reported error. Apply the
relevant approved setup remedy, then rerun the specific readiness check; a successful image build
does not establish authenticated remote access.
• The repository contains two Dockerfiles. The one in .devcontainer builds the dev container, and the
one at the root is the Astro image for Airflow. Use the correct runtime boundary when diagnosing a
failure; the beginner appendix explains which image each file builds.
• Stale cached container images can cause failed builds even on fresh clones. A clean rebuild without
cache, or recloning the repo, fixes it. Preserve local work and record the failure before rebuilding or
making a fresh clone; a merge conflict requires understanding and resolving the conflicting changes.
Avoid cloning into OneDrive.
• Windows line endings have bitten before. Windows pulls can re-add carriage returns, which breaks
shell scripts run inside the Linux container (shell scripts must be LF).
To set up the Databricks connection from inside the container, run the Mise task (mise run setup:
databricks, which uses OAuth by default). It prints a workspace URL. Keep pressing enter until you

reach the login page, authorise the permissions request, then select the workspace and warehouse. You
won’t use it today, but you need it from tomorrow, so set it up now.
How do the skills reach Databricks? There’s no magic connection. Catalyst generates Python that uses
the client scripts in the repo, and those scripts read the credentials that setup saved.
Credentials and packages
Use OAuth in class. The supplied setup uses interactive OAuth; Catalyst’s connection skill has its own machinecredential requirements. Follow the approved setup route rather than creating a token to bypass it. Python
packages come through Capital Group’s internal Nexus (cgrepo-aws.capgroup.com, index cgpypi), so don’t
install straight from public PyPI.

So what’s on the whiteboard? Code lives in GitHub, and Harness builds it and promotes it through the

On screen: Data contracts

Close Tuesday by following a dataset through the platforms you have just met. The names are familiar now;

Knowledge check: Before following the pipeline
Your team has a repository, a green deployment and an Airflow DAG. Another team says its source data is ready.

piece of evidence you would request and the person who should provide it.

Start with the operating problem
A shared Airflow estate can contain thousands of DAGs from many teams. Coordinating configuration,
upgrades and remediation at that scale creates dependencies beyond any one product.
A team may need to deploy tomorrow while a vulnerability prevents its release. If the fix depends on a
central backlog, that team’s schedule depends on work it cannot prioritise. An expensive pipeline can also
consume capacity needed by other products. Federation addresses ownership and isolation, but there
are two different boundaries here. Separating Airflow deployments changes orchestration ownership;
protecting Databricks compute also requires appropriate job, capacity and workload configuration.
The paved-path response is to retain common conventions while giving teams responsibility for their
deployments. A blueprint can help teams start consistently. It cannot decide whether a source is fit for
purpose, whether a release is compatible, or whether a consumer should trust yesterday’s result. Those
remain product decisions with named owners.

Why Airflow and Astronomer were retained
Airflow already supported ingestion and curation dependencies. Keeping it preserves an orchestration
model teams know while changing how the service is operated. Astronomer is described as the choice
for vendor support, local development with its CLI, and disaster-recovery arrangements. The decision is
about operating Airflow as well as expressing DAGs.
Compare three operating approaches. Terraform modules could give each team an Airflow installation on
EKS, but teams would still need an operating and support model. AWS Managed Workflows for Apache
Airflow, or MWAA, was considered with concerns about support, executor choices and recovery at the
time. Astronomer was selected for the combination the team wanted. Assess each service against

In this example, workspaces group deployments organisationally, and deployments are owned at team
level. A project might justify another deployment, but one deployment per dataset is not the default. Ask
who should be able to remediate a runtime problem without negotiating another team’s backlog. That is
a stronger basis for choosing the boundary than counting how many DAGs a product contains.
Disaster recovery also needs a concrete question: what must be restored, how quickly, and how much
loss is acceptable? Vendor support or a recovery feature does not establish that a particular product has
a tested restoration plan. Thursday develops run and recovery evidence; Tuesday establishes who owns
that question.

Cross-team dependencies without shared runtime access
Consider an asset-reference product that depends on another team’s instrument data. The consumer
needs to know when the agreed input is available. It does not need broad administrative access to that
team’s Airflow deployment.
In the example architecture, a custom bridge connects Airflow asset events across deployments.
The producer emits an update, its bridge sends a readiness message to Kafka, and the consuming
deployment’s bridge receives the message and updates its local scheduling state. Each team’s DAG can
then express a dependency through the supplied integration. Kafka carries the notification; the table is
consumed through its governed data-access route.

Separate governance, execution and physical storage
The Databricks story begins with notebooks and workspace-local metadata. Copying a dataset to another
workspace made sharing easier in one sense, but risked divergent access rules and duplicated data. Unity
Catalog is introduced as a common governance and metadata layer.
Keep three responsibilities distinct. Databricks compute executes queries and transformations. Unity
Catalog describes and governs the registered data objects.

S3 holds the underlying files in this

architecture. A table’s qualified name has three levels: catalog.schema.table. For example, domain_
assets.reference.asset_reference is an illustrative governed name, not a supplied production

destination. Databricks’ Unity Catalog overview explains the namespace and governance model.

These are design roles, rather than built-in Unity Catalog object types. Application data is described as

A dependency may be in a transitional catalog. Finding useful data there does not prove that it will remain
the long-term dependency. Record both the current source identity and the intended migration owner
before promising a consumer a stable location.

Delta and UniForm: metadata is different from a publication copy
The example uses Delta tables. A Delta table combines data files with transaction metadata; the metadata
enables the engine to identify the relevant table state. UniForm provides a way for other engines to read
the data using Iceberg-compatible metadata.
More precisely, UniForm generates Iceberg metadata alongside Delta metadata, using the same underlying
Parquet files. Generation can be asynchronous, and supported readers and table features matter. It is
not two independently written copies of the data. See Databricks’ Iceberg-read documentation.
This distinction matters later:

UniForm adds a compatible metadata representation; deep-clone

publication copies data to another table. A consumer using a different engine still needs an agreed
access route, compatible configuration and evidence about the table version it can actually read.

Why dbt sits over Databricks compute
dbt lets creators express transformations in SQL, reuse macros and keep models close to tests and
documentation. It reduces some authoring complexity while Databricks remains the execution platform.
dbt defines the transformations and sends work through its configured adapter. On the Databricks route,
the selected Databricks compute executes that work. Installing dbt locally is useful for development; it
does not make the remote dataset or its permissions local. In this course, offline parse and CSV checks
support the assigned Databricks execution; they do not replace it.
Bitemporal data supports being able to ask what was true for a business date and what the system knew
at another time. Consider an instrument classification effective on Monday but corrected on Thursday.
A report reconstructed with Tuesday’s knowledge can differ from one reconstructed after Thursday’s
correction.

What the vended repository gives you
Vending is described as supplying an Airflow deployment, Databricks workspace arrangements and a
repository that deploys to those platforms. The repository contains conventions as well as code: SQLFluff,
pre-commit configuration, tool setup, blueprints and shared components. Their presence helps teams
begin consistently; a generated scaffold still needs review against the product requirements.

Observability gives you somewhere to look
Monitoring must be accessible to the people responsible for the product. Confirm the assigned logging
destination and permissions before an incident.
Use that operational view to connect a symptom to a particular deployment, DAG run, Databricks job and
candidate. An upstream event received, a job submitted, a transformation completed, a quality check
passed and a release published are separate milestones. Logs help explain where progress stopped; the
consumer still needs the resulting business date, meaning and freshness. Verify the assigned logging
destination and access before relying on it during an incident. The course’s local log evidence has its own
scope and does not establish a connected Datadog integration.

Contracts connect the design to schema changes
DDL, or data definition language, describes structures such as tables and columns. It cannot by itself
express the complete consumer agreement.

An ODCS contract holds schema alongside sensitivity,

support ownership and other metadata. Use the platform’s supported conventions within that standard.
Contract tooling can generate DDL and migrations from a reviewed ODCS schema. Inspect the supplied
repository tooling and the proposed migration before applying it; source prose is not a CLI command.
Follow the chain from reviewed contract to generated schema change to the actual governed table. If the
contract says a field is required but the deployed schema or transformation permits missing values, you
have found a mismatch that a successful deployment may not reveal. Likewise, a support-group name
entered in a contract must correspond to an accountable operating arrangement.
A metadata file in Git does not establish that the marketplace can discover its contents.

Verify

registration and the consumer-visible listing. Product documentation explains meaning and use; platform
documentation explains how to build. DAG documentation can provide an additional operational view.

Worked change: carry a currency name through the product
A consumer of the AED listing product requests currency_name_lower alongside the existing currency
code. The existing interface identifies eligible listings at the agreed listing grain. This request changes
the interface without changing that population.

Treat it as one reviewed product change spanning

requirements, contract, transformation, tests, migration and consumer use. A generated column is useful
only when those artefacts describe the same meaning.

Begin with a concrete acceptance example: an eligible listing whose currency code is AED should carry
uae dirham when its authoritative English currency name is UAE dirham. Lowercasing AED produces aed,

which is a code, not a name. Neither a plausible expansion invented by an assistant nor an unreviewed
lookup can establish the authoritative name. Locate the governed reference source, its owner, language
and join key before accepting the derivation.
1. Requirement and consumer agreement. Record the request in the PRD or maintained requirement:
an English lower-case display name for the listing’s currency, derived from the authorised currencyreference name. Agree whether surrounding spaces are meaningful and what happens when a code has
no matched name. In this worked case, retain the eligible listing and publish a null name rather than
inventing one. State that consumers must continue to use the currency code for identity and calculations.
Name matching is a display concern; it is not a new currency conversion rule. The acceptance examples
must include missing reference data and must preserve the existing listing population.
2. Contract. Add currency_name_lower to the reviewed ODCS schema with the supported string type,
nullable status, description, authoritative origin and lower-case meaning. Keep the existing key, grain,
classification, ownership and service promises explicit. Record the reference-data coverage rule agreed
with the consumer rather than assuming that a nullable field needs no quality control. Under a policy
that treats nullable additions as compatible, this is a candidate minor version change. Check actual
consumers before settling that decision: a strict schema validator or positional export can still fail when
a column appears. A version label records the agreement; it does not provision a parallel interface.
3. Integration model. Join the listing’s currency code to the approved currency reference and derive
the field from the reference name. Confirm that the reference contributes at most one eligible row per
currency code under the chosen date policy. If the reference is historical, define which business date
selects its name; an unrestricted join to all versions can multiply listings. A left join implements the
agreed retention of listings without matched names. For the chosen no-trimming rule, the derivation
is conceptually lower(currency_name); use the actual project column and supported SQL conventions.
Lowercasing must occur after the authoritative name has been selected, not after a guessed mapping
from the code.
4. Final model and consumer documentation. Project the new field explicitly into the final interface,
alongside the unchanged currency code and listing identifiers. Inspect the output model and published
interface: adding a field to an intermediate model does not make it visible to a consumer. Document the
null meaning, language and source. Check that the DAG or bundle still selects the intended model graph,
and that the candidate-to-domain publication step carries the additional column. This request needs no
new schedule merely because its schema changed. Existing access groups and discovery metadata must
continue to describe the actual published product.
5. Tests and independent examples. Use a small fixture whose expected results are written before
inspecting generated SQL. An active AED listing with the reference name UAE dirham produces uae
dirham; an eligible listing without a reference name retains its key and has null; an inactive AED listing

remains excluded. Include an instrument with two distinct eligible listing IDs: both survive, proving
that the change preserves listing grain rather than collapsing to instrument grain. Add a reference-key
uniqueness check and compare candidate key sets before and after the change. Compilation checks
references and syntax; successful execution checks runtime viability; the fixture and key comparison
establish the requested meaning and population. A lower-case check alone would accept the erroneous
value aed.
6. Migration, historical rows and release. In the client repository, commit the reviewed ODCS contract
change: CI is the canonical SQL generator, and the Harness bot owns commits under flyway/migrations/.
Review its generated additive DDL, exact target, type, nullability and dependencies. Local SQL under
gitignored .local/migrations/ is throwaway review output, not an artefact to commit in place of CImanaged migrations. Preserve applied migration history through the supported workflow; do not manually
94

rewrite deployed history to make it resemble a fresh installation. The client tooling README defines this
ownership boundary. Adding a nullable column changes structure but can leave existing rows null. If the
consumer needs historical names, specify a bounded backfill, the authoritative name history available
for those dates, reconciliation checks and recovery before promotion. Today’s reference name must not
silently stand in for unavailable historical truth. DDL review and a backfill plan are separate evidence.
Review these changes together on a short-lived branch from main. The reviewed commit can move
through environments according to the deployment policy, with checks at each target. Local compilation,
fixture review and a private candidate do not establish that a production migration or consumer transition
has occurred. Production readiness also requires the approved migration, any required backfill, candidate
quality evidence, publication and the affected consumers’ compatibility checks. The capstone does not
require applying these migrations.
REVIEW — finite change assessment. Using only this case and the supplied repository conventions, write
six short review comments: one each for requirement, contract, integration, final interface, tests and
migration/release. Identify the mistake if the generated integration uses lower(currency_code), the
missing evidence if a reference join doubles a listing, and the uncompleted work if DDL adds the column
but historical rows remain null. Decide which consumers need a compatibility check before a minorversion release. Your result is a local review note, with no new live commands or deployment required.
A complete review connects the expected uae dirham value to its source, preserves the listing keys and
separates schema readiness from historical-data readiness.

Quality checks belong before domain publication
Publication creates a critical quality boundary. If a pipeline writes to a shared table and checks quality
afterwards, a consumer can read the bad data during the gap. A failed check cannot undo a decision
already made from it.
The example writes a candidate into the application catalog, runs quality checks there, and publishes
to the domain catalog only after those checks pass. Publication uses a deep-clone step. Databricks
documents deep cloning as copying data and metadata; a shallow clone references source data
files instead. The extra copy here is a deliberate cost of separating private preparation from shared
consumption.

Use the quality framework supported in the assigned environment and verify that a failed required rule
blocks publication. A rule library cannot protect consumers when the DAG publishes despite its failure.
Publishing also does not solve all quality questions. A dataset can be unique and complete while using the
wrong classification rule or excluding a consumer’s intended population. Monday’s agreement supplies
the acceptance examples; Wednesday’s model and tests make them executable; Thursday’s orchestration
preserves the order.

Migration preserves dependencies and consumer agreements
Plan a migration in observable steps. Ingestion first changes orchestrator while retaining the existing
execution stack; later work moves execution and publication towards Databricks and source-aligned
catalogs. Separating those changes reduces the number of moving parts to diagnose at once.
An upstream pipeline may remain in Caspian while its downstream product moves to Astronomer. A
supported dependency-check blueprint can provide an interim way to inspect legacy DAG completion
through an authorised API route.

That transitional route has a different access boundary from the

federated event design. Neither is an invitation to grant every deployment access to every other one.
A migration may preserve a virtual-dataset interface while changing its underlying physical source. Verify
the queries, schema, values and access rather than assuming the unchanged interface makes the change
transparent.

Versioning and roadmap questions need separate answers
Parallel versions require a supported design.

A contract version records a change; it does not

automatically create two independently usable datasets. Altering a table can still break a consumer
using the previous schema or meaning.
Suppose the producer changes asset_class from a descriptive label to a code. Four version questions
now arise: which code revision ran, which contract described it, which schema was deployed, and which
data release the consumer read. Aligning those identities helps explain a result. Incrementing only the
contract version does not preserve the earlier interface.
With trunk-based development, short-lived reviewed changes can flow into a shared main line;
deployment to each environment and activation for consumers remain separate concerns. Feature flags
or parallel branches alone do not establish consumer compatibility. Do not promise dual-version support
because a branch or flag exists.

Context use, retrieval and durable decisions
A prompt can include visible user text, higher-level instructions, a skill, retrieved documents and tool
output.

Some of that context may not be visible in the same chat message.

Retrieval-augmented

generation supplies selected source material to a generation request; it does not make every generated
claim a faithful quotation of that material.
A finite context window imposes a capacity limit.

Conversation summarisation or compaction can

preserve the broad task while losing a column, exception or unresolved decision. Keep authoritative
briefs and correction logs in files. On a new request, identify the current versions and ask the agent to
reread the relevant sections.
Position and presentation can matter as well as capacity. Lost in the Middle found sensitivity to where
relevant information appeared in its tested long-context tasks. The result is bounded by those models
and tasks. For your contract review, make the evidence packet focused, label each source, and test
whether the draft used a critical condition instead of assuming a universal ordering rule.
Separate role and purpose from examples. “Equity”, “active”, “real time” and “available” need productspecific definitions. A long thread with several conflicting examples can leave the interpretation unclear.
Starting from a short, confirmed brief may produce a more reviewable result than adding another
paragraph to the thread.

Why code gives useful but incomplete validation signals
Code offers checks that prose alone may lack: parsing, compilation, tests and comparison with expected
results. Those checks help expose defects, but the strength of the signal depends on what they measure.
A programme that always returns 4 passes a single “2+2” example without implementing addition. A
model that hard-codes one row can make a superficial pipeline check appear successful.
A useful review therefore separates several questions. Does the code load? Do references and declared
columns resolve? Does the selected input produce the expected output? Does the output preserve the
agreed meaning, grain, units and exclusions? Does the structure support maintenance and review? The
final two questions need product and engineering judgment as well as tools.
Automated feedback helps inspect coding output, while software-size anecdotes do not establish a
universal line-count threshold for useful AI assistance. Evaluate a bounded model change or contract
review in the repository you actually use, with representative dependencies and edge cases. A small
change can be consequential; a large file can include much generated or repeated material. Size alone
does not settle risk.
A second model’s critique can help generate test ideas, but a shared assumption can survive both
generations. Tests that repeat the same generated formula also repeat its error. For the CG product

How can a consumer use AI without Catalyst?
First establish the consumer’s approved tools and data access. A workspace may provide a conversational
interface such as a Databricks Genie space, an editor extension or another approved assistant. Availability
and permissions are environment-specific; access to a dataset does not automatically grant access
through every assistant. Ask the platform owner which route is supported and verify the answers against
authorised data and definitions.

How should a team investigate an AI-assisted workflow?
Start with a real, authorised example of the finished artefact and a small task that can be evaluated.
Identify the required sources, meaning, style and approval criteria. Test one part, inspect the result, and
record what changed when the input or instructions changed. Do not begin with a large autonomous
system before establishing the work it must perform.
Turn a useful, reviewed iteration into maintained instructions or a skill, then test it on a second
example. Transfer to another person, department or product may require different terms and evidence.
Reviewer agents can suggest issues, including unclear language or missing terminology, while human
and independent checks decide whether the artefact is usable.
Retrieval, an internal application or orchestration may be appropriate once you understand the task,
source volume, permissions and evaluation. Retrieval is a way to supply relevant context, not a universal
first step or a guarantee of factual output. Follow the sequence of investigation, product design and
engineering at the scale the evidence supports. See deliberate prompting.

A meaningful model review
Suppose an agent proposes a query that joins holdings to a reference table and sums market value. Is
the reference key unique at the join? If it has two rows per key, each holding is counted twice, and both
the SQL and the row-count test can still pass. So check the unmatched rows and how many matches
each key gets, as well as the final total.
Each type of mapping needs its own kind of test, and the table under Mapping types, failure modes and
versioning lists them. Decide what a failure means before you write the test. Does it block the batch,
flag suspect records, or go down as a known limitation?
When a model is still a stub, don’t build a wide downstream selection and then blame the platform for
the failures. The client guide uses selectors to build just the step you’re writing and skips the tests that
depend on unfinished models. Once everything is written, widen the selection and run the whole graph
before you hand off.
Change the model, the mapping and the tests together. If you change a business rule but leave the
description and the acceptance criterion alone, the code can be right and the product still misleading.
For the handoff to Thursday, write down which models you built, which sources they read, and what’s
still unresolved, such as access or data problems.

Data systems: database, warehouse, lake and lakehouse
With Docker done, we turn to the systems the afternoon’s dbt work runs in, and to how you write down what
a data product has to do.
THIS SESSION ANSWERS

• What are a database, a warehouse, a lake and a lakehouse?
• What is a data pipeline, and what is grain?
• What goes in a source-to-target mapping?
• What do an SLA, an SLI and an SLO promise?

Knowledge check: Storage and processing
Which requirements would make a database, warehouse or lake a suitable home for a product? What would
you need to know about schema, query patterns and governance before choosing?

A working glossary
• A database is structured storage. It’s tabular, with a schema nailed down by the software using the
tables. Typically online/transactional systems with daily inserts; the schema is rigid.
• A data store holds raw files: each individual piece may have structure, but the system as a whole
has no unified structure. When you hear “data store”, you can almost always just think files and
folders.
• A relational database: what is a relation? A relation is a table. It’s a mathematical word (a relation is a
set of tuples). Relational databases are not about relationships; that’s a common misunderstanding.
Keys and joins express relationships between the tables; their correctness depends on the declared
identity and multiplicity.
• OLTP (online transactional processing) — systems optimised for writes/inserts; better thought of as
systems of record, where data is written atomically. Why “transaction”? The original OLTP databases
were retail databases (Sears-era department stores, 1950s onward), and the transactions were literal
financial transactions. Today the word means any write operation that must succeed or fail as a
whole. Retail needs this for double-entry: withdrawing from one account and adding to another
must succeed or fail together, otherwise you get double spending. (Aside: the one famous solution
to double-spending without transactions is, arguably, Bitcoin, in 2009.)
• OLAP (online analytical processing) — optimised for reads; analytical databases, often with large
numbers of columns. Rule of thumb: write-heavy databases have few columns and many rows;
read-heavy analytical databases have many columns. Transactional systems are more sequential
(transactions must succeed or fail in order); analytical systems parallelise well. You very rarely see
a GROUP BY in a transactional database.
• A data warehouse — an analytical (OLAP) database that also tracks history: tabular, but with a much
more flexible schema; tables often have large numbers of columns, typically fitted to reports, and
somewhat arbitrary. You keep adding columns to make your report work. Worth knowing: OLTP
systems generally don’t timestamp changes. When a user changes their username, the record is
updated in place. If you need a log of changes, that’s a separate system, and that log is what gets
inserted into the analytical database, which is why the data most of you see always has timestamps
everywhere.
• A data lake stores files in varied formats, usually in object storage. It can hold tables, images,
free text and contract files without requiring one tabular schema for the entire store. Versioning,
ownership, discoverability and access still need explicit controls; flexible storage does not make
those guarantees automatic.

+44 (0)20 3583 0972 | info@decoded.com | decoded.com

DECODED

Wednesday — Data systems and dbt

Compare a database, warehouse and lake by their storage flexibility, processing needs and governance
responsibilities.
In these examples, structured data means fields governed by a declared schema. Tabular storage is a
common form. Semi-structured or other file formats can also carry useful structure, so name the actual
format and schema requirement rather than treating “structured” as a complete design.

Parquet
To store tabular data in a lake you can simply add a CSV or Excel file, but more commonly a Parquet file
(also ORC, Arrow): like a CSV that is compressed and stored column-by-column rather than row-by-row.
It’s effectively a pivoted CSV.

The lakehouse
The lakehouse sits between the warehouse and the lake on the flexibility scale. It is like a data lake in
the storage layer, still just files (Parquet etc.), but the difference is in the querying layer. A database has
a querying layer and a storage layer; a data lake has only storage.
A lakehouse combines lake-style file storage with table management and analytical query capabilities.
Transactional table formats and metadata add schema, version and concurrency controls over files. The
useful design question is which guarantees the chosen format, catalogue and query engine provide, and
how those guarantees support the consumer’s workload.
Why does it matter? This is the heart of how you’ll use Databricks. When dbt queries Databricks, it
relies on the fact that Databricks isn’t just files and folders. There’s a SQL layer on top that dbt can use.
Even inside Databricks everything is still files underneath; Databricks provides a single management layer
(ACID and so on) over them.

ACID: transaction guarantees
ACID describes four transaction guarantees:
• Atomicity: a transaction commits as a whole or has no effect.
• Consistency: committed data satisfies the constraints enforced by the system; business validity
still needs explicit rules.
• Isolation: concurrent transactions do not expose an incomplete write to a reader.
• Durability: committed changes survive a failure.
For Delta tables, data files and transaction metadata identify committed versions. This is different from
claiming that every distributed operation executes in one universal real-time order. Check the supported
isolation and transaction scope when choosing a design. Databricks explains its ACID guarantees.

Worked demo: Delta time travel
One command shows the mechanism Databricks built those guarantees on. Against any table the project
materialises (staging models are views, so pick one from the prepared layer) in your training_<initials>
schema:
DESCRIBE HISTORY training_ab.prepared_orders;

Every write to a Delta table produces a version: the table you query is just the latest one, and the
earlier versions are kept. Run dbt run twice more and run the DESCRIBE again. Two new versions have
appeared, one per write, each stamped with when, which operation, and by whom. Then read an earlier
state directly:
SELECT * FROM training_ab.prepared_orders VERSION AS OF 2;

108

+44 (0)20 3583 0972 | info@decoded.com | decoded.com

DECODED

Wednesday — Data systems and dbt

That’s how the lakehouse keeps its ACID guarantees on top of plain files. A write either produces a
complete new version or it produces nothing, so a reader never sees a half-written table (atomicity), and
switching things off between versions loses nothing that was committed (durability).
A separate product case uses Parquet with custom bitemporal logic. Table-version history and businesshistory requirements are different; choose a design that records the dates and corrections the consumer
needs.

On screen: S3 data lake
Buckets and object prefixes are how the files are physically stored. Catalogs, schemas and tables are
the governed view of the same data, and they’re what you query. A folder called curated is just a name.
The quality promise lives in the product’s tests and contract. The Iceberg example keeps metadata files
beside the data files, and together they make up one table.

You won’t browse or configure S3 here. For the client dbt work, reach the data through the tables and
views your project and profile point at. You need to tell a path, a table and a product apart, and you can
leave administering the storage to the platform team.

The lakehouse and ACID
A lakehouse adds table management and transaction metadata to file storage. The ACID explanation
covers committed writes and concurrent reads; it does not imply that arbitrary files acquire those
guarantees.
Expert
The supplied architecture calls its lakehouse Caspian. This course example does not establish the current
enterprise service boundary or support owner; confirm those in the internal service documentation. In that
architecture, S3 holds data files and table metadata, while Databricks executes queries and Unity Catalog
governs registered objects. Delta uses Parquet data files with a transaction log; it is not a sorted CSV. Parquetonly and Iceberg examples have different table-management arrangements. Delta Lake documents the table
format and guarantees.

Dimensional modelling still matters
A lakehouse changes the storage engine, but consumers still need tables organised around the questions
they ask. Dimensional modelling separates measurable events into facts and descriptive context into
dimensions. In the prepared or curated layer, that gives BI tools predictable joins, gives several products
the same definition of a fund or client, and lets a reader find measures without decoding the source
system.
This example star uses a territory scenario because its design shows the privacy decision clearly. Its grain
is one row per client, per territory, per asset, per date.

Erasure removes time-travel history
On Delta Lake, erasure has four technical steps. First, DELETE the subject’s PII from the table. Second, REORG
TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE) where deletion vectors are enabled. Third, run the approved VACUUM operation to

remove historical files. VACUUM ... RETAIN 0 HOURS destroys time-travel history, so it must never be copied
from a teaching example into production without the approved retention and safety settings. Fourth, rebuild or
delete the same subject from staging, integration, prepared tables, materialised views and streaming outputs.
Deleting only the current dimension row leaves historical files or derived copies behind.

Fit and lock-in
A warehouse remains a sensible home for structured relational data, stable BI queries and strict
governance when the team accepts a proprietary storage and compute model. A plain data lake suits
mixed raw formats and low-cost storage when a separate governance system can supply schema,
transactions, ownership and access control.
Without owners, metadata and quality controls, teams may create conflicting copies because they cannot
find or trust the existing data. Cheap object storage does not remove governance and maintenance costs.
The lakehouse is only partly portable. Delta stores data in an open format that Spark, Trino and DuckDB
can read. Unity Catalog’s grants, masks, filters and lineage records are a platform commitment; they do
not migrate with the Delta files. If an RFD chooses this stack, write down the work needed to recreate
the governance somewhere else.

Publishing through two catalog tiers
Teams build and validate in an app-aligned catalog such as caspian_ig_dev. After the DQ gate passes, a
publish task copies the table into the consumer-facing domain catalog:
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ig_dev.exposures.fact_fund_exposure
DEEP CLONE caspian_ig_dev.exposures.fact_fund_exposure;

Why split it this way?
• Work in progress stays away from consumers.
• The publish step runs only after DQ has passed, so any table you can see in the domain catalog has
passed that gate.
• The domain gets its own copy of the table, separate from the build area.
• The same validated product can be copied into more than one authorised domain.

Figure 41: The two-tier publish path keeps work in the application catalog until data-quality checks pass,
then clones the validated table into the domain catalog.

The marketplace listing from the consumer’s side
Register a product through the supported marketplace process so consumers can find its purpose, owner,
schema, glossary and access route. Search the same catalogue before a new build: an existing positions
product may meet the need or supply a reusable component. Verify the listing and its definitions instead
of inferring registration from a completed pipeline.
What a consumer of the exposures product would see on its listing:
• Sample data and the actual table, plus a glossary tab defining the columns. Some of the data
dictionaries are AI-generated, so check them before you rely on them, the same as the glossaries
behind an STTM.
• A request-access section if you don’t have access, which connects into ServiceNow.
• For highly sensitive data (HR, say): without access you see no sample data and no schema, just the
business context.
• A section for how to use it and how not to use it, worth populating when it’s your product.

Wednesday — Data systems and dbt

Data meant to be shared across domains, or that anyone might reference, should be discoverable and
searchable. Otherwise we’re just creating data silos.
Unity Catalog is the Databricks side of the same discoverability. Anything in Caspian (tables, shares) is
registered in Unity Catalog, and its namespace has three layers, the same ones your dbt profile named.
At the bottom is a table, above it a schema (the database, or container for the data), and above that a
catalog. So catalog, schema, table. The marketplace is available to everyone, but Unity Catalog doesn’t
necessarily let you see everything. Consider the discoverability trade-off. Should everyone be able to
browse all schemas and views (without the data) so they can find what exists? Without browse access,
the only way to know what’s in a catalog is to ask, and discoverability can’t really work. The practical
request you’ll make as a creator is catalog-to-workspace binding. Catalogs are bound to workspaces,
and not every catalog is bound to every workspace. “I have this catalog in the Caspian workspace, and I
need it in my research workspace. Can you bind it?” For a Caspian catalog, more than likely yes. Binding
a domain catalog into another domain’s workspace is less likely to be available by default. People often
don’t realise a catalog needs to be bound to their workspace before they can use it.

Unity Catalog controls at query time
Column masks protect a sensitive value while preserving access to the table. This shortened form shows
the mechanism:
CREATE FUNCTION mask_tax_id(v STRING) RETURNS STRING
RETURN CASE WHEN is_member('compliance_team') THEN v ELSE 'REDACTED' END;
ALTER TABLE prepared.dim_client
ALTER COLUMN tax_id SET MASK mask_tax_id;

Row filters apply the same idea to records:
CREATE FUNCTION fund_filter(fund_family STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN
RETURN is_member('global_team') OR fund_family = current_user_fund_family();
ALTER TABLE prepared.fact_fund_exposure
SET ROW FILTER fund_filter ON (fund_family);

Unity Catalog evaluates both controls in the engine, whether the request arrives through SQL, a notebook,
a BI tool or an API. Per-table functions become hard to manage across hundreds of products, so governed
tags provide the scaling route: tag a column as PII or a table as restricted, then bind a policy to the tag
so later objects inherit the control when they are classified. The governance decisions behind these
snippets are worked through in Appendix B.

Data mesh
• Data mesh is the opposite of data siloing / a centralised data team: data product creators are spread
throughout the business and can create and self-serve their own products. It is an organisational
concept, not a technology.
• Summary mind-map of the supplied course architecture: data mesh (human/organisational side) +
data lakehouse (infrastructure side) + dbt (code/data side) + SLAs (promises).
• Assess a proposed organisational pattern by the ownership, access and support problems it solves.
A fashionable label alone is not an architecture decision.
Learning Review
Retrieve the differences between retention, access control and publication. Apply them to a client dimension
linked to a long-retention trade fact: which attributes and relationships require a recorded policy decision?
Check that the proposed retention and erasure treatment, masks/filters, owner and catalog publication route
agree with the product contract; technical deletion alone does not establish a policy outcome.

Data pipelines, the medallion system and grain
With the lakehouse as our system (files and folders plus SQL, as far as we’re concerned), how do we use
it to create data pipelines?
Knowledge check: Layer, alignment and grain
What does one row represent in your source and proposed output? How does that differ from the layer or
folder in which the model lives?

A data pipeline is automated (prefer that word over “CI/CD”) movement of data from one place to another.
The data flows, and at every stop an operation is applied. The operations come in a few kinds:
• Ingest / save-and-load — taking data from the source, landing it.
• Transformations (sometimes called rules).
• Joining and combining — enriching across data sets (called curation in the supplied course examples).
• Exposing to the consumption layer — publishing without changing the data.

The medallion system
The generic industry framing is bronze / silver / gold:
• Bronze — where data is initially dumped from an outside source; raw.
• Silver — the first layer of transformations.
• Gold — the final layer; e.g. report-ready.
These are relative terms (each team defines what they mean), but there are often agreements between
phases, sometimes enforced automatically on release. The layers might literally be folder names: an
agreement might say that by the time a file reaches silver there are no missing values, all currencies are
the same, everything is timestamped; gold might mean report-ready.
Nothing in the medallion system is inherently about sources and consumers. Two software systems
could ingest from different apps, normalise, and dump back out, system-to-system. A bronze model
may preserve source structure and a gold model may serve a consumer, but those names do not
determine product alignment. A reusable domain product can contain several processing stages, and
another product can consume its output as a source.

Capital Group’s stage names
The course examples use these stage names:
• Staging — raw data as landed (e.g. from MFT), plus metadata such as timestamps. Single-source;
data still looks like its source.
• Integration — joins, lookups, enrichment; intermediate data artifacts. Still largely single-source and
raw-shaped; data quality work happens between staging and integration.
• Prepared / curated (the terms are used for the same thing) — curation logic across multiple sources;
this is where the grain changes.
Other layer names you’ll hear
Some teams also described two golds: an application gold and a business gold exposed to the business.
Another set is landing / ingest / curate. The industry uses bronze / silver / gold widely, and internal names
vary by team.

Use source-, domain- and consumer-aligned to explain whose requirements shape a product. Use the
assigned repository’s model names to explain processing: the supplied projects include stg_, int_ and
prepared/report models. There is no universal one-to-one crosswalk and no claim that every Catalyst
version generates the same layout. State both the product boundary and the model stage; a source can
be another internal CG team rather than an outside supplier.
For a consumer-aligned mart, the kind of query decides the prefix:
• rpt_ names a report-shaped query, such as one Morningstar exposure roll-up per fund.
• agg_ names a measure grouped by a dimension, such as exposure by asset class.
• ts_ names one row per entity and period, such as daily exposure by fund.
• api_ names a low-latency single-row lookup, such as the latest fund exposure.
The training project itself uses folders named after the layers.

Grain
Grain states what one row represents: an event, an entity at a specified time, or an aggregate over
a defined population. Name its identifying keys and time boundary before joining or grouping. For an
aggregated metric, a larger group produces a coarser result, as the following example shows.
Take LA crime data, with crimes scattered unevenly across the city. Compute the mean crime rate per
square mile across all of LA and you get one number, say 3, which is very non-granular. Replace all the
detail on the map with “3” and you can’t see anything.
Split LA into districts (Pasadena, Long Beach and so on) and compute the same metric per district, and
you get more numbers, each with a smaller group behind it: finer grain. Smaller groups, finer grain; you
change the grain whenever you do a group-by.
You could also define grain by level/categorisation (a key change often goes with it). Maximum granularity
is generally at the source. In principle joining in additional data sets can add detail later, but mostly a
pipeline lowers granularity (makes things more general) as data flows through the stages.
Organisational context has the investment glossary, a worked fact-and-dimension join and two windowfunction examples.

Grain changes across transformations
An aggregation changes what one row represents, so check the grain on both sides of it. Before summing,
check the lookup keys are unique and look at the unmatched rows. After summing, write down the
grouping columns and reconcile the total to the eligible inputs. An offering count can be arithmetically
correct and still include repeated catalogue/detail records or lose offerings with unknown expenses.

Where dbt and Databricks fit
dbt defines models and tests; the configured Databricks compute executes their SQL over governed
tables backed by storage. A model can materialise a view or table rather than move a physical file
between folders.
Why not just do it all in Databricks? Databricks does provide SQL (and Python, but PySpark pipelines get
complicated fast, so set that aside). Databricks SQL handles reporting queries fine, but as soon as you
want to create tables (actually materialise each hop), it gets more complicated. What dbt gives you:
• Simple SQL: you write what looks like a series of SELECT statements; behind the scenes dbt does
all the table creation and insertion for you. As an analyst you just write selects and dbt does the
flow.
• Versioned models, documentation generation, tests, enforced contracts and CI integration. Other
transformation approaches need their own equivalent controls.
It remains an architect’s trade-off. You could use Databricks alone; there’s no single right answer.

Source-to-target mapping, transformation rules and traceability
This is the technical half of product design. We have done the non-technical design (requirements,
interviewing), and we still need to specify the data product to the person developing it: the source-totarget mapping rules, the SLAs and SLIs, what we measure and how. It’s quick, because writing the rules
isn’t the hard part. Implementing them in code is, and that’s dbt. dbt is how we write the data product.
Git is how we version it, and Docker is how we bundle it for release, dependencies included.
Knowledge check: Rules before SQL
Which facts belong in a source-to-target mapping row? How would you describe a conversion, join or null rule
so another creator can implement and review it?

The STTM
The source-to-target mapping (STTM) specifies how source records become target records: source and
target names/types, transformation rule and null treatment. Record renames, unit conversions, joins,
filters and aggregation explicitly so another creator can implement and test the same meaning.
One row is harder than all the others. Morningstar and FactSet each carry their own security identifiers,
and deciding that two of them mean the same asset (and then assigning one internal identifier) is the
hardest row in the mapping. For an individual-account product, such as retail or retirement accounts, data
may arrive from two to four sources. The sources are joined, duplicates removed, and a unique internal
identifier assigned, and that last step is one of the hard areas. The classic case is police databases.
Officers fill out forms at crime scenes, names are spelled differently across reports, and it’s very hard to
know whether any two reports are about the same person. Day 1’s identifier-misalignment pain point is
this row, and the “No join condition” omission below is what happens when it is left out of the mapping.
The STTM travels with a glossary: the mapping rules don’t tell you what the language and values mean, and
meanings shift in realignment. “Returns” in one column may be risk-neutralised while another consumer
wants raw returns. Same word, different operational meanings, so the glossary must pin them down.
Suppose a fund-attribution product ships money-weighted returns when the portfolio managers needed
time-weighted returns. Nobody wrote down which “return” was meant, and the fix is weeks of rework. So
one glossary entry records term ID, term, definition, synonyms or aliases, authoritative source, example
values, related terms and owner. Give each term one owner. Version every changed definition with an
effective date and tell the consumers, and review the glossary at launch and at each major version.
