The supplied marketplace example lists data sets with glossary sections defining column meanings, as
the marketplace listing below shows. But some of those glossaries are currently AI-generated, and they
need to be very carefully scrutinised before you rely on them.

Mapping types, failure modes and versioning
Poor source quality complicates the rules and can rule out a transformation without you knowing it,
so profile the data before you map it. discover-data ranks candidate Unity Catalog tables. For the
Morningstar work, run data-profiling on the exposures candidates to see null rates, distinct counts,
ranges and fitness flags. Do that before transformation-spec drafts the STTM, so every source column
in the mapping comes from a table you’ve looked at.
The mapping type tells the builder which kind of test the row needs:
Mapping type

Test implied by the mapping

Direct

Compare source and target values after any rename or compatible cast.

Derived

Recalculate the expression independently and compare the result.

Constant

Check that every target value equals the declared constant.

Aggregated

Reconcile sums or counts to the lower-grain input.

Lookup

Check join-key validity and return every unmatched key — country code GB looked up to
United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, with any code the table lacks
returned.

Join

Column 1 from one source, column 2 from another, combined into the target: check the
key on both sides and count rows lost or multiplied by the join.

Filter

The rows kept on a condition: check that no kept row fails the condition and reconcile the
count dropped.

Union

Rows of two sources joined end to end: check the row count equals the sum of the inputs
and the column types agree.

Conditional

A value chosen by an if: exercise every branch with a row that reaches it.

Six things get left out of mappings again and again, and each one causes rework:
• No null rule. The builder has to guess whether to reject, default, flag or quarantine a null, and
what empty means differs by kind of data. State whether null means unknown, unavailable or not
applicable.
• An ambiguous transformation. “Calculate return” leaves TWR versus MWR, gross versus net, and the
time window unresolved.
• An ambiguous connective. The word if has several senses, and or can be exclusive or inclusive (“left
or right” meaning either, or possibly both). In English, add words rather than relying on if and or:
“either this or that”, “both this and that”.
• An unscoped term. “Phone number” — US phone numbers only, or worldwide? State the scope of
every technical term the rule uses.
• An assumed stable source name. An upstream rename invalidates a mapping that records no sourceschema version.
• No join condition. A multi-source mapping needs the join key and a rule for when the sources
disagree.

Every mapping is relative to a schema, so put the source-schema version in the STTM header from the
first draft. When Morningstar changes a column, the header tells you which version of the source the
mapping was written against, and the impact analysis starts from there.

The traceability matrix
A traceability matrix and design canvas are structured records for different review questions.
One aspect of traceability is that the promises we make about the data product (in particular the
promises about these transformations) are tracked and enforced. A row of the matrix links: the business
outcome / consumer promise (e.g. “refreshed by 7 AM, national coverage, complete”), the columns and
transformations relevant to that promise, the glossary terms needed to understand them, and the risks,
accountabilities, dependencies and findings. In short it is the mapping, the glossary and the risks laid
alongside the actual promise and the data consumer. It’s just record keeping.
Take the Morningstar exposures. The consumer wants fund exposures by 07:00. The STTM columns give
source and target, the types, the rule and the null handling, and they link to the glossary. The quality
commitment covers freshness, completeness and range checks, and the RAID record holds the risk that
goes with it.
The design canvas includes everything else (risk register, traceability matrix, reuse assessment and the
source-to-target mapping), and the mapping in turn refers to the glossary.

Traceability is not lineage
Lineage records where data came from and which transformations or outputs depend on it. Traceability
links a requirement to its implementation, check and acceptance evidence. Use lineage to inspect change
impact; use the traceability matrix to show that the consumer promise is covered.

the pipeline

Three files implement this schematic rule. The names illustrate the mapping; use the assigned project
paths for your own attempt.
First the staging model, which does the rename and nothing else. Staging models are meant to be boring:
-- models/staging/stg_morningstar_exposures.sql
select
fund_id,
us_exposure as exposure_us,
loaded_at
from {{ source('morningstar', 'exposures') }}

Then the integration model. This row’s transformation rule contains no arithmetic (a rename plus a
validation), so the integration model simply passes exposure_us through while joining it onto the fund
reference data, which is the job that layer is for:
-- models/integration/int_fund_exposures.sql
select
f.fund_id,
f.fund_name,
e.exposure_us
from {{ ref('stg_funds') }} f
join {{ ref('stg_morningstar_exposures') }} e
on f.fund_id = e.fund_id

Last, the two right-hand cells of the STTM row become tests. The null-handling cell says “fail the pipeline”,
and that’s what a failing not_null test in schema.yml does:
# models/staging/schema.yml
models:
- name: stg_morningstar_exposures
columns:
- name: exposure_us
tests:
- not_null

The range rule becomes a test too. It’s written today as a one-off SQL file (any row it returns is a defect;
the afternoon explains why every dbt test works that way), and can be turned into a reusable generic
test; see dbt further study:
-- tests/exposure_us_in_range.sql
select fund_id, exposure_us
from {{ ref('stg_morningstar_exposures') }}
where exposure_us < 0 or exposure_us > 1

Git and the paved path: a recap
The paved path is Capital Group’s supported tools and conventions for product development: Git/GitHub,
Docker, dbt, Airflow, Databricks and Harness, with Catalyst and documentation alongside.
Knowledge check: History and execution
What can Git tell a reviewer about a change? What separate configuration decides which service or database
the changed code can reach?

Git: versioning the data product
Git is a version-control system for code. It’s a bit like a wiki for code, where you can go through the
history of edits to a file. Software engineers want three feature sets from it:
1. The log — a history of changes. Engineers make mistakes constantly and need to undo them by
walking back through the edit history.
2. Branches — multiple simultaneous versions of a product.
3. Sharing — push and pull: distributing the code between people and machines.
Why use a software-engineering tool for a data product? Historically a data product might have been an
Excel file, an Access database, or a SQL file. Odd things to put under Git. The supplied data-product
124

+44 (0)20 3583 0972 | info@decoded.com | decoded.com

DECODED

Wednesday — Data systems and dbt

projects use dbt, whose transformations are SQL and configuration under version control. That project
choice does not describe every CG data product. So to version data products and test them, we use Git
the way software engineers do, on the code of the data product.
If you’re comfortable with SQL but new to the software-engineering side, versioning and sharing SQL via
Git may feel unusual. It’s standard engineering practice, applied to data.

Git vs GitHub, and the pull request
A Git repository holds files, commits and branches. GitHub hosts repositories and adds collaboration
workflows, including pull requests and review checks. Git also works locally without GitHub.
You don’t have to use GitHub. Git works fine on your own laptop or on CG infrastructure. Why pay for a
proprietary hosted system?
• Collaboration — a watering hole: a standard place everyone knows how to use to share code.
• Workflows — GitHub adds workflows that are not part of Git itself, and the key one is the pull request:
a GitHub feature (not a Git feature) that puts in front of an approver the request to take one version
and make it the released version. Technically it requests a merge; conceptually it is an approval
request to promote one version of the software, usually to become the release. That review flow is
one reason the supplied development process uses GitHub; integration and environment promotion
remain separate decisions.

The line: development vs live
Separate development artefacts from their execution.

Git versions the code; Docker packages

dependencies. Airflow schedules data tasks and Databricks executes the configured SQL. The branch,
deployed version and connected runtime are separate identities.
• Databricks is a platform. From our point of view, it’s where the data side of the data product lives:
where products are discovered and the actual tables can be accessed. Everything above the line is
just code that runs and does something, and the something it does is create tables in Databricks.
(Caveat for later: the data doesn’t literally live on Databricks. It lives in S3 on Amazon. But for
working purposes, Databricks is the release target.)
• Airflow — everyone says “orchestration”, but what does that mean? Automated sequencing: a task
runner and scheduler. If you remember Windows Scheduler from the Windows 98/XP era, it’s that
idea; if you’ve used Linux, it’s essentially a cron wrapper. It defines, in code, when to run a task, on
what condition, how often, and what to do if it fails. Airflow is the system that actually triggers the
data product’s code to run; the code, when run, modifies Databricks.
• Harness is a wrapper around all of this, which we leave until later in the week. For a data creator,
detailed knowledge can stop before Harness.

What the data creator actually does
Creators mainly author and review dbt mappings, models and tests. The platform supplies the supported
environment; engineers may manage orchestration and deployment. The assigned Airflow phase also
asks you to author a small DAG. Retain a reviewed diff and checked output, then use the agreed handoff
rather than assuming a push completes the product.
Python appears in Airflow and supporting helpers. The amount you author depends on the selected route:
the assigned v2 Airflow activity writes a small Python DAG, while platform examples may use prepared
configuration.

A pull request proposes a change against one base branch. Pick the wrong base and you can hide

Collaboration clinic: a merge conflict
In a separate collaboration clinic, use the disposable v2 Git workspace and an agreed reviewer. Stage
conflicting changes to the same lines only after saving the work you intend to keep. This clinic has its
own time allocation; it does not interrupt dbt practice.
Distinguish two failure states:
• Machines with uncommitted local edits fail before any merging starts: error: Your local changes
to the following files would be overwritten by merge. Nothing is conflicted. Git stops early

to protect your uncommitted work. The exit is the safe sequence from the top of this block. Run
git status, then commit or git restore, then pull again.

• In the prepared collaboration clinic, competing branches edit the same contract lines, so their merge
produces a deliberate conflict. Now both sides have changed the same region, and the file itself
gains markers: <<<<<<< HEAD above the local lines, ======= between, >>>>>>> below the incoming
ones. Git has written both candidate versions into the file and paused the merge, because choosing
between them is a human decision.
git status is the map throughout. It names the files in conflict and lists the commands available, so

read it before touching anything. Then the two exits:

Docker: the problem containers solve
Code that runs on your laptop often breaks on a colleague’s, because their machine has different versions of
everything underneath. Docker is how the industry deals with that.
THIS SESSION ANSWERS

• What problem does Docker solve?
• What is a container, and how is it different from a virtual machine?
• Why run more than one container?
• How do you describe and build a container?

Knowledge check: The container boundary
How does an image differ from a running container? Which resources and files come from the host, and what
would you inspect when the app stops?

Before reading the definition, distinguish an image, a running container and its host. Describe where the
process runs and what filesystem it can see.
A definition must distinguish a container from a zip archive: the image packages files, while the runtime
starts processes with configured filesystem, resource and network boundaries.
Start instead with the alternative. Here’s a laptop (or any environment, such as a remote machine). It
has a set of key resources: RAM (the temporary, ephemeral memory), disk (persistent storage), CPU, and
a network connection. Suppose I have my git repository with some code (say my dbt code), and I just run
it directly on my laptop. What’s the problem?
1. Drift. There are lots of different laptops in the world, with different background environments and
different things installed. Even if two environments start from the same position, they eventually
drift apart. Code that runs on my machine may not run on yours.
2. Encapsulation (call it security). The code in my git folder can access anything else on my system,
such as passwords, configuration and other areas. And it cuts both ways: if the dbt project holds
Capital Group-specific keys and passwords, a virus on my machine can access those too.
3. Resource management.

The operating system doesn’t give very good control over how many

resources a piece of software uses. A misbehaving application can consume everything and make
the machine unusable. There’s also a diagnostic angle: if I declare that an application requires a
certain amount of disk and RAM, then if it’s using more than that, something is wrong with my
software.
So what we want is a uniform environment across many machines, an encapsulated environment where
everything inside the bundle can see itself but nothing outside, and carefully managed resources, so we
understand what our application actually requires.

The definition
Expert
Docker is both the container (the bundle) and the runtime, the program that runs containers. Here’s the
definition we use.
A container is an isolated process or group of processes running from an image, with its own filesystem view
and configured access to host resources. The image supplies user-space files and libraries; it does not contain
a running kernel. To run a container is to load that simulation into a runtime (the Docker runtime), inside which
your application runs.
An image packages user-space files and libraries. A Linux container shares a Linux host kernel; Docker Desktop
provides that host through a VM on Windows or macOS. It is not a complete simulated laptop.
When we run a container, we tell Docker how many resources to allocate: this container has no network
connection, this much RAM, 16 GB of disk, one CPU thread.
The image is the layered bundle; a container is one running instance of it. Removing that instance leaves the
image available to run again, while changes made only inside the removed container do not become part of
the image.

Containers vs virtual machines: the syscall explanation
This sounds like a virtual machine. So what’s the difference?
• A machine (your laptop, a server) has CPU, RAM, and storage.
• A virtual machine is software running on a machine that pretends to have a certain amount of CPU,
RAM, and storage, plus a complete copy of an operating system and everything else. A radical level
of isolation.
• A container is like a virtual machine, but it does not fully simulate the operating system. It simulates
having some CPU, RAM, and disk, but when it needs to do something like open a network connection,
it asks the host operating system to do it. It shares a large amount of functionality with the host
OS.
Mechanically: Linux provides syscalls, a set of functions the operating system offers (opening a file, for
example). A container simply asks the host operating system to run its native syscalls. A virtual machine
runs a guest kernel, which provides those system calls to guest applications; the hypervisor virtualises the
underlying hardware. Since all Linux systems open files basically the same way regardless of distribution,
containers don’t need to simulate that layer.
So a container is less isolated than a virtual machine, and that’s fine, because in most real deployments
people run Linux containers on Linux machines, where the container’s OS and the host’s OS are very
similar if not the same. The sharing is reasonable and adds very little overhead. The physical machine is
called the host, and the containers running on it are guests. Because each container is lightweight, you
can run many containers on one host cheaply.
Two distinctions help interpret the example.
• Can you run two different versions of Linux as two containers on one host? Yes, generally. Different
distributions share the same syscall interface, so the host can serve both.
• One caveat: if you’re on Windows and you want your system to fail the way Linux fails, you sometimes
want a Linux virtual machine. Running Linux containers on Windows (or macOS) can throw up errors
you wouldn’t see running Linux containers on a Linux host.

Container networking
Suppose we have multiple applications on the same system and want them to talk to each other. Between
two containers on the same laptop we establish a network connection: this container exposes a port (say
8000), that one exposes another (say 9000). Think of a port as an in-tray/out-tray inside each container.
The containers are allowed to swap messages via those trays over a pretend network connection between
them.
So on one laptop we can have multiple containers, each with a custom network configuration, seeing and
communicating with only the specific containers we configure. That gives an entire live environment on
a laptop with relatively high security: things inside the environment can’t see the laptop, and we have
fine-grained control over which containers talk to each other.

Why would a data creator need multiple containers?
Examples: multiple Airflow instances, multiple dbt instances; multiple branches of a feature; multiple
product lines, with one team making feature one of a data product, another team making feature two,
both live at once on the same server, each team seeing its own version.
More generally, multiple containers are incredibly common. Say you have a login service and a user-profile
service, and the login service needs to request something from the profile service. They run as different
containers. Why? Often because one team looks after the profile service and another the login service,
and they release their containers separately.
The structure of software is decided by institutional factors more than technical factors. Technology
tends to follow the organisation and structure of the business. (Databricks is often chosen mostly for
institutional reasons too.) With one team, you wouldn’t necessarily split things this way.

Development and production benefits
For development:
• Reproducibility — you can copy and paste your entire environment, cheaply. Copying a virtual
machine (VirtualBox, VMware) means a very large image that is slow to start and stop; containers
are much faster because they share the host OS.
• Everything installed at particular, pinned versions.
For production (live environments):
1. Isolation / security. On one Linux host you might run two data pipelines and a reporting/UI layer. You
want them fully isolated, not talking to each other and not seeing each other’s files. If an attacker
gets into one environment, they don’t automatically get into the others.
2. Modularity and encapsulation, which also stops teams tripping over each other. The big problem in
software is complexity. If each piece of software runs in its own small environment, teams can’t
casually see, use or modify another team’s code and files. Encapsulation means a capsule around
things (barriers and protections), and modularity means reuse and composition.
Then came the Docker revolution. Around 2015–2016, before Docker took hold, developers ran lots of
virtual machines locally, which was slow, while the live environment (where performance matters) looked
completely different. One of Docker’s big wins is similarity between dev and live, because containers are
efficient enough to use in both.

Inside a container
Docker plays two roles on the paved path:
Knowledge check: Editor and runtime
Where do files, shell commands and data processing live in your development environment? Which of those
locations would survive recreating the container?

1. Development — the container bundles all dependencies so code runs anywhere (the dev container).
2. Release — to make software live is to deploy the container. We release the bundle itself, so the
development environment mirrors the production environment.

What’s inside a container
An image is a packaged filesystem built from layers; a container is an instance created from it. The recipe
commonly specifies:
1. Operating-system user space — commonly Linux distributions and their libraries. The container
uses the kernel of its Linux host; Docker Desktop supplies a Linux VM when necessary on Windows
or macOS.
2. System packages
3. Your code (copied in, plus dependencies)
4. The command — the one command that runs when the container runs
From the outside we treat a container as if it were just that command. If the command were 2 + 3,
running the container would be an absurdly expensive way to get 5. OS, packages and code, all to run
one sum. So the commands are things worth the overhead: a dbt run, an Airflow server.

How the OS layering actually works
Docker itself includes client and daemon components. Docker Desktop normally runs Linux containers in
a Linux virtual machine on Windows or macOS. When the containerised code asks the OS to do something,
the Linux container runtime makes system calls against its Linux host kernel; Docker Desktop uses a Linux
VM on Windows/macOS rather than forwarding Linux system calls directly to a different host kernel, which
is why containers are so much cheaper than virtual machines (and why Windows quirks can leak through
into your “Linux” container). The system-call distinction explains why an image’s user-space files differ
from a complete virtual machine; keep that distinction when reading the deployment examples.

Does a data creator need to build containers?
The platform supplies the standard development image. The EDO repository you cloned is the standard
container, prepared by the EDO team for data product development. It has everything you need, and it’s
the one container you really deal with. You create dbt code inside it and submit to Git; the engineering
process that deploys containers to live systems (Harness) is outside the data creator’s scope.
But awareness matters: you’ll sit in meetings with dashboards, logs, and errors from these systems, and
knowing how they work helps you integrate with the teams deploying your code. (And besides, Docker is
one of the tools on the course, so we teach it.)

Runtime controls: the other reason Docker matters
When running a container you can allocate its resources from the host: RAM (temporary memory), storage
(long-term), and CPU/compute. Take a laptop with 32 GB of RAM, 8 cores and 1 TB of storage. The
container is told which slice of that it may have. At its simplest a container does two things, compute (2
+ 3) and run a command (dbt run), and the limits decide how much of the machine that command gets.

136

+44 (0)20 3583 0972 | info@decoded.com | decoded.com

DECODED

Wednesday — Data systems and dbt

• Locally, resource limits can keep one development workload from consuming the host’s available
capacity.
• In production it’s the main event: physical servers run many containers, and resource limits keep
applications well-behaved. If a container capped at 2GB of RAM starts demanding more, something
is wrong with it, and it fails alone instead of starving the host and bringing the system down.
• Networking is the most important control:

containers can be restricted to talk only to the

containers they’re allowed to. Traditional development installs everything on one machine where
every programme can see every file. In a live system with high-value data, you assume you will be
hacked, so a compromised container that’s forbidden from communicating with anything else has
strictly limited impact. That’s defence in depth. Put up as many barriers as you can and keep the
blast radius small.

What is a dev container?
A dev container is a Docker container plus a VS Code feature (plugin) that runs VS Code inside the
container. VS Code starts itself inside the container as if the container were your laptop. Your terminal
executes inside the container (no need for docker run -it to get a bash prompt), files you create are
created inside the container, and every command picks up the pre-wired configuration. It’s not touching
your host OS.
What’s in the EDO dev container:
• Mise (short for mise en place) — a cross-language meta package manager: one tool, configured once,
that drives system packages, pip, npm, Maven and the rest. The project configuration pins tools and
names its setup tasks.
• Astronomer — Airflow wrapped in a container… inside our container. Containers within containers
is strange and somewhat fragile; more on why on Thursday.
• Databricks CLI — needed by dbt, and by Catalyst: when Catalyst runs a query for you, it goes through
the Databricks CLI.
• Docker (inside Docker) and dbt.

Where did your work go?
One consequence of “your terminal executes inside the container” is worth a minute, because it
determines whether a rebuild preserves your work. A container’s writable layer is thrown away when
that container is removed or replaced. Stopping and restarting the same container normally keeps it.
Rebuilding or recreating the container is what usually loses it.
The exception is the workspace mount. The dev container maps your cloned repo folder on the laptop
into the container (the workspaceMount setting in .devcontainer/devcontainer.json), so files in that
folder live on the host and survive any number of rebuilds. In raw Docker the same mechanism is a
volume flag:
docker run -v /Users/you/edo-repo:/workspace my-image

That line runs the container and makes my laptop’s edo-repo folder appear inside it at /workspace. Writes
under /workspace land on the laptop; writes anywhere else land in the container and die with it.
Check where every edited file was saved before removing or rebuilding a container. Files under the
mounted repository survive; files in an unmounted home directory or /tmp may not. Verify an agent’s
reported path in the filesystem.

Reading a Dockerfile
A Dockerfile is the build recipe.

Read its instructions to distinguish the base image, installed

dependencies, copied files, runtime user, working directory and startup command. The example includes
these common instructions:
• FROM — which image to start from. An image is a blueprint/template for containers (ten containers
can share one image). Here: the official Airflow image, so we begin from a template that already
contains Linux, Airflow, and its libraries.
• LABEL — tagging the container with metadata about what it’s for.
• RUN apt-get update … — updating/installing system packages (apt-get marks this as Debian/
Ubuntu Linux).
• USER airflow — switching to the airflow user.
• WORKDIR — setting the folder we’ll copy things into.
• COPY requirements.txt + RUN pip install … — the Python dependency list, copied in and installed.
• COPY … — the application code.
• CMD — the one command the container runs: the Airflow server.
• EXPOSE 8080 — opens the networking: “you’re allowed to plug a cable into this container on port
8080.” Strictly, EXPOSE only records the port. The actual mapping from container port to laptop port
happens when the container is run, with docker run -p 8080:8080, which is why, on Thursday, the
Airflow UI running inside a container appears in your browser at localhost:8080.

Anatomy of a Dockerfile
How do we describe and build a container? With a Dockerfile, a file that specifies how the container is
built from its layers. It’s built up line by line: each line (typically, not always) builds a layer in the bundle.
Walking through the example Dockerfile in the challenge material:
Knowledge check: Build and run
Which Dockerfile instructions affect image contents and which select the running command? Why could a
build succeed while the app still fails?

• FROM python:3.11-slim — the base image, and a very unusual name when you’re new to this. A
base image supplies the filesystem layers your image extends. The name reads as if we’re installing
a Python package; we’re not. We’re importing an entire Linux system (for a -slim image, Debian
Linux) with a full set of system packages and a Python 3.11 environment. The image is simply named
after the one key package it carries, to tell the reader that Python is the point of this container. A
less confusing name would be “Linux + Python 3.11”. Starting points are named after the thing they’re
most useful for: there are base images for Airflow, for dbt, for git. FROM some git image would mean
“load an entire operating system with git installed”.
• Where do base images come from? A registry, a store of published images that docker pull
fetches from, layer by layer. Docker Hub is the public one; large companies typically run an
internal mirror of the images they’ve approved, and the paved-path images come from CG’s
own infrastructure rather than the open internet (the specifics belong to the platform team).
Pulling layer by layer explains two things you may see today: the first build on a machine
is slow, because the base layers have to come down the network (simultaneous first-time
pulls can saturate a shared connection), while every later build is fast, because the layers
are cached locally. It also explains a familiar failure: a VPN that intercepts traffic can break
pulls, because the connection to the registry doesn’t trust the VPN’s certificates. Which is the
practical argument for the FROM line you’ll actually meet at CG: a CG-approved base image
138

+44 (0)20 3583 0972 | info@decoded.com | decoded.com

DECODED

Wednesday — Data systems and dbt

with the SSL certificates already baked in, so everything built on top of it can talk through the
corporate network without each team re-solving the certificate problem.
• WORKDIR /app — our working folder; all subsequent commands run from /app and copy things into
it.
• COPY — copies everything from the local location into the app folder within the container (there’s a
slightly strange interaction between the WORKDIR and COPY lines that we won’t unpick here).
• CMD python summarize.py — the command Docker runs when the container starts: once the
operating system and everything else is established, this is what runs at the very end.
That’s the whole example file. Three more instructions turn up in almost every production Dockerfile, so
learn to recognise them:
• RUN pip install -r requirements.txt — a command executed while building, its result frozen into
a layer. This is where dependencies get installed: RUN happens once, at build time, and everyone
who runs the image afterwards gets the already-installed result. (CMD is the opposite case. Nothing
happens at build time, and it’s executed at run time.)
• USER appuser — up to this line, everything in the container runs as root. Switching to an unprivileged
user before the application starts means that if the application is compromised, the attacker gets
an unprivileged account inside an isolated container. It’s the encapsulation argument from earlier
again. Production Dockerfiles almost always do this; toy examples usually skip it.
• EXPOSE 8080 — a documentation line. It records which port the application intends to listen on and
opens nothing. As in the first walkthrough, docker run -p 8080:8080 does the actual mapping at
run time. (The in-tray/out-tray from the networking section is created by -p; EXPOSE only labels the
tray.)
Treat the versioned image and its runtime configuration together: the image packages the pipeline
dependencies, while mounts, credentials and reachable external services determine what the running
process can use.
Will you ever write one? Mostly no, as above. The supplied project includes a configured Dockerfile.
For live work, confirm the current base image, certificates and support responsibility with the assigned
platform team. A data creator reads Dockerfiles, and dbt is the core skill.

The eight commands: live demo
You’ve been using Docker Desktop since the environment setup. The command line does the same
operations without the buttons. Here are the eight commands, run once on screen against the example
container, with the Docker Desktop tab each one matches:
• docker build -t summarize . — read the Dockerfile in this folder, build the layers, tag the result
summarize. This is what fills Docker Desktop’s Images tab.

• docker images — list every image built or pulled onto this machine: the CLI form of that same
Images tab.
• docker run summarize — load the bundle into the runtime and execute its CMD. (The example
container runs its script and exits, so for the exec step below start one that stays alive: docker run
-dt summarize bash.)

• docker ps — what is running right now; add -a to include containers that have stopped. The
Containers tab.
• docker logs <name> — everything the container has printed. When a container dies, this is the first
place to look.
• docker exec -it <name> bash — a shell inside the running container. Run cat /etc/os-release:
it prints the Linux distribution, and there is the operating system the theory promised. You are on a

Mac or Windows laptop, and inside the container is whichever Linux the base image chose (the file
tells you which, so you don’t have to guess from the image name). Look around; exit to leave.
• docker stop <name> — shut the container down.
• docker rm <name> — remove the stopped container. The image stays (docker rmi removes that),
so stopping and removing costs nothing you can’t rebuild.
The challenges use only these commands, and tomorrow you’ll diagnose the Astronomer environment
with ps, logs and exec.

Kubernetes: infrastructure as configuration
Kubernetes coordinates deployed containers through declared desired state. It controls where workloads
run, how their instances are grouped and how unhealthy instances are replaced. This explains part of the
platform behind the release demonstrations; the assigned local Docker and dbt activities do not require
cluster provisioning.
Knowledge check: Workload orchestration
What does a shared platform need to coordinate beyond one local container? How do workload placement and
data-task dependencies differ?

Orchestration coordinates separate work. Airflow orders tasks and observes their execution; Kubernetes
places and manages container workloads. The two graphs solve different problems. A model dependency
does not tell Kubernetes which nodes to use, and a Kubernetes deployment does not establish a dataquality rule.
A pod is Kubernetes’ unit for one or more closely related containers that share specified runtime resources,
including a network namespace and configured volumes. Group containers according to their lifecycle
and communication requirements; do not put unrelated products in one pod just because the same team
owns them. The scheduler places pods on nodes, while controllers reconcile declared configuration with
observed state.
For a product platform, configuration can describe a workload’s image, replicas, resource requests and
limits, environment, storage mounts, service access and recovery behavior. Review that configuration
alongside the application’s expected files and connections. A container can be healthy as a process
while its output is incomplete or late; the data promise still needs separate checks.
A local Docker command starts a scoped instance for development or diagnosis. A shared cluster needs
placement, isolation and recovery across many instances and teams. The platform team owns that
infrastructure boundary. When you review a deployment demonstration, identify which image/version is
selected and what evidence shows that the workload is ready. Do not treat the diagram as permission
to deploy.
Versioned configuration makes a change reviewable: inspect the diff, required settings and chosen
environment before applying it. It can help reproduce a workload in another prepared environment,
but portability depends on external services, identity, storage and infrastructure capabilities. Kubernetes
does not by itself provision every cloud account, network or managed service; tools such as Terraform
address infrastructure responsibilities shown separately in the platform material.
Expert
Amazon EKS is a managed Kubernetes service; ECS is a separate AWS container service. The supplied platform
examples discuss both and a Capital Group managed-platform direction called Helix. Use current internal
platform documentation and the responsible architecture team to choose an approved service; a historical
screenshot is not a current approval list. Harness and deployment conventions can vary by team. The creator’s

dbt run builds selected models; running tests afterwards leaves a gap in which downstream models may

Case study: A successful build with an incorrect population
Situation. A fund-exposure model builds successfully and produces a plausible total. The lookup table contains
two versions of one fund key, so enrichment duplicates a holding. A consumer asks whether the reported

Repair the selected lookup grain, then run the negative case and the independent

reconciliation again.
Reasoning. The model’s own total and a downstream total can agree because both inherit the same duplicate.
A green command reports execution; independent evidence checks the intended business result.

review below; advanced fan-out repair belongs to Diagnose a join fan-out before repair–Write reconciliation
that detects the negative case in the separately timed clinic.

Repeatable development and small tests
A useful development loop makes a small change, executes it in an isolated workspace and inspects the
result. Git retains the version and diff; dbt selects the model/test scope; the prepared local runtime
keeps one learner’s experiment from overwriting another’s result. Each tool makes the evidence easier
to inspect without deciding whether the business rule is correct.

Tests alongside a build
Tests shorten the interval between an incorrect change and its diagnosis. Choose a test for a plausible
failure: a required identifier, duplicated row key, invalid category, orphan relationship or wrong total.
Keep a known negative case so the test demonstrates that it can fail. Run the selected model while
it is unfinished, then widen the build to include all required upstream and downstream checks before
handoff.

Layers and reusable transformations
Staging preserves a source’s meaning while normalizing names, types and units.
transformations express reusable joins and calculations.

Intermediate

A mart supports the consumer’s stated

decision and grain. Use the layer and alignment table to explain both technical structure and business
purpose; a folder name alone cannot establish either.

Dependency edges and compiled relations
ref and source resolve configured relations, and references between models declare the dbt dependency

graph. They let dbt order a selected build and let a reviewer trace a source-to-consumer path. See the
dependency explanation and macro example. A dependency edge identifies what a model reads; it does
not establish key uniqueness, freshness or correct units.

Reference question: history and bitemporal requirements
A history requirement must name the time it describes. Business-valid time answers when a fact applied;
record/system time answers when the system learned or stored it. A requirement to reproduce both
perspectives needs an explicit bitemporal design. A dbt snapshot preserves changing records through
validity intervals; do not assume that one snapshot interval automatically implements both timelines.
The snapshot and history reference introduces observed-state history. Historical data and bitemporal
loading develops two-clock corrections, master and balance grains, supplier-file policies, and recovery.
Its temporal-history clinic is optional and separately timed; the protected dbt practice block remains
focused on the assigned Portfolio Analytics tasks.

Reference question: reusable SQL macros
A macro turns a named reusable operation into compiled SQL. For example, a shared date conversion can
make a legacy field rule explicit in several models. Inspect the compiled query and test representative
inputs; hiding repetition in a macro does not validate the transformation. Macros and incremental/history
variants are advanced reference topics, outside minimum Phase 1 completion.

Choosing a transformation tool for the workload
dbt is designed around analytical transformations and their dependencies. A low-latency transactional
service needs a workload decision covering concurrent updates, application interfaces and latency. Do
not treat an analytical model as an application’s transactional write path solely because both use SQL.
Record the operating requirements and involve the appropriate engineering role.

Review challenge: find the defects in a generated model
Knowledge check: Review the specification
Which mapping decisions would you trace into the proposed SQL first? What would convince you that its prose
summary describes the actual query?

No code is written in this challenge. You get an STTM extract and a model presented as agent output,
and you mark every place the model breaks the mapping. Work in pairs, ~30 minutes; you only need to
read SQL, so non-technical participants pair with technical ones and interrogate the STTM side.

The agent produced the model below, with this summary: “I’ve implemented the integration model
as specified: renamed the columns, rescaled weights to 0–1, handled nulls, and joined the sector

with holdings as (
select * from {{ ref('stg_holdings') }}
),

select * from {{ ref('stg_security_reference') }}
)

h.fund_id,
s.sector,
sum(h.weight / 100)
as weight,
max(h.as_of_date)
as as_of_date
from holdings h
join security_ref s
on h.security_name = s.security_name
where h.weight > 0
group by h.fund_id, s.sector

Brief

OUTPUTS A reviewed generated change

The challenge takes about 35 minutes. Ideally, use the setup skill to create a new dbt project. If that hasn’t

the one you know works. You need to end up with a new model, and a new project is optional. If you finish

Practical checks before requesting a generated change:
• The setup skill walks you through creating a new project rather than silently overwriting an existing
one.
• Files Catalyst creates may land in odd places (e.g. under the Catalyst artifacts folder). The Catalyst
folder is just a folder of files, so keep your projects somewhere else.
• A selected model may interpret the same skill/context differently across runs. Inspect whether it
asks for missing facts, changes the requested scope or chooses an unsupported default. Judge the
observed change against your contract and evidence rather than a vendor stereotype.

Amendment: verify with git before you accept
After Catalyst has generated or modified models, and before you accept, commit, or build on anything,
run two commands in the project folder.
• git status lists every file the agent created, modified, or deleted. Compare that list to the agent’s
own summary of what it did. The summary is generated text like any other output, so it has the
self-reporting problem from Tuesday’s AI-agents talk. Trust the file list over the summary.
• git diff shows the exact line-by-line changes. Read them. The specific task in this amendment
is to find one thing the agent did that its summary did not mention, such as a renamed column,
an edited schema.yml entry, a deleted test, a changed materialization. In practice there is nearly
always at least one.

And when the diff shows a change you don’t want: git restore <file> puts a modified file back to its

Cases: reviewing a generated change
Case study: A skill invocation with incomplete context
Situation. Two creators request a dbt model using the same skill. One supplies the project, source fields and
expected grain; the other leaves those decisions unstated. The resulting changes take different paths, including
clarification questions or guessed file locations.
Decision and reasoning. Inspect the context, requested output and actual diff before comparing the results. A
skill supplies instructions to a probabilistic model; its name does not guarantee identical behavior. Clarify the
missing fact and rerun a bounded request.
Lesson. Retain the prompt/context and the reviewed change. Do not equate a skill invocation with a completed
requirement.

Case study: Fast generation increases the review workload
Situation. An agent creates a large model set and converts an Excel input into CSV. It also reduces the sample
to 1,000 rows. The build succeeds, but the consumer expected complete coverage.
Decision. Confirm which transformations and sampling limits were requested. Review a small representative
change first, compare the full expected population and retain excluded-row evidence before expanding the
build.
Reasoning and lesson. File conversion, successful execution and plausible summaries do not establish coverage.
A small training sample can be useful when it is explicit; silently applying it to a product changes the promise.
The creator owns the units, membership, tests and handoff limitation, including review effort when generation
is faster than inspection.

Learning Review
Retrieve the distinction between skill instructions, supplied context and generated behavior. Apply it to a
model that builds successfully after dropping part of its input. Check git status and the complete diff
against the requested files, population and tests. Name one independent result that could reject the agent’s
summary and one unresolved assumption with an owner.

Primary variant: the contract-to-tests round trip
Use the group’s own design artefacts instead of a generic new model. Feed Catalyst the data contract
your group generated with Catalyst on Tuesday and ask for two things: the schema.yml tests that enforce
its data-quality section, and the source freshness configuration that enforces its arrival SLA (freshness
itself is covered on Thursday morning). Then review the output against the contract, sorting every promise
in the quality and SLA sections into three piles:
• Promises that became tests. Key rules become unique and not_null, and categorical rules become
accepted_values. Range rules (exposures between 0 and 1) become a range test, and the arrival

SLA becomes warn_after and error_after on the source.
• Promises that were mangled in translation. Typical finds: a completeness threshold of 99.5% silently
turned into not_null, which demands 100%; a range rule attached to the wrong column; a test placed
on a staging model when the contract’s promise is about the published table. Each one is plausible
YAML that enforces something other than what was agreed, the same kind of defect you looked for
in the review challenge.

Review challenge: find the defects in a generated model

Back to the section

Generated-model review — defect key

Defect key and evidence limits
1. Wrong join key, silently dropping rows.

The STTM joins on security_id; the model joins

on security_name, a name field, which will not match cleanly between a vendor feed and
internal reference data. And it is an inner join where the STTM specifies a left join with an
'UNCLASSIFIED' default, so every unmatched security’s holdings vanish from the output with

no error, no log, no rejected row.
2. A filter that deletes the most important rows. where h.weight > 0 removes short positions,
which the STTM declares valid. Tuesday’s AI-agents talk warned about this kind of script, one
that does everything right except delete the rows you need tomorrow.
3. Missing null handling. The same predicate makes null weights disappear silently (null > 0
is not true, so the row is filtered). The STTM requires nulls to be rejected to an error table;
nothing in this model routes anything anywhere. The rows are simply gone.
4. Grain broken by a stray GROUP BY. The target grain is fund × security × date; the group by h.
fund_id, s.sector collapses it to fund × sector. security_id does not even appear in the

output, and max(h.as_of_date) papers over any mixture of dates in the input.
5. The summary is false in checkable ways. “Handled nulls”? It deleted them. “All rows are
preserved”? The inner join and the filter both drop rows. “At the fund/security/date grain”?
The GROUP BY changed the grain. One thing it did do correctly: the rescale (weight / 100)
matches the STTM. A reviewer who checks only that line will pass the model.
Return to the mapping and generated-model brief.

Knowledge check: What does an arrow promise?
Which part of a pipeline diagram describes data movement, and which part describes a prerequisite? Which
missing input would make you stop publication?

Group challenge
OUTPUTS A flip-chart flow of your pipeline

As a group, choose one real pipeline that someone at your table works with and draw its flow on flip-chart
paper. Use the scheduled morning activity slot; reserve the final part for comparing dependencies and checks.
Answer these on the drawing.
• What must happen first? What can happen at the same time? Which steps must wait on others?
• Where should checks happen between steps?
• What happens if something is missing or late? What happens on success vs failure?

Use the drawing to review an Airflow graph later. Explain each dependency so colleagues with different
roles can assess its business consequence.
Case study: Source readiness and delivery
Cases: source readiness and delivery
Integrated positions product. Sources: IMAP (positions) and Compass (the portfolio-master system, supporting
different roll-ups such as account, segment and equity or fixed-income portions, to measure performance),
plus reference data (asset classification, country, security details). Ingestions are daily: positions land ~9–10
PM, reference data ~8 PM. The goal is the final integrated positions table by ~12 AM (midnight) so downstream
consumers can start. Daily SLAs were defined for IMAP and Compass availability. Data is staged into IPAC tables
(IPAC acting as the centralised calculation engine), positions and portfolios are integrated (active portfolios
holding positions as of a date), first/last-trade calculations run on the integrated set, and a file publication is
broadcast to Caspian and on to consumers.
Checks are split into in-motion rules (duplicate checks, null and primary-key checks and contract conformance,
which stop the pipeline if they fail) and at-rest rules (value checks, e.g. return percentages must sum to 100%,
weight percentages in range). In-motion failures are rare and usually system issues; when they happen, whoever
is on call gets paged. On missing/late data, a notification goes to a wide distribution list of consumers of the
data. Checksum/file-hash validation detects a changed transfer. In this example it belongs to the NFS transfer
boundary, while row-level rules belong to ingestion and curation.
Advisor-level view. Building an integrated advisor-level view (a row = a 360° view of an advisor: AUM, activity
involvement, etc.) from individual data sets already standing and QA’d in Caspian, plus benchmark survey data
to be added. Mostly daily (some weekly) SLAs; the pipeline waits on all of them before triggering. Staging, then
joins/integrations/transformations, with completeness checks in motion and a proposed escalation process
with the operations team when an SLA is missed. A useful discovery question is whether consumers need a
combined product that the existing stable sources do not yet supply.
Market-close price delivery. After US market close (~1 PM Pacific), a third-party vendor publishes end-ofday prices into a shared Snowflake database. An internal Snowflake notebook runs a batch of queries and
cross-references, writes the results to a CSV, and sends it downstream to consuming applications.
Morningstar ingestion contract. A pipeline design identifies the source systems and primary keys for dataquality purposes, then defined the data contract per data set (four Morningstar data sets, e.g. holdings) with DQ
rules (e.g. completeness ≥ 99.5%, often set to 100%), dependencies between ingestions, arrival SLAs (holdings
by 8 AM; prices/FX ingestion from 6:30 using T-1 close; benchmark data needed only for the later benchmarkrelative/alpha calculations, so not blocking), schemas, and operational support when files are missing.
Checks run at both the ingestion and curation layers. Critical failures stop processing and alert consumers,
and the pipeline is re-run after a fix. Non-critical checks run weekly for statistics without blocking the flow.

Review a pipeline diagram by classifying every box as a task, rule or design decision, then label its arrows.

Figure 52: Morningstar task order: arrival and contract checks precede transformation. Critical failure
stops the run and alerts consumers; successful checks allow calculation, publication and notification.

Source freshness as an SLI
The Morningstar contract includes a measurable promise: holdings arrive by 8 AM. Wednesday defined
the SLI as the indicator you measure to know whether you’re hitting the agreement; dbt ships one for
arrival SLAs, and it takes four lines of YAML on the source declaration:
sources:
- name: morningstar
tables:
- name: holdings
loaded_at_field: loaded_at
freshness:
warn_after: {count: 24, period: hour}
error_after: {count: 28, period: hour}

loaded_at_field names the timestamp column written when rows land. Running dbt source freshness

takes the newest loaded_at in the table and compares its age to the thresholds. For this example, a
check after 8 AM against a previous delivery older than 24 hours identifies a late arrival. An age threshold
is not by itself a proof of the business date: verify the expected delivery identity and timestamp as
well. That’s the warn_after line. Older than 28 hours means it’s now badly late and downstream models
shouldn’t build on stale data. That’s error_after.
The thresholds come straight from the contract’s arrival SLA. That’s why Wednesday’s contract-to-tests
round trip had Catalyst generate this block from the SLA section, and why you check its arithmetic
yourself.
This afternoon, Airflow decides when things run. Source freshness measures whether the data arrived
when it was promised. Airflow will happily start the 10 PM run on time whether the file arrived or not. Run
dbt source freshness as the first step, and the pipeline notices the late file before it builds anything

on top of it.
Learning Review
Retrieve the three arrow meanings without looking at the diagram: data flow, task order and an external
delivery dependency. For a holdings feed due at 8 AM, place a source-arrival check before transformation and
explain which tasks must stop when it fails.
Self-check: your drawing has one meaning per arrow style, a named input owner, a critical gate before
consumption, an explicit restart step and an evidence check on the recovered output. Explain why a 24-hour
freshness threshold alone may not identify the expected business-date delivery.

The DAG file, in full, is the Cosmos form pointed at Wednesday’s project, with the schedule line set from
the SLA:
from datetime import datetime
from cosmos import DbtDag, ProjectConfig

positions_dbt = DbtDag(
dag_id="positions_dbt",
project_config=ProjectConfig("/usr/local/airflow/dbt/positions"),
schedule="0 22 * * *",
# the drawn arrival SLA, as one cron line
start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
catchup=False,
)

Every model in the project becomes its own task that can retry by itself, and the tests run alongside the
models they test. The retries and callbacks from earlier go in through default_args, as in any other DAG.
Harness releases this repository, and Astro runs what was released. That’s two separate cycles, and the
release session later today keeps them apart. One is the release: someone changed the code, so it gets
reviewed, approved and deployed. The other is the run: 10 PM came round again. The running system
only changes when a change to this repo is released. After that, the schedule line runs it every night with
no human involved.

Challenge zero: the Airflow UI tour
Once astro dev start has the local instance running, open the address it prints in a browser. In the
challenge repo that’s a per-project hostname on port 6563, and a plain Astro project uses localhost:8080.
Everyone does this tour before writing or generating anything. Why? Because most data creators will
read this screen far more often than they’ll ever write a DAG. This is where you find out whether last
night’s run delivered.
• Grid view. Each column is one scheduled run and each cell is one task in that run. Green succeeded,
red failed. A missed morning delivery is a red cell with a date on it, and you answer “when did this
last work?” by scanning left.
• Graph view. This is your flip-chart diagram as the >> lines encode it, including which tasks sit in
parallel. If the picture doesn’t match what you meant to draw, the dependency line is wrong.
• A task’s logs. Click a task instance, then Logs. That’s the output of that one task for that one run.
It’s the first place to look at a red cell, and where a failed dbt run prints which test or model broke.
• Pausing and unpausing. The toggle beside the DAG name. A paused DAG doesn’t get its scheduled
runs. Triggering it by hand is a separate button, and what that does to a paused DAG depends on
your Airflow version. New DAGs usually arrive paused, so “my DAG isn’t running” usually means “my
DAG isn’t unpaused”.
• Clearing a failed task to rerun it. Select the failed task instance and choose Clear. Airflow resets
that task so the scheduler runs it again. Downstream tasks are only included if you tick them,
so check the run, the task IDs and the options before you confirm. This is the everyday fix once
the upstream problem is sorted, and repeat it only after checking the task’s replay behavior and
publication boundary. Verify that a repeat does not duplicate side effects and that the recovered
business output matches the expected state.

If the environment misbehaves
When the prepared runtime fails to start, record the failing command and environment before applying a
targeted repair.
• Read the first error before rebuilding. Check the configured runtime, dependencies, paths and
service logs. Preserve learner files before recreating a container; remove only the identified stale
training resources. A separate clean clone can help isolate a setup problem without discarding the
existing attempt.
• Working out of OneDrive breaks permissions. Clone to the local file system (Documents or similar)
instead.
• Airflow does not really work natively on Windows. Many operators use bash, which is a Mac/Linux
tool, so on Windows you must use the container, which is what you’re doing. One root cause found
on Windows laptops was a .env file with Windows carriage-return line endings being parsed by bash;
hidden characters differ between files written on Mac and Windows, and Tuesday’s core.autocrlf
setting is the fix.
• After a rebuild, rerun the documented settings setup and check the new terminal/worker
configuration. Do not copy credentials into review evidence.
• For registry or certificate failures, retain the reported host and failing operation and use the approved
image/network setup. Do not change the Astro base image merely because another laptop had a
similar symptom.
• Check where work is saved before stopping or rebuilding a container. Files under the workspace
mount survive a rebuild; anything written elsewhere inside the container does not.
Plan on roughly an hour and a half of self-paced challenge time.

Count the containers: what astro dev start actually started
With the local instance running, open a terminal on the host (not inside the dev container) and run docker
ps. The challenge runs Airflow 3, so you should see five long-running containers. Match each one to its

job:
• the scheduler — the part that decides what runs and when; the actual orchestrator;
• the dag-processor — reads the files in dags/ and turns them into DAGs the scheduler knows about;
• the api-server — serves the UI you just toured;
• the triggerer — looks after tasks that are waiting for something (the deferred waits that sensors
can hand over to it);
• postgres — Airflow’s metadata database. Every run, task state and retry count lives here, and the
grid view is drawn from it.
An older Airflow 2 project shows a webserver in place of the api-server, and no separate dag-processor.
Wednesday separated container roles by teams and product lines. Here’s a second answer, running on
your own machine: one application split into parts that work together. Astronomer’s local runtime is a
ready-made multi-container setup, and the development-container and Astro-runtime boundary remains
explicit. The Astro CLI writes the container configuration and starts the set, which is the job a Docker
Compose file does by hand.
Stretch, for those who did Wednesday’s Docker stretch goals: find the Compose configuration the CLI
generates and read the service definitions (the CLI’s help output lists the export command for your
version).

Closing challenge: generate a DAG, then interrogate it
This block ends the way Wednesday’s dbt review did: an agent writes something and you check it. In pairs,
run the generate-dag Catalyst skill against your group’s flip-chart pipeline from this morning. Describe
the tasks, their order, the schedule and what should happen on failure, and let the skill produce the file.
generate-dag writes YAML for the DAG’s name, schedule, defaults, dependencies and generic tasks. A

person or a template then picks the operators that actually get deployed, so open what the skill produced
and read it.

The skill supports several patterns and production controls. Read these before the orchestration request so
the offered capability is not mistaken for assigned course scope. The course follows its offered v2/Cosmos
route; production callbacks, provisioning and alternative carriers remain outside that assignment.

Before you run anything, check it against this list:
• Does the schedule match the SLA you drew? Decode the cron line by hand. If the skill reached for
@daily, remember that means midnight, and check whether midnight is what your drawing says.

• Are there retries, with a plausible retry_delay? Or does one dropped connection go straight to a
failure?
• Is there an on_failure_callback? The supplied production convention routes a Datadog event to
the responsible team. The assigned v2 local callback records the observation in its log; it does not
configure Datadog or demonstrate an on-call page.
• Is catchup set, either way? If it’s missing, the replay behaviour is a default nobody chose.
• Do the >> lines reproduce your arrows? Look for anything you drew in parallel that came out serial,
and the reverse.
Correct the review findings and identify the emitted carrier: Python, dag-factory or an existing blueprint
framework. The assigned v2 starter uses its provided Python DAG and local execution command. A
generated YAML carrier is not executable merely because it looks plausible; keep it as reference unless
the prepared runtime explicitly supports it. Optional extensions follow the core evidence gate and use an
isolated training copy. Review the schedule, retries and failure behavior before any additional execution.
On the paved path, CI checks every DAG for <domain>__<dataset>__<frequency> naming, an on_failure_
callback, all five MDS tags, no email_on_failure and at least one retry. cimon runs those checks on each

change in Harness, and scaphe scans the whole estate for DAGs that have drifted. Check the platform
docs for the current list. A DAG can run happily while failing all five. Missing callbacks and tags fail
silently, because no routable Datadog event reaches on-call.

Review your use of AI and Catalyst
Review how Catalyst has affected your product work: which decisions improved, which assumptions
needed correction, and which results you can now verify without relying on the agent.
What hints would you share? Write down the two or three you’d give a colleague starting this course
next month.
Exploration versus exploitation. Is the request too broad or too narrow? Every session with an agent sits
somewhere between exploring (wide questions, to find out what is possible) and exploiting (driving one
known approach to completion). Both are right at different moments. The trouble starts when you don’t
notice which one you’re doing. Go too broad and nothing ships. Go too narrow and you commit to the
first plausible answer.

Check the review workload.

Fast generation can create more assumptions and changes than you

have time to inspect. If useful outputs arrive inconsistently, narrow the request and compare several
representative results rather than accepting one impressive answer.
How can you correct the pattern?

Two remedies.

First, ask whether you’re getting good results

consistently. One impressive answer tells you very little. Second, simplify the output and focus on one
thing at a time. In practice that means mixing Catalyst with manual work, which the Docker and dbt
blocks already asked of you.
Four prompts worth keeping, because each one gets the agent to dig into the assumptions:
• “Ask me some questions about things that have been assumed.”
• “Give me a plan to do X.”
• “Explain to me what I need to know in order to plan to do X.”
• “What are the things I’m missing?”
What is the role of the human in the loop? Tuesday introduced what humans bring that LLMs don’t:
purpose, judgment and taste. Tuesday’s talk, “The Human Role When Working With AI Agents”, turned
that into a way of reviewing what an agent hands you. Now use the same habit on yourself. Notice what
heavy use is doing to your own attention and assumptions, and correct for it.

What the client gate proves
Use mise run challenge:v2:verify-starter airflow phase-one-certified to check the supplied
starting state.

A baseline pass is not completion.

The phase’s connected verification needs fresh

scheduled run/task identities, the controlled failure and repair, and independent Databricks checks.
Start the prepared Astro runtime and use the address it prints. Select your owned DAG, run and task
instance before inspecting logs. The final publication_evidence task records a checked training handoff;
it does not grant access or register a production marketplace listing.

Controlled failure, recovery and replay
Work on a disposable training copy and your own training schema. First run the working path and check
the output yourself. Then break it the way the instructor shows you, and keep the original file so you can
put it back. Note which task fails, what the log says and which tasks after it don’t run. Those later tasks
show as upstream_failed, which means the failure above them blocked them.
Fix the cause before you retry. Pick the DAG, run and task instances you mean, and read the clear dialog
or command options before you confirm. A calendar-day range can include several runs; use the run/
task identity to establish which execution the clear action should affect. Don’t use an unscoped clear
command as a shortcut. If a task writes or publishes data, work out what happens when it runs twice
before you include the downstream tasks.
After the fix, check the task state and the data. A task can go green and still run the wrong query, or
finish without doing any work. Compare the model outputs with the contract checks, then run it again
and show the rerun doesn’t duplicate or corrupt anything. Keep the run IDs and model versions so you
can show which run produced what.

Tools you watch but don’t configure
Some of today is about tools you’ll see but won’t touch: Datadog, Harness, Kafka, S3 and Lambda. On
the paved path, a task that fails after its retries calls its on_failure_callback, which sends an event to
Datadog, and Datadog routes it to a person. The challenge DAG has its callbacks in the same place, but
they only write a line to the task log. The challenge runs Airflow 3, so its DAG has no sla= argument
either. The two-minute practice timetable demonstrates scheduled execution. A production deadline
needs its own business timezone, source-arrival promise and retry allowance.

The product
• Problem: reporting teams (INA, and soon others) were working from scattered data in sandbox
environments with no single source of truth for institutional client data.
• Goal: centralise client, product, assets, client-interaction, opportunity and territory data into a single
source of truth for institutional data (retail to follow), consumed initially by two teams and growing.
• Sources: data producers already registered in Caspian (Capital Group’s enterprise data lake) via
ingestion DAGs owned by the source teams.

The stack and execution boundaries
• Airflow orchestrates the curation pipelines. The territory DAG opens with three or four dependencycheck tasks that call the Airflow REST API or metadata to verify that upstream ingestion DAGs, such
as the CDM team’s, ran successfully within a time constraint. Only then does curation start. If
a dependency fails, alerts fire to the team and to the business, and processing stops rather than
joining against wrong data.
• Databricks runs the actual work: Airflow triggers a Databricks job (e.g. the territory job), whose
tasks are the same dbt commands learners had been running by hand, dbt seed and dbt run for
the models. Jobs are defined in YAML using Databricks Asset Bundles, which deploy them into dev/
SQA/prod. (A design review asks If orchestration lives in Airflow on purpose, to avoid Databricks
lock-in, why is there orchestration-looking YAML on the Databricks side? The answer was that all
dependencies resolve in Airflow, and the bundle YAML only defines the jobs that run the dbt models.)
• Harness provides CI/CD: automating the path from integrated code to released product. Airflow
automates scheduled data workflows; Harness automates software releases. Release automation
and data orchestration have different owners and evidence requirements.

Pipelines exist per

environment (dev, SQA, prod), and separate IaC pipelines (Terraform) create the infrastructure itself,
meaning clusters, warehouses and the S3 buckets for each medallion layer.
• Storage: medallion architecture (bronze/silver/gold) on external tables. The data sits in the team’s
own S3 buckets instead of Databricks-managed storage. The architectural reason was disaster
recovery. At design time managed tables didn’t support cross-region (east/west) replication, and
external S3 buckets can be replicated with full control. Databricks is configured to pretend those
folders are its own; the files actually live on Amazon.
• Layers of control: Harness on the outside (it sets up everything, including the S3 layout), then
Airflow (schedules, watches, resolves dependencies), then Databricks (runs the jobs), then dbt (does
the transformations). The control question is which layer runs the final tasks. Databricks runs the
dbt, Airflow wraps Databricks, and Harness wraps the lot. Why Harness and Airflow? Specialisation:
software-release tasks vs data tasks.
• Consumption and governance: gold-layer products are replicated from each team’s application
catalog into platform-owned domain catalogs in Unity Catalog. Access is role-driven: raise an
access request, get approval, and the domain catalog binds into your workspace. Two consumer
types appear here: analytical consumers, such as Power BI through the Databricks connector, and
other teams consuming the data into their own curation pipelines. Their source-aligned catalogs
bind into their workspaces just as Caspian catalogs bind into GCC’s workspace. Unity Catalog holds
descriptions, column metadata and read and write grants, so it’s where governance happens as well
as where you look at data. On the paved path you register a product in the in-house Marketplace
at Phase 6, and its metadata goes to Collibra and the Unity Catalog marketplace. Before you build
a product, search those catalogues to see whether it already exists.
• Scale for reference: a ~20-table data set, on the order of a billion rows for assets, roughly 100–200
columns per table.

The simplicity argument
ETL transforms data before loading it into the target system; ELT loads first and transforms there. dbt
fits the ELT pattern by expressing SQL over already available source tables.
Start an architecture review with the actual input, transformation and consumer output. Then justify the
added services through access, scale, recovery, vendor integration, audit and operating requirements. A
small prototype can clarify the logic, but it does not establish that a laptop meets production obligations.

Case review: changed values and lineage
• Upstream logic changes (schema unchanged, values change): the only defence is data-quality rules
with acceptance criteria at your end. For example, a column expected to take three values suddenly
produces a fourth and your check fails. But checks encode the assumptions made when they were
written. The business changes, so checks need looking after, and with vendor data you often get no
warning until something breaks. For change diagnosis, because everything here is code (Terraform,
YAML, Python, dbt), a clean git history is an audit trail. Nothing changes the system except through
versioned code changes that someone has reviewed.
• Duplication/lineage: check the domain catalogs for an existing product before building another one,
then follow its recorded lineage.
• Lineage across dbt projects (each team has its own project, and lineage works within it): inside
Airflow, task lineage plus Datadog spans the whole pipeline. Once the dbt tasks sit in the DAG,
Datadog gives you observability and logging across the run. The supplied example proposes to
co-locate teams’ dbt and YAML so lineage can be followed upstream beyond your own team.
• “Where does the end product actually live?” In S3, behind the scenes; consumers see it through
the domain catalog and don’t need to care.
:::

The dependency-check pattern has a name: sensors
A curation pipeline must not start until an upstream team’s ingestion has succeeded. The GCC territory
DAG hand-built this with tasks calling the Airflow REST API; Airflow has the pattern built in, in two forms.
A sensor is a task that waits for a condition instead of doing work:
from airflow.sensors.external_task import ExternalTaskSensor

wait_for_cdm = ExternalTaskSensor(
task_id="wait_for_cdm_ingestion",
external_dag_id="cdm_ingestion",
poke_interval=300,
# check every five minutes
timeout=3 * 60 * 60,
# give up, and fail, after three hours
)

Put that first in a DAG (wait_for_cdm >> stage >> …) and curation can’t begin until the upstream run
has succeeded. The timeout gives you GCC’s “within a time constraint”. After three hours of waiting the
sensor fails, the failure callback fires, and nothing downstream joins against missing data.
The trade-off to know is poll versus event. A sensor polls: it re-checks every poke_interval, so there
is delay of up to one interval between the upstream finishing and downstream starting, and a waiting
sensor occupies resources (deferrable sensors mitigate this by handing the wait to the triggerer container
from the docker ps exercise).
The event-driven alternative is dataset-aware scheduling: the upstream task declares the dataset it
updates, and the downstream DAG’s schedule is that dataset instead of a cron line. It runs when the
data changed, with no polling at all. The catch is that both DAGs must live where the same Airflow can
see them, whereas an authorised API check or a suitable external-system sensor can check a different
runtime. The ExternalTaskSensor example above checks runs in its own Airflow environment; it does not

Data operations: the tools around a product
The last session today is the “everything else” session. It covers the tools and systems around a data product
that data creators don’t drive directly but should understand end to end, and the umbrella theme is data
operations.
THIS SESSION ANSWERS

• What does “ops” mean in DataOps?
