• What does a real paved-path product look like in production?

Knowledge check: Choose the right operational record
Which record tells you a change was released, and which tells you the nightly data task ran? What should an
owner record before escalating a failed delivery?

So what does ops mean in “DataOps”? Operations means systems (systems, programming and control)
and the practices around that: operational practices, CI/CD, release practices, and so on.
The plan:
• The interfaces of the tools you don’t drive. GitHub, Harness, Astronomer, the data marketplace,
Unity Catalog and Datadog, shown live wherever possible by an authorised instructor with prepared
access. Expect a pull request under review, Harness pipeline stages, an approval step and the
environment selector, the Astronomer DAG list, a marketplace listing, the Databricks workspace
home and Catalog Explorer on a domain catalog, the SQL editor and job logs, and a Datadog monitor.
• Docker and containers in more depth; Kubernetes, and briefly Terraform and Harness (this is not a
Terraform course).
• The end-to-end infrastructure picture. How a change becomes a release, where things get deployed,
and how all the layers stack up.
• Mopping up. Catalyst workflow phases and terminology, plus outstanding questions from the group.
The framing for this session, in terms of Monday’s asset view: a data product is code plus infrastructure
plus data plus promises. The week covered data, promises and code, and this session is the infrastructure.
It’s a peek behind the curtain at how dbt, Databricks and Airflow actually run, and how everything fits
together. This layer is beneath your feet. You’ll rarely touch it, but it’s part of the paved path’s context
and worth understanding. The stack itself is the list Tuesday gave you: Git and GitHub, Kubernetes, dbt,
Airflow with Astronomer and Cosmos, Databricks, S3 and Harness. The supplied platform example also
includes Kafka event delivery, Lambda handlers and SQS queues. The event triggers later in the session
show the last two.
The course objective is to make everyone capable of producing a data product with Catalyst, while
understanding what’s going on under the hood. Catalyst can generate all the code for you, but you
must be able to read what it produces and judge whether it is right, because data products go into the
hands of people making big decisions, and being wrong is expensive. Manual inspection and observed
checks let you evaluate generated work and retain ownership of its outcome.

The supplied product example follows Average Advisor and Next-Gen Portfolio Construction, built on the

The product and its purpose
• The product tracks advisor interaction data from web tools (portfolio construction being one): when
an advisor runs a fund comparison, what they compared, portfolio health at run time, whether the
same tickers persisted year over year, whether swapping to a custom portfolio would have been
healthier.
• The pipeline owner needs the consumer’s interpretation even when the dataset’s business meaning is
outside the owner’s specialist role. Use the contract to connect operational checks to that meaning.
• Code management, deployment, quality checks and access remain necessary as tools change. Learn
each tool through the responsibility it serves, and retain evidence that the responsibility is met.

Documentation: from requirements to solution delivery
• The product manager maintains Confluence documentation covering the pain point/opportunity,
strategy, and measurable, achievable and realistic objectives, using the product decisions introduced
earlier in the week.
• A conceptual architecture diagram starts the project (inputs, staging, expected outputs). Because
it’s written by architecture, it’s conceptual and not always accurate (arrows don’t always match the
final build), but it explains data flow to a net-new engineer.
• A roadmap precedes committing the team: use cases per data source, objectives and deliverables.
These are tasks that are computable, so delivery time can actually be estimated.
• When finished, the team writes a solution delivery page: the tables delivered, frequency, owners,
the inputs required (Argo, CDM, SFDC, MAI and FinMason, a mix of internal teams and vendors), and
the engineered data flow as actually built. Every data product gets one, so anyone on the team can
triage support issues when the owner is out.
• A current triage guide lets a responder trace failed dependencies when the original engineer is
unavailable. Check any AI-drafted guide against the repository and an observed recovery; stale
documentation can send support to the wrong step.

The data layers
• ~15 raw files arrive from Pecan (the foundation data set of advisor activity/analysis runs) with ~15
correlative FactSet files; these land in staging, with per-file checks and balances in the dbt models.
That’s the pattern from the dbt days.
• Integration is where transformation happens. Staged sets are merged or unioned (e.g. Pecan fund
detail combined with FactSet fund detail).
• Prepared (also called curated) is the consumer-facing zone; access controls mean users effectively
only ever see prepared tables.
• Identity enrichment: activity data carries only an ID; CDM maps the party ID to a name, email and
role, and from there a whole web journey can be reconstructed. Foundation data vs supporting/
metadata data (identity being metadata relative to Pecan).

Change-to-production walkthrough (Harness + Airflow)
The supplied demonstration follows a column rename from change to release:
1. New engineer creates a feature branch in GitHub, makes the change.
2. In Harness (described as “an orchestrator for infrastructure”, with GitHub-Actions-style pipelines),
select the feature branch as an expression, run the pipeline: it grabs the code and deploys it to the
test environment in ~5 minutes.
3. Schedule the Airflow job in the corresponding environment and verify the renamed column appears.
4. Once approved, a prod-level Harness instance builds/releases, and the normal Airflow scheduler
(defined in YAML) triggers the job on its nightly schedule.
Airflow specifics from the demo:
• DAGs are chains of dependency checks and hand-offs; the example DAG depends on four other
Pecan jobs. The Airflow code itself is very thin, “almost just handing off to dbt”. Jobs are described
in YAML, and business logic lives in the SQL and dbt layer. Some steps (e.g. curation sync to Azure)
are macros rather than hand-written.
• Naming conventions are one-to-one between DAGs and repos, so any job can be traced to its code
in GitHub (their team repo: Advisor Touch Point).
• Branches of the DAG that are independent (e.g. Dremio sync vs historical sync to Azure) can finish
at different times, but all must complete before the team notification is sent. Notifications are
success-based to the team; a few high-priority reports notify user distribution groups directly.
• Airflow replaced Autosys as the scheduler; the win is that orchestration now lives in the same repo
as the code (previously two separate repositories, two check-ins per change). Astronomer may be
adopted underneath, but “from a data creator point of view it changes nothing”.
• Runtime ownership. Trace the DAG to its deployed environment, released code and execution logs.
In the supplied paved-path example, Harness deploys into Astronomer; another runtime must be
established from its own configuration. The release section separates that deployment from each
data run.

Case study: Consumer value and service reliability
Case study: value and service reliability
An investment-data product supports analysis and advice, while operational systems make that service available
and reliable. A product owner must decide where a proposed change creates value: improved decision data,
more reliable delivery, or a better consumer experience.
One view starts with the core business decision: data and advice are the service being sold, and software
enables it. Another starts with retention and competitive differentiation: a consumer may leave when the
service channel fails even if the underlying advice is sound. The engineering decision is to assess both the
analytical benefit and the service promise, rather than infer priority from the software’s size.
An engine is necessary for a car, but the journey explains its value. In the same way, operating software
successfully is necessary without exhausting the value of the product. The transferable lesson is to name the
consumer outcome and the reliability constraint together when prioritising a data-product change.

How does a data product get released?
A release takes a change on GitHub and puts it live in the cloud. We follow one change from pull request to
production and look at the layers it runs on.
THIS SESSION ANSWERS

• What does a release involve, and what is CI/CD?
• Why release every day or week instead of every three months?
• Where do things get deployed, and what are containers and Kubernetes for?
• Where do you look when the nightly run fails at 3 a.m.?

Knowledge check: Keep approval and correctness separate
What can an automated test establish that a human approval cannot? What can an approval authorise that a
passing test does not?

Take a data product. For our purposes right now it is code: some dbt code, some Airflow code, maybe
some YAML configuration. On what conditions does this get released? Where does the code live? GitHub.
Release processes are attached to, or driven by, GitHub actions. The actions we can take:
• Push and pull — pushing and pulling changes to code. These are Git actions.
• Pull request — a special action that only GitHub-like providers give you, because Git itself has no
pull requests. A pull request is literally a request to pull your changes, and the reason we request
rather than just pull is so the changes can be reviewed before they go in. It also leaves a record.
When something breaks you can return to the exact commit that last worked and see what changed.
So the flow: you have code on GitHub, you open a pull request, someone approves it, GitHub pulls the
code in. Attached to that pull (or to a push) there can be a release process.

What does a release involve?
A data-product release can involve the following changes:
• Building code — resolving dependencies, compiling/packaging
• Testing — before we release, we test the changes
• Deployment — to some remote environment, which may mean creating the infrastructure itself:
renting and configuring machines
• Configuring services — any services the system uses

CI/CD
• CI = continuous integration: continuously merging and building code. CD = continuous deployment:
automating the infrastructure so code goes live. “Continuous” means you don’t wait for a release
window. Code goes as and when it passes its quality checks, in practice daily or weekly, where
traditional software releases came every 3–6 months.
• A CI/CD process takes you from code in Git to a product running (typically in the cloud) at that
frequency. CI/CD is to operations people what data mesh is to data people. It’s a set of practices.
• Triggers: timing makes no sense for code (developers don’t produce hourly changes), so triggers
hang off Git, such as a push, a merge or PR, or a tag. A typical pipeline pushes, tests the code,
builds a container, pushes the image to a registry, deploys it onto cloud infrastructure and runs it.
Between build and deploy the image goes through a registry (a store of built container images). The
build pushes it there, and the deploy, usually on a different machine from the one that built it, pulls
it back out.
• Harness is the configurable system that does this at Capital Group. If you’ve only ever used Harness
to run Airflow jobs, that’s just the one task your team configured. Harness will sequence any CI/CD
tasks: renting cloud infrastructure, configuring containers, triggering Airflow.
A release keeps the same commit SHA from the Git merge onwards. The code is built and tested, passes
the data-quality gate, gets Harness approval and a change record, and is deployed. Then you watch the
released product.

Why release continuously? Feedback loops
A long batch release cycle delays evidence about whether a change works for its consumers. Smaller
reviewed releases shorten that feedback cycle, provided each change keeps its contract and passes the
appropriate quality and delivery gates. The useful trade-off is the size and risk of a change against the
cost of review, testing and recovery; speed alone does not establish a sound release.
Releasing something means the customer can see it, the team can see it, the engineers can see it. You
get a shared understanding, and you get it often. Continuous integration forces developers to see the
latest version of the code; continuous deployment forces the customer, or whoever views the system, to
see the latest release. If there’s a mistake, an issue, something not happening, you find out fast, and your
understanding of the system is always current. In a large organisation without it, every three months the
whole thing collapses and it’s a nightmare to resolve.

Inside Harness: projects, pipelines, input sets and executions
The supplied Harness example follows an application release into Kubernetes. Creators inspect the
project, branch, input set, stage results and approval evidence; an authorised platform operator controls
the release.
• Getting a pipeline into your repository. You have a repository with your code and you want to deploy
it. For that you need a Harness account and a Harness pipeline. There are templates on DevHub
from which you import the Harness files directly into your repository: you tell it which repository
you’re adding to, and it adds a .harness folder containing a YAML file, which holds the structure
of your pipeline configuration. Where Airflow had lines pointing between tasks, here you write the
stages out in YAML. Once that’s committed, the pipeline shows up in Harness.
• Projects and pipelines. In Harness you have projects, and within a project a list of pipelines. You
name a pipeline after your repository so you can keep track of all your deployments. Harness’s job
is to keep track of each deployment and each execution run: where it failed, on which path, and
the full logs of what happened. A lot of debugging happens here: you deploy and follow the errors.
• Importing a pipeline from Git. Choose the Git provider and a connector (Capital Group has these
enabled already), pick the repository, pick the branch (the maintained pipeline definition lives on

main; its execution inputs select the reviewed revision and target environment), then give the YAML

• Input sets. A layer inside the pipeline that distinguishes types of deployment: straight to prod, only

• Team practice. Each developer manages their own application from build through dev to QA. Only
three or four people are dedicated to the production pipeline, to restrict usage; code reviews for
prod happen between those people.

Two cycles, kept apart
Separate these two cycles before diagnosing a failed delivery.
1. The data cycle. Infrastructure is set up once, with Airflow ticking away on its own daily schedule.
2. The code cycle. Someone changes the dbt, ETL or YAML in GitHub, and that push (in the guest
demo’s team, via a manual Harness run in test, then a prod-level Harness release) redeploys the
code that the nightly Airflow run will pick up.
In this pattern, Airflow keeps its data schedule and Harness releases the code it uses.

Event triggers: when a vendor file lands
A data-ready event can replace a clock trigger. In the supplied vendor-file pattern, an S3 arrival creates
a queue notification, an SQS-fed Lambda submits a trigger to Airflow, and the resulting DAG starts
the downstream work. Separate the event acknowledgement, accepted DAG trigger, successful task
execution and correct published result; each is a different evidence boundary.
This is the event side of the poll-versus-event trade-off from the sensors section, sitting outside Airflow:
a sensor polls from inside the DAG, whereas here the cloud tells Airflow the file has arrived and nothing

polls at all. It’s also why the GCC case and this demonstration both start from S3. Vendors integrate by

Integration and environment promotion
The paved-path convention uses short-lived branches from main, reviewed squash merges, and an explicit
promotion record. Integration combines an approved change with the team’s main code line. Promotion
selects the exact commit or artifact version an environment receives. A merge can trigger Harness without
making every environment adopt that revision immediately.
Consider reviewed commit C104, which adds a required quality check. Development can use C104 while
SQA and production continue using C103. After validation, SQA receives C104; production follows only
after its required approval and ServiceNow change record. The promotion record, such as promotions.yml,
identifies those selections. A deployment execution binds the selected revision to its actual target and
result. A current main checkout alone cannot tell an operator which revision is live in each environment.
A designated live branch or tag is another possible release design. In that arrangement, a merge or
tag update can trigger delivery to a named environment. It needs its own approval, desired-state, and
deployment reconciliation rules. It is not the standing-branch convention used for this course’s paved
path, and a Git webhook by itself does not establish a complete GitOps operating model. Follow the
repository and promotion conventions rather than combining incompatible branch policies.
In the platform release flow, a developer submits a focused change, addresses review feedback, and
integrates the approved pull request. Harness uses the selected environment inputs and pauses at
the required ServiceNow change gate before production deployment. The release record identifies the
commit, environment, approval, and change request. Keep upstream dependency identities alongside
that record so a failed refresh can be routed to the right owner.
Work in progress can remain behind the maintained include_wip gate in an isolated development target.
Check enabled downstream dependencies and keep promotion intent out of duplicate _v2 model files.
Consumer compatibility is a separate product decision: selecting a code version does not automatically
create two compatible consumer interfaces.

Why redeploy the whole product on every change
A partial release can leave uncertainty about which compatible components are running. A repeatable
build and a recorded deployment help establish the intended code/configuration identity and expose
cross-layer interactions, such as a dbt change affecting an Airflow command. Rebuild or replay only
within a defined boundary: verify that the particular tasks are idempotent, that repeated publication
does not duplicate external side effects, and that the expected output still holds. The weekend-outage
example explains why repeatability needs this evidence rather than an assumption.

Why Airflow orchestrates even when Databricks does the work
An Astronomer-managed Airflow DAG can submit one Databricks notebook job and wait for its result.
The Airflow graph then contains one task; detailed execution is in the Databricks job logs. Inspect both
records to connect the scheduled run with the transformation it performed.
So why schedule with Airflow rather than as a Databricks job? Standards, basically. Say you have a few
data products that are fairly important. If they were just executed as Databricks jobs, the data operations
group, which is there to oversee with “eyes on glass” across the important DAGs, wouldn’t have the same
visibility. The jobs can do the work, but what orchestrates and triggers them should be Airflow, which
gives the operations side one place to see what’s happening. The other argument you’ll hear is the vendor
lock-in one from Tuesday’s Databricks session. Use as much open-source software as possible so vendors
can be switched out later. Remember the caveat from Wednesday’s lock-in discussion, though. Unity
Catalog’s grants and lineage stay behind if you move.
The supplied projects invoke dbt from Airflow and do not use a dbt Cloud scheduler. This describes
their execution route, not an enterprise-wide CG dbt version, licensing decision or historical adoption
sequence.

In an emergency the delivery gate still applies. You raise an Emergency change request instead of the
standard one, and it has to link to an active incident. The incident is the reason you’re allowed to go faster,
and it keeps the record attached to the change. Lower environments could promote automatically, but
the supplied paved-path template pauses even at deploy-into-dev for an ADM ID and a change request,
because one template serves every environment.

Breaking changes at release time
If you know a release will break your consumers, you declare it in promotions.yml. The model’s row in
that file needs acknowledge_breaking: true. The tempting shortcut is a second model alongside the
old one, something like fct_exposures_v2.sql. Don’t do that. You end up with two versions of the same
table and the lineage splits across them. Ask the product owner for the current notice period and who
signs off the change.
The usual pattern has four steps. Tell registered consumers five working days before the change. Publish
the new contract version. Keep compatibility views running alongside for ten working days. Remove the
old view once the owners have confirmed they’ve moved. The flag is only the declaration, so you still
owe consumers the notice and the migration window.

Recovery crosses software and data boundaries
A rollback plan must identify what has already changed. Reverting a commit does not reverse every effect
of the released implementation. Use the retained release and run identities to select the recovery action.

Warranty and the launch package
For the first 30 days after a production release, the team that built the product still owns it. That’s the
warranty period. You tidy up the runbook, the alerts and the known failure modes while the people who
built it are still on the hook. DataOps can refuse to take the product over if the runbook is missing or
unusable, and the Data Domain Lead settles any dispute.
The hand-off checks two things. The product pillars ask whether the team built the right thing, built it
well, tested it properly and documented it well enough. Monday’s six quality dimensions check the data
itself: completeness, freshness, accuracy, validity, uniqueness and consistency.
Before you announce a product like Morningstar exposures, run it quietly in production for at least three
days in a row. The consumer guide has to answer five questions: what the product contains, where to
find it, how to connect, what its limitations are, and who to contact. The Marketplace listing is the Phase
6 gate. It has to be live and validated, with the right entity type, domain ancestry and contract reference,
and at least one downstream consumer has to have confirmed access. Three roles sign it off:
• the DPM submits it;
• the Data Steward signs off completeness;
• the Data Domain Lead approves visibility across domains.
After launch, watch four numbers: distinct active consumers, query volume, support tickets tagged with
the product, and how often it meets its freshness SLA. Remember Monday’s Excel workaround? If the
product is green while people still refresh their own spreadsheets, find out why before you touch the
pipeline. Can they find it? Do the sample queries work for them? Does it use their words?

Group exercise: approve or request changes?
So where does a release start? With a pull request. In this exercise you sit on that gate.
Group exercise
OUTPUTS An approve or request-changes decision with its reasons

Review a supplied pull request against the Morningstar-style reference project. It’s a plausible dbt change
(a rename, an added filter, a touched schema.yml) with one planted contract violation. In one variant a nullhandling rule from the STTM has been dropped from a staging model, and in the other a test has been quietly
deleted. In groups of three, take ten minutes with two artefacts, the rendered GitHub diff and the data contract.
Decide as a reviewer would, approve or request changes, and explain the evidence for your decision.

Review criteria:
• Every promise in the contract is kept or broken by what merges. The PR is the last screen where
anyone can say no.
• You don’t need to be able to write the change to review it. You need to know the contract: which
columns may never be null, and which tests encode which promises. That’s the data creator’s
knowledge. Non-engineers can and should review these PRs, especially now that much of the
change is generated.
• A deleted test shows up in the diff as a block of red lines, and it’s easy to skim past. Read the red
lines as carefully as the green.
Use ten minutes for the review and ten to fifteen minutes to compare decisions, retain the evidence and
identify the contract correction.

Deployment environments at Capital Group
Knowledge check: Separate storage and compute
Where would you locate persistent source/consumer data, transformation compute and the orchestration
runtime? Which dependency can a green deployment leave unverified?

Where do things get deployed? Distinguish storage, compute and application-runtime destinations:
• S3 — strip away the Amazon branding: it’s a storage service, meaning files and folders.
• EC2 — virtual-machine compute.

An instance supplies configured CPU, memory, storage and

networking; the product still needs its own runtime and dependencies.
• Serverless services — the provider manages the execution infrastructure. The team supplies the
supported code/configuration and checks duration, capacity, access and billing limits.
• Databricks — as far as Capital Group is concerned, mostly used as a compute platform: you run
things like dbt on it. Databricks can store data and run other kinds of compute, but here much
of the data sits externally (S3) and Databricks is essentially your SQL engine. S3 is your storage
and Databricks is your compute, and together they form your database (mostly, though there are
exceptions and some internal stores).
• Airflow — the system that triggers events across this infrastructure.

Airflow can run in local

containers or managed remote infrastructure. The supplied case discusses EKS and Astronomer; it
does not establish the current CG deployment topology. Identify the scheduler, worker runtime and
platform owner for the assigned environment.
• Astronomer — also in the picture, running Airflow on top of EKS. It’s the Airflow vendor from earlier
today: local containers on your machine, and managed Airflow in its cloud.
For all of this infrastructure there are dev, QA (SQA in some teams’ configuration) and prod environments.
This part isn’t about the data, which is what flows through at the end. This is about software: how a
piece of software configures this infrastructure. This part of the job is software engineering more than
data analysis. The rented infrastructure is duplicated, across regions and within one place, so different
processes can be tested in different environments, and for reliability: if one goes down, another picks
up.

Containers in deployment
Knowledge check: Know the packaging boundary
Which dependencies travel in a container image, and which remain external? What would you check when the
same image behaves differently in two environments?

One more idea is needed before the deployment picture makes sense: containers. This is a recap of
Wednesday’s container session, now in its deployment context.

Virtual machines first
When we say something “runs on a VM”: a virtual machine is an abstract box with an allocation of harddrive space, an allocation of RAM, and an allocation of CPU time, and we rent all of these. The physical
machine has 100% of the CPU, RAM and disk; a virtual machine is a share of those resources that we
treat as a machine.

177

+44 (0)20 3583 0972 | info@decoded.com | decoded.com

DECODED

Thursday — Orchestration and operations

What a container is, and what it is not
A container packages an application process with the user-space files and dependencies it needs. It
shares the kernel of the host/runtime environment rather than carrying a complete guest operating
system. A virtual machine supplies a guest operating system with its own kernel on virtualised hardware.
Containers commonly run inside VMs in cloud environments. Docker explains these boundaries.
Packaging cannot include an external database, live credentials or supplier data.

Host/runtime

configuration and mounted files also remain dependencies. Line endings, paths and permissions can
differ between development hosts; check the actual prepared container/runtime instead of assuming
the image erases every environmental difference.

Why wrap code in a container at all?
Two responsibilities explain the additional layer around a VM or physical host.
1. Portability and repeatability. A versioned image fixes packaged code and dependencies, reducing
configuration drift between development and deployment.

Repeatability still depends on a

compatible runtime, explicit configuration and reachable external inputs. Keep those conditions in
the readiness record.
2. Isolation and interfaces. Process, filesystem, resource and network boundaries limit interactions
and make service interfaces explicit. Their effectiveness depends on the runtime configuration,
privileges, mounts and exposed interfaces; a container is not an assurance that any untrusted
process is harmless. The platform team supplies the approved configuration.

Docker
Docker provides tools to build images and run containers. A production platform can use a compatible
container runtime while retaining the packaged application identity. Separate the image build from the
environment and workload configuration that make it run.

Kubernetes and the layers of orchestration
EKS is Amazon’s hosted Kubernetes (K8s, really “the container configuration service”). Kubernetes is an
orchestrator for containers. It is to containers what Airflow is to data tasks. It configures, connects and
automates the containers on the rented machines. (Kubernetes was originally written by Google.)
Each orchestrator manages a different boundary: Kubernetes places and manages workloads; Airflow
orders and observes data tasks. Automation makes these operations repeatable, while the team still
defines dependencies, failure responses and ownership.
Knowledge check: Read the runtime state
What does pod readiness tell you, and what data-product promise does it leave unproved? Which image and
namespace identify the workload you intend to inspect?

The whole picture
When we deploy something, the way to think about it:
1. A container orchestrator (Kubernetes) drops containers across the infrastructure.

That’s the

outermost orchestration layer.
2. Inside those containers runs Airflow, the orchestrator of the data work, moving files around and
triggering jobs.
3. Airflow triggers dbt, which does the analysis and transformation. You could even see dbt and SQL
as the innermost orchestrator, a row-and-column orchestrator.

4. Driving the outermost layer at Capital Group is Harness: inside Harness sits Kubernetes and

The configuration languages underneath:
• Terraform (.tf files) — the code handed to Harness that asks Amazon/Azure/GCP for machines, S3
buckets, RAM.
• Kubernetes configuration — connects and automates the containers on those machines.
• Inside those containers: Airflow, which triggers DAGs, which run dbt, which moves the files.
These platform responsibilities form the paved path introduced on Tuesday. A successful data run still

Harness, indirection and Conway’s law
Knowledge check: Explain a platform boundary
Which responsibility belongs to Harness, Airflow, Databricks and dbt? What coordination problem would remain
if their code were combined into one script?

• Harness at this level: versioned release control. It can call infrastructure and application deployment
steps, while the released Airflow runtime subsequently manages its data runs. Keep the release
commit and execution record connected to deployed code and observed runtime behavior; a Git log
alone is not proof of the live state.
• This layering is the engineering technique of indirection:

introducing something that causes

something else rather than doing it directly. Each layer localises one concern:
• Harness — infrastructure (GitHub, Docker, cloud, “renting the building”)
• Airflow — timing and SLAs
• Databricks — running the code
• dbt — the business logic itself
• The small-program thought experiment: a script can illustrate downloading code, scheduling
work, deploying it and checking a result. A shared platform separates these concerns to manage
environments, identities, resource lifecycles, approvals and operational responsibilities. Review the
purpose of each boundary before adding another layer.
• Conway’s Law: software systems evolve to match the communication structure of the business.
Communication and ownership boundaries influence where interfaces are placed. The paved path
looks the way it does because of how Capital Group is organised.

Case study: Decoupling teams through file delivery
Case study: decoupling teams with file delivery
A file-delivery platform separates teams whose systems change at different speeds.

In the supplied CG

example, direct database-to-database integration made replacement costly because consumers depended
on the producer’s implementation. The decision was to exchange files through stable product boundaries.
Three considerations explain the choice. Organisational ownership makes a published contract preferable to
dependence on another team’s database internals. Large data volumes also benefit from distributed storage
and processing rather than one machine’s limits. Finally, domain sharing and supplier feeds already use object
storage: a Morningstar file arrival can participate in the existing S3 event ecosystem.
This approach still needs schemas, arrival promises, quality checks and ownership; folders alone supply none
of them. The transferable lesson is to improve an established exchange boundary with explicit contracts and
observable delivery rather than assume replacing the whole platform will remove its coordination problem.

The cloud
Knowledge check: Name the service before the acronym
What is being supplied as a service: infrastructure, a managed platform, or an application? How would you
calculate a continuously running resource’s cost from an illustrative hourly rate?

• “Cloud” means three things: SaaS (what a businessperson means, like Word or Google Docs), PaaS,
and IaaS. For this course, IaaS matters most: renting machines, or slices of machine time, from a
cloud vendor. PaaS = IaaS plus pre-installed, vendor-managed programs (e.g. renting a managed
database).
• What you rent: virtual machines (RAM, CPU, disk, network access) plus vendor services for security
and networking configuration.
• Cost arithmetic.

Use the illustrative rates $1, $10 and $100 per hour to practise estimating a

continuously running resource: multiply by the billable hours, about 750 in this example month.
At $1/hour that is about $750/month. These are arithmetic examples, not current vendor prices or
a margin estimate; real decisions use the approved service, region, usage and billing terms.
• Translate the service name. EC2 provides virtual-machine compute; S3 provides object storage.
Explain the service role before relying on an acronym.
• Infrastructure as code. Versioned configuration describes resources, so a reviewed process can plan
and apply changes consistently. The platform team owns provisioning and access; creators review
the dependencies their product needs.

Getting onto the paved path after the course
After the course, use the platform onboarding route for your application and account. The training material
is good for hands-on, but most of you have applications and AWS accounts connected to them, and
you’ll more likely be building data products off those accounts. The platform team has built templates
for onboarding those accounts, meant to be end to end: the paved path needs GitHub, dbt, Databricks,
Astronomer and Harness, and the template has all of those elements built in, with a guide to what you
get.
The supplied platform example calls its onboarding template Lake Launch. Lake Launch onboards the
account, and catalyst-domain-template (listed in Appendix C) starts the repository.
• Three prerequisites. You’ll need an ADM ID (the application identifier), an Astronomer workspace and
a Databricks workspace or bundle. If you don’t have one you get onboarded and given a Databricks
connection. The documentation lays all that out; then you traverse the template and fill in the
requirements to provision all of it.

Reading a release pipeline
Read any release pipeline for these four things.
• The trigger — what starts a delivery execution. In the integration and promotion pattern, a reviewed
merge or approved promotion can trigger Harness; the execution must still select the exact revision
and satisfy its target environment’s gates.
• The stages — provision the infrastructure, deploy the data jobs and validate, in dependency order.
• The environments — dev, SQA and prod, and how a release moves from one to the next.
• The approval gates — where they sit, and who holds each one (a role is fine where a name isn’t
known).
The three kinds of arrow from this morning turn up in a release pipeline too. A trigger arrow says this
event starts that one. A stage-order arrow says this stage must finish before the next starts. An approval
arrow says someone must say yes before the release goes on.
Compare two real examples. The supplied dev-to-prod promotion runs a change in a lower environment
first, and the prod release follows approval. The stage graph in Harness shows a real pipeline’s stages,
with one run paused at an approval step. Use the Harness anatomy (projects, pipelines, input sets,
execution history) to name what you see.
Learning Review
Trace a reviewed change through its commit, release execution, approval, deployed code and the next
scheduled data run. For a failed morning delivery after a release, choose the first release log and Airflow
task log you would inspect and explain why.
Self-check: the same intended change is identifiable across the release record; conditional/skipped stages
and waiting approvals are explained; the runbook names an owner, recovery decision and consumer update.
Successful infrastructure provisioning alone does not establish correct published data.

Knowledge check: Make a recovery decision
A dependency check fails before the consumer deadline. Which evidence would you inspect first, and
what must be true before you replay and publish?
• Airflow task logs — did the job run at all, and which task failed?
• Databricks job and query history — did the SQL itself fail, and on which query?
• Harness execution history — did someone deploy last night? A failure the morning after a release points
first at the release.
• Datadog — the observability platform where the data-operations group keeps DAG monitors (did the DQ
check pass, did the DAG finish inside its window) and per-product dashboards; who was alerted and
when, and which dashboard shows the SLA breach? The routing table from earlier today is what fires
from it.
Then someone has to tell the consumer. The message says who is being told, by when, what’s known, what’s
still uncertain and when the next update will come.

The drill leans on three things you already have.

The first is the runbook from earlier today, with

the full template in Operations: ownership, dependencies, dashboard and log links, alert-to-response
steps, rollback choices, communication routes and recovery checks. The second is alert thresholds. A
metric that drifts raises an alert without paging anyone until it crosses the agreed threshold, while a
failure that threatens the SLA pages the responsible role. A production illustration might compare a run
duration with its recent baseline; the assigned v2 phase does not configure that monitor. The third is the
difference between monitoring and observability. Monitoring watches the measures we chose in advance.
Observability lets the operator dig through logs, metrics, lineage and run history when the failure doesn’t
match anything we’ve seen before.

Operations reference
So what happens after your code is merged?

Harness releases it, Terraform and Helm set up the

infrastructure it runs on, Airflow runs it and Datadog watches it. The platform team drives most of
these tools. You still need to know which tool owns which part, so that when something breaks you
can tell the right team what failed and where. This reference covers runbooks, alerts, the incident log,
scheduling and the deployment tools.
The worked examples use Morningstar exposure data, so swap in the names, thresholds, owners and
commands from your own product.

Runbook template
Keep the runbook in the same repository as the DAG. If a pull request changes a task, a dependency, an
alert, an owner or a recovery command, it changes the runbook too.
A runbook has seven sections.
1. Service overview.

The product, what the consumer uses it for, the dag_id, repository, owner,

timezone, schedule, delivery promise, normal duration and normal row counts.
2. Architecture. The path source → ingestion → transformation → publication → consumer,
who owns each dependency and how you know each input is ready.
3. Access. Links to Airflow, Databricks, Datadog and source control, plus a query that checks the
product.
4. Common alerts. Use the alert table below.
5. Escalation. The on-call groups, the business contact, the response window and the P1 route.
6. Manual procedures. The retry, restore, full-refresh and backfill commands, written out in full, with
how to check each one worked.

Incident-log schema
Write one row per incident. These seven fields are enough.
Field

Content

incident-id

Stable INC-YYYYMMDD-NN identifier shared by Datadog, the incident thread, and
follow-up

severity

P1, P2, or P3, matching the alert tier

first-seen

UTC timestamp emitted by the alert

root-cause

One-line cause, distinct from the visible symptom

resolution

Action that restored service or data quality

runbook-step

Entry used, or none — new failure mode

owner

Responder who resolved it, or the current escalation owner

Write the row at resolution time and keep it beside the runbook. When runbook-step is none, add the
new failure mode and its recovery procedure. When a listed step did not resolve the incident, revise that
step using what the log shows.
Keep timestamps in UTC so Datadog, Airflow and the incident thread line up without conversion. For the
root cause, write down what started the incident. The alert text usually only describes the symptom. A
resolved incident looks like this:
- incident-id: INC-20260824-01
severity: P1
first-seen: 2026-08-24T10:05:00Z
root-cause: Morningstar exposure file arrived three hours late
resolution: source arrived; freshness check and downstream tasks reran
runbook-step: failure-scenarios/source-freshness-error
owner: wealth-management-data-oncall

Capital Group alerting
In the supplied CG alerting convention, Datadog receives automatic events. The severity and routing tags
on the event decide what a person does next.
Priority

Typical condition

Human response from the Datadog event

P1

SLA breach, or failure after retries

Support manually pages xMatters.

P2

Quality or freshness warning

A human posts to Microsoft Teams.

P3

Performance or capacity warning

The team creates a Jira ticket.

The supplied alert-routing case disallows email_on_failure; validate the current policy with the
operating owner before applying that restriction to a live product. xMatters, Teams and Jira are human
actions from the Datadog payload.

Every event carries l1_domain, l1_xmatters_group, lifecycle_

phase, data_classification, and criticality.
Expert
Group related failures, deduplicate by incident ID, and link P1 and P2 events to the runbook. Audit 30 days of
P2s monthly; when more than 20% led to no action, move the condition to P3 or remove it.

and the marketplace has one. Ask the platform team which monitors your product has.

Timezone and scheduling
Work the schedule out from when the business needs the data. Cron expressions are one supported
scheduling rule; Airflow also supports timetables and data-ready triggers.

For a local-time promise, use a timezone-aware start date so daylight-saving changes do not move the
local hour. In Python, for example, set start_date = pendulum.datetime(2026, 4, 7, tz="America/
New_York") after importing pendulum.

A fixed 05:00 UTC schedule runs at midnight during Eastern Standard Time and 01:00 during Eastern
Daylight Time. That may be right for a UTC source hand-off. If the business promise is tied to a New York
clock time, set the DAG timezone and state the local-time rule in the runbook.
usable buffer = SLA deadline − latest planned start − normal runtime − retry allowance

For a 07:00 ET delivery, 03:00 start, 25-minute run and 20-minute retry allowance, the buffer is 3 hours 15
minutes: four hours between start and deadline, less 45 minutes for the run and one retry. Compare that
remaining buffer with the source delivery promise. If likely source delay consumes it, move the planned
start only when the source can be ready earlier; otherwise use a readiness trigger and renegotiate the
downstream promise.

These are release-control responsibilities, not commands assigned in the local learner task. Current

Harness supplies the production gate and records who approved the release. A Databricks bundle has no
approval gate of its own. Apart from the target workspace logs, it keeps no record of what was promoted
where. When Harness calls databricks bundle deploy, the approval and the promotion record stay with
Harness.
Each deploy command ships only its own side. A DAG-only deploy releases DAG source to Astronomer, and
databricks bundle deploy creates the jobs and other resources in the Databricks workspace. Airflow

can then trigger a deployed Databricks job and wait for it. The DAG still decides the schedule, the
dependencies, the retries and what runs next. The bundle packages the Databricks resources, and the
transformations inside them are still dbt, PySpark, SQL or whatever else you wrote.
When a release goes wrong, look in the tool that owns that part. Harness shows the commit, target,
approval and command result. Astronomer shows whether the expected DAG version is registered. The
Databricks workspace shows whether the named resource exists with the released configuration.

Releasing while a workflow is running
Assume a daily run has completed staging and is waiting to start integration. A release changes the
integration output column that its publication task reads. Before deploying, establish which code and
dependency versions the pending tasks will use, whether that behavior is configurable, and whether both
task interfaces remain compatible. Executor and runtime behavior determine the answer; an active run
is not a universal guarantee that every later task stays on its original revision.
Choose an explicit transition: deploy a compatible change, drain the affected work before release, or
use a supported version-consistent execution mechanism. Record the run, input partition, code/image
identity, remote job, and candidate so the operator can distinguish a mixed-version failure from bad
supplier data. Test this boundary in a prepared non-production environment rather than infer it from
a DAG-only deployment’s speed. Astro operations develops runtime ownership, configuration authority,
upgrade checks, capacity, and release consistency.

Three Harness terms come up all the time.
• Input sets are saved groups of parameters, one per environment. A production deploy becomes a
click into a template, so nobody retypes the inputs and gets one wrong.

• Triggers are GitHub webhooks to Harness. They fire on a pull request, a merge or any code change.
• Trigger and promotion are separate decisions. A reviewed merge can trigger delivery, while the

A typical pipeline is set up like this.
• A .harness folder in the repository holds the pipeline YAML, which started life as a DevHub template.
• A Harness project holds pipelines named after their repositories.
• Each pipeline has an execution history with one entry per run. Every stage has its own log (build,

Thursday review
Use one product journey: source arrival, freshness/quality gate, transformation, publication, consumer
delivery and recovery. Connect it to the reviewed commit and the runtime that executed it.
Learning Review
Retrieve: explain DAG/task/run/operator, schedule/dependency/retry, and release/run/approval. Then identify
which promise each control serves.
Apply: the scheduled run used yesterday’s source after a new release. Decide whether to pause publication,
inspect the release, repair the input, or replay. Name the evidence needed before each decision; an attractive
green dashboard is insufficient.
Self-check: your handoff states the business date and deadline, source identity, released commit, run/task/
attempt, failed gate, recovered output and consumer communication. You separate log-only learner evidence
from production alerting and keep infrastructure changes with the platform owner.

On screen: Pull requests in practice
What this sequence controls
A pull request proposes changes for discussion and review before they enter a branch. Its diff and
checks supply evidence about the proposed commit; its description connects that change to the product
contract. A review decision is a release input, while a later deployment/run provides separate evidence
about the live product. GitHub defines this review workflow.
These are pull requests on a real infrastructure repo. The disaster-recovery PR is a documentation
proposal. Its timings are unmeasured and its implementation decisions remain open. Passing automated
checks does not satisfy the outstanding review gate or demonstrate failover. Read the proposal and
approval state together.
When you hand over a change on this course, write the description the same way. Say what changes for
the consumer, which files you touched, which tests cover it and what you know is still missing. A dbt fix
may need a contract or glossary change too. You’ll practise on a small training diff.

What this sequence controls
AWS Lambda runs a handler in response to an event without the product team operating a dedicated

Airflow DAG, together with a recorded trigger result. It does not transform the holdings or prove that a
downstream job finished. AWS describes the event-driven handler model.

an accepted trigger into the named DAG run and then check its publication evidence. This is a platform

An arrival event can start a DAG through several routes. Here are three. In the first, a Kafka source
invokes a notification Lambda. Its handler decodes the record, works out the target dataset and asks
MWAA to trigger a DAG. In the second, S3 events go through EventBridge to a Lambda. In the third, SQS
feeds the Lambda. Each one gets different inputs, wraps its events differently and retries differently.
The schema and the target-dataset list show why an event needs more than “data arrived”. The consumer
has to work out which dataset it is, ignore events it doesn’t care about, and cope with the same event
arriving twice or a trigger that fails. A triggered DAG has only started, so check its run to see whether the
transformation finished.

On screen: DAGs that trigger DAGs
What this sequence controls
A TriggerDagRunOperator requests a run of another DAG. The waiting option determines whether that task
also waits for the child run’s completion; the default is not to wait. Thus the runner’s status must be
read with its configuration, and each required child’s delivery still needs evidence. The operator reference
documents this completion boundary.
The runner starts report DAGs in parallel. The shown code sets wait_for_completion=True, so each
trigger task waits for its child run. The default without that setting would only confirm the trigger. Inspect
each child’s run and output; a completed child can still produce the wrong data.
If many reports share one source, a runner like this is a tidy way to start them together. You still have to
decide what fresh means for each report and how you’d rerun just one of them.

A release execution is a chain of observed step results, not one undifferentiated green/red signal.

On screen: Terraform in the repository
What this sequence controls
Terraform describes infrastructure resources in versioned configuration.

Providers translate those

declarations into operations against services; inputs parameterise the configuration, and state relates
declared resource addresses to managed infrastructure. A plan previews intended changes and apply
performs them. HashiCorp explains the configuration/plan/apply workflow.
Terraform controls infrastructure such as the demonstrated ECR registry.
holdings transformation or prove consumer data quality.

It does not express the

Read the recovery/design requirement,

resource definitions and environment inputs together; platform owners execute provisioning, while
creators explain their product’s dependency on those resources.
Terraform is a way to code your infrastructure. The .tf files basically say “go to AWS and give me an S3
bucket, give me a machine with this much memory”. Here they sit in the repository next to the Helm charts
and the documentation. The variables file declares each input with its type, and each environment gets
its own .tfvars file with values like the ADM ID and namespace. The ECR module creates the container
registry that built images are pushed to.
The design document in the same repository says what all this is for, which here is disaster recovery. Read
it before you review the Terraform, because the code can be valid and still miss a recovery requirement.

On screen: Terraform Cloud
What this sequence controls
The supplied screenshots use the name Terraform Cloud; current HashiCorp documentation calls the
hosted product HCP Terraform. Its workspace binds configuration, variables, managed state and a history
of runs. A run records the proposed plan and, when performed, the apply result. The official run guide
shows commit, status, timeline and command output.
Treat state as Terraform’s record used to manage resources, not a measurement of data freshness or
a guarantee that application code works. Check workspace/environment identity before reading plan,
apply and state history. The demonstrated role-based dynamic credentials are a platform-managed
access mechanism; learners do not copy credentials or apply cloud changes.
Terraform Cloud has one workspace per component and environment. Each workspace shows the latest
run, the linked repository and the resources it manages. A run has two stages. The plan works out what
would change, and the apply makes the change. Successful infrastructure changes are recorded in state
history, which is Terraform’s record of the infrastructure that exists.
The dynamic-credentials screen shows Terraform borrowing short-lived AWS credentials through a role,
so nobody has to store a static key. The platform team looks after the variables and credentials. If a
support report mentions a failed plan or a stale state, it’s an infrastructure problem. A failed job or a
missing row in your table goes to whoever owns the product.

On screen: Helm charts
What this sequence controls
A Helm chart packages Kubernetes resource templates with values. Rendering those templates produces
resource definitions such as the demonstrated Deployment; the values select image/configuration/
resource settings for an environment. Helm documents chart templates and values.
Terraform and Helm control different boundaries here: Terraform manages infrastructure resources; Helm
packages the application’s Kubernetes configuration. An edited chart/value is an intended change until
an authorised release applies it. Compare the rendered configuration with the cluster’s observed pod
state; a chart alone cannot establish that the product delivered correct data.
Compare environment values—image, CPU, memory and variables—with the rendered Deployment and
observed workload after release.

On screen: Datadog and Retina
What this sequence controls
A Datadog monitor evaluates a defined query or check against alert conditions; a dashboard groups
observations for investigation. The chosen evaluation window, threshold and no-data behavior affect
interpretation. Datadog documents those monitor controls.
Retina is the named job/cost view in the supplied platform sequence: the visible evidence is EMR job
runs and costs. No broader product capability or current tenant availability is inferred. Keep a healthy
backend, a current serving date and a successful business-output check separate. In learner practice,
callbacks remain local log evidence; live monitor configuration is a platform demonstration.
Datadog is an observability platform. A product dashboard puts service status, data freshness and
monitors on one screen. Look at the serving date as well as the backend health, because a perfectly
healthy backend can still be serving yesterday’s data. A monitor checks one condition you set up in
advance and sends an alert when it trips. Anything you didn’t think to set a threshold for, you find by
digging through the dashboards and logs. Retina shows EMR job runs and what each one cost.
Your part as a creator is to say which promise needs watching, who responds when it breaks and how
you’d know it has recovered. The platform team sets up the monitors.

Figure 125: EMR jobs in Retina

On screen: Kubernetes with Lens
What this sequence controls
Kubernetes manages workloads made of pods; a pod contains one or more containers sharing execution
resources.

Lens presents cluster/workload state and container logs through a graphical interface.

Kubernetes defines the pod boundary, and Lens documents selecting a pod and container log.
Read namespace, workload, image and selected pod before interpreting readiness or restart counts.
Readiness determines whether a container is ready to serve; a failed liveness probe can restart it.
Neither alone proves fresh or correct consumer data. Kubernetes documents these different probes.
This sequence is observation, not a learner cluster-management task.
Lens is a desktop app for looking inside a Kubernetes cluster. A deployment runs pods, a pod runs one
or more containers, and a CronJob starts jobs on a schedule. The pods screen shows each pod’s status
and how often it has restarted. Lots of restarts usually means something is unstable, though it won’t tell
you what that does to your data. The containers screen shows which image is running and its CPU and
memory limits, which ties the workload back to a release.
There are two probes. The readiness probe asks whether the pod should get traffic yet. The liveness
probe asks whether it’s stuck and should be restarted. A CronJob is basically cron in a container. It has
no task graph, so you don’t get the dependencies between tasks that an Airflow DAG gives you.

On screen: Reading a pod spec
What this sequence controls
A pod specification declares the requested containers, image, environment, resource settings and lifecycle
behavior. Its status reports observed conditions. Workload controllers manage the intended number of
pods, so read the owning Deployment as well as an individual pod. Kubernetes describes the Deployment’s
desired-state role.
In these screenshots, connect the image and environment to the released configuration, then read probes,
termination hooks, topology placement and volumes as separate controls.

A Datadog environment

variable shows intended integration configuration; successful telemetry still needs observed evidence.
The pod spec is not the data contract, and editing it is outside learner scope.
The pod YAML declares what you asked Kubernetes for. That’s the environment variables, CPU and
memory, probes, lifecycle hooks and where the pods are placed. Some of the environment variables
wire the pod into Datadog. A preStop hook runs just before a container shuts down. Topology spread
constraints spread the copies across machines, and volumes attach storage. The status at the bottom is
what Kubernetes actually observed; the spec above is the requested state.
You’ve met the same split in Airflow. The DAG file says what should happen, and the task states and the
data tell you what did, so check both.

Friday briefing and course review

Course review
Follow one product from a consumer’s decision to a checked result. Monday established who needs the
data and what it must mean. Tuesday turned interview evidence into a draft specification while keeping a
creator responsible for its accuracy. Wednesday gave those promises a technical form: a grain, a mapping,
models and tests. Thursday placed the work in an execution sequence with failure and recovery evidence.
Friday brings those decisions together in the CG product-information capstone. A successful command is
one observation in that chain. The consumer still needs to understand the population, units, limitations
and owner of the output.
Use this review in the final consolidation slot. Begin with the product journey and a short team explanation,
then choose the application questions that expose your weakest link. The longer scenario and self-check
can continue after class. Keep your own contract, mapping, diff, test results and output open; answers
backed by those artifacts are more useful than recalling a tool name.

The product journey
Suppose an advisor needs a summary of portfolios with qualifying trading activity. Before choosing a
dashboard or model, establish the decision the advisor wants to make. Does the summary explain recent
activity, current positions or every portfolio they oversee? Those are different products. A report of
active portfolios can correctly omit portfolios with no qualifying trades. A report of all portfolios needs to
represent the unknown-cost population as well. The contract makes that choice visible before a query
turns it into an accidental filter.
Interview the consumer about their current work, the producer about the source and its limitations, and
the creator about feasibility and the checks needed to maintain the promise. Ask for a recent example, the
decision made from it and what happens when the information arrives late. Record unresolved questions
with an owner. A statement such as “we need better data” is a starting point; an agreed population, unit,
freshness rule and acceptance example can guide implementation.
The design canvas collects these choices so that the team can inspect them together. Consumer value,
reuse, feasibility and viability matter together: a technically possible product can still be too costly to
operate or too difficult for a consumer to adopt. Search the existing catalogue before proposing a new
source or output. Explain the gap in what is already available, then decide whether to reuse, adapt or
build. The interview activity and canvas are linked in Monday’s route; the stakeholder reference helps
with interests and adoption when that depth is useful.
A service promise needs an observable measure and a response. “Fresh each morning” leaves several
questions unanswered: which business timezone, which qualifying source delivery, which deadline and
what happens after a missed deadline? Record what is measured, the threshold and who acts. A quality
test can protect a promise only if the model population and failure treatment agree with that promise.
Quarantining invalid events, blocking publication and warning a consumer are different decisions.

Specifications, Catalyst and responsibility
Give Catalyst the interview evidence, the intended artifact and the boundaries of the task. Useful context
includes the consumer decision, source fields, grain, exclusions, units, known examples and unresolved
questions. Request a draft that distinguishes supplied facts from assumptions. Review it against the
actual skill instructions and output structure rather than accepting a fluent paragraph as an agreed
contract.
A creator owns the resulting decisions and checks. Read the generated contract for invented fields,
unstated access, contradictory units and promises that the team cannot measure. When a skill produces
a model or test, inspect the files and the diff, identify which source rule each change implements
and retain independent evidence. If an output is wrong, supply the specific discrepancy and verify the
237

+44 (0)20 3583 0972 | info@decoded.com | decoded.com

DECODED

Friday briefing and course review

correction. Repeating “try again” until a command succeeds can conceal a changed requirement or an
omitted test.
Judgment is choosing an appropriate action from the available evidence; taste is recognizing whether the
artifact is clear and useful for its reader. Apply both to an acceptance example. A technically valid field
list may still fail to tell an advisor which portfolios are included. A clear explanation can still contain an
unsupported valuation. Ask a teammate to read the artifact without your spoken explanation, then ask
them to identify the population and limitation. Tuesday’s worked review demonstrates that handoff.
For an unfamiliar task, keep the correction small enough to inspect. Check a representative source row,
explain the proposed transformation and compare an expected result before widening the build. Model
performance can vary across similar tasks; specialist discussion belongs in the AI reference. The practical
response is to retain ownership, use bounded changes and choose evidence that could reveal a plausible
error.

Grain, mapping and a trustworthy model
State what one row represents at every stage. Distinguish source representations, selected offering rows
and return observations. Explain the two authored phase-1 models and the supplied fee-normalization
support, then show how phase 2 extends the population to 109 offerings.
Trace one mapping rule from source to consumer. For example, converting a published expense from
percentage points to basis points multiplies by 100. Selecting a net expense component and a source
representation requires explicit rules. A return comparison needs a declared basis, kind, period and
reporting date. Write those rules in the mapping and ensure the SQL, descriptions and tests implement
the same meaning.
Before enriching facts, test dimension-key uniqueness and inspect unmatched rows. Joining one fact row
to two dimension rows can double a total while producing valid SQL and a successful build. An inner join
can lose eligible rows when a lookup is missing. A left join retains rows but introduces null descriptive
fields; that does not automatically satisfy the contract. Choose the join from the intended relationship
and explain the treatment of unmatched keys.
Reconcile the output independently. Compare exact offering IDs and selected expense values with the
frozen source. Reject duplicated representations and unsupported fee components. Missing expense
ratios remain unknown; return comparisons require matching basis, kind, period and reporting date.
A useful test checks a plausible failure of the promise. Uniqueness protects row identity. Non-null
tests protect required identifiers. Accepted values constrain event meaning. A relationship test checks
a declared key connection, and a reconciliation checks the relevant population or amount. A count alone
can miss a duplicated row that replaces a lost row. Use representative rows, key membership and totals
together when the failure could preserve an aggregate count.

Development and runtime boundaries
Git records the changed files and their history. A branch makes a change reviewable, but code on that
branch can still reach a shared database through its configured connection. Read the diff, identify the
target runtime and keep learner work in the copied v2 workspace. A merge-conflict clinic practices
collaboration after branch/diff concepts; it should not interrupt the protected dbt practice block.
The development container supplies an editor-connected shell and tools.

Docker images describe

packaged dependencies; a running container is an instance with its own processes, mounts and
environment.

The separately started Astro environment runs Airflow tasks.

A remote Databricks

workspace executes connected jobs under an assigned training identity. A path or variable available in
the editor terminal is not automatically available to an Airflow worker. Appendix H gives the beginner
walkthrough and command/runtime map.

Friday briefing and course review

Offline file checks and CSV calculations support review but do not establish a Databricks run. Likewise,
installing a CLI does not prove warehouse access. Record the actual runtime, command, output and
limitation; when access is unavailable, retain the completed work and name the check that still needs
the training environment.

Orchestration, recovery and release
Draw the dependency graph from the data promise. Identify what must complete before a model builds,
where quality checks belong and which consumers may use the output after validation. dbt expresses
model dependencies; Airflow schedules and observes a wider execution sequence. Running the same SQL
through a scheduler does not make it correct. The task graph should preserve the model/test contract
established on Wednesday.
For each failure, decide whether retry can change the result. A transient connection failure may recover.
An invalid-data test will continue to fail until its input or rule is corrected. Record the failed task and
evidence before restarting a whole pipeline. Check whether replay would duplicate data or repeat an
external side effect, and use the supplied recovery procedure within the training scope.
Inspect task logs and output after a successful run. A scheduler’s green state shows that its tasks
reported success; it cannot replace a consumer-level reconciliation. A failure callback in the assigned
local route writes log evidence. It does not prove that a remote notification, monitoring platform or
production escalation is configured. Thursday’s platform demonstrations explain release and operations
controls without assigning learners to provision them.
Release control answers a different question from orchestration. A reviewed commit, a promotion record
and an approval identify what version is allowed in an environment. Terraform describes infrastructure,
Helm packages Kubernetes deployment configuration, and monitoring observes the running system. Read
the demonstrated evidence and role boundaries; the course’s local checks do not confer production
access or approval. Link your runbook to the actual contract, owner, failure treatment and retained
evidence.

Evidence area

What a reviewer should be able to verify

Consumer and contract

The named decision, intended population, grain, units, acceptance examples and
limitations agree.

Catalyst ownership

Supplied evidence is distinguishable from assumptions; generated files were read and
corrected by a named creator.

Mapping and models

A business rule is traceable to authored SQL and a test; supplied baseline stages are
identified.

Quality

Representative rows, key membership and an independent reconciliation support the
claimed result.

Runtime and recovery

The actual local or connected environment is named; failure, repair and replay evidence
match that boundary.

Handoff

The consumer can interpret the output; unresolved checks, responsible owners and
next actions are explicit.

For each evidence area, use a simple self-check: 0 means absent or contradicted; 1 means a plausible
claim with incomplete evidence; 2 means an artifact, an observed result and an explanation that agree.
A teammate should be able to find the evidence without reconstructing your terminal session. Use a
named pending gate when a required environment is unavailable; retain the valid local result rather than
claiming a connected run. Select the next activity from the weakest link in the journey, not from the
number of commands completed.
Continue with a focused next step. Repeat a core task if you cannot yet explain its evidence, choose an
advanced clinic when the core is clear, or use the reference for a specific question. The v2 challenge
reference preserves the full offered material and optionality. The Questions and answers reference
addresses recurring questions; the worked contract reference provides another artifact to inspect. Keep
the distinction between learning evidence, runtime readiness and approval when you carry the habits
into a real product.

How do you know when a data product is done?
Agree acceptance criteria with the consumer and the accountable product roles. A consumer-aligned
table containing rows is necessary for some products, but it does not establish that the required decision,
quality, timing, access or support conditions are met. A percentage-complete claim needs a declared
denominator and evidence.
Trace each criterion to a test, review or sign-off. Include the relevant consumer classes and unresolved
conditions, rather than relying on one enthusiastic user’s approval for every use case. Completion is a
decision against agreed criteria; later operation and evolution remain ongoing responsibilities. Tuesday’s
worked review shows why a complete-looking contract is still a draft.

Git collaboration
Projects contents · Task index
• Foundation core — page 248
• Advanced core — page 256

git challenges
Git makes a data-contract change inspectable through snapshots and ancestry. Foundation practice
stays local: distinguish working/index/committed content, make intentional commits, combine branches,
resolve a business ownership conflict and restore only an accidental edit. Advanced practice carries
a prepared independent contract through an authorized private sandbox PR, real review revision and
concurrent upstream change. The result is preserved requirements and an understandable history, not
merely a command count.
Before you start
Prepare an isolated attempt through mise and check its repository root before any change. Keep the
baseline contract and evidence at the attempt root and local Git work in the inner lab. Foundation
requires only delivered Git and a local training identity. Advanced requires an instructor-designated
private repository, permitted branch prefix, CLI identity and arranged reviewer. Missing remote or human
preparation remains pending; a local simulation can teach mechanics but does not establish peer review.
Neither route authorizes publishing the course checkout or modifying a production branch.
Suggested timeline and tasks
Estimates include reading, practice, checks and explanation. Allow additional time for environment setup
and optional extensions.

git: Phase 1 — foundations
Purpose and outcome
Learn to preserve and explain a small data-contract change using local Git. You will distinguish working
files from staged content and committed history, make intentional commits, combine branch work,
resolve a meaningful ownership conflict and restore an accidental edit. The contract is small so the
tool behavior is visible. The point is reviewable changes and preserved requirements, not memorizing a
long command sequence.
Dataset and pipeline
The starter is an ordinary holdings contract with owner, grain, currency and daily delivery.

It is a

documentation fixture, not the later Databricks dataset. You will refine its deadline and escalation
promises while keeping the original grain and currency facts. An untracked notes file demonstrates
that a file can exist without entering the next commit. Compatible branches edit deliberately separated
facts; competing owner edits create a known merge conflict. This local history becomes the evidence for
your explanation of how requirements were combined.
Prerequisites and workspace
Use the delivered Git executable and a configured training identity. Prepare an isolated attempt from the
training project root through mise, then create a new inner lab repository inside that copy. Confirm the
repository root before running change or restore commands. The course repository and another learner’s
directory are outside the exercise boundary. Keep the copied baseline contract and evidence note at the
attempt root, with only the inner lab under its new Git history.
mise run challenge:v2:prepare git phase-one-certified
cd .local/challenges-v2/git/phase-one-certified
mkdir lab
cp contract.md lab/contract.md
cd lab
git init -b main
git --version

Record your configured author identity without changing another repository’s global settings. If Git does
not support the initial-branch option in the delivered version, inspect its help and create the main branch
explicitly; record that measured variation. Use a new workspace for another attempt instead of resetting
existing work. This phase performs local actions only and does not require a hosting account, production
branch or public repository.
Starter behavior
The supplied contract is valid text and there is no intentionally broken repository. Initial status shows an
untracked contract until you stage it. The first task deliberately creates an additional notes file so you
can identify exactly what enters a commit. A later ownership merge is expected to stop with a conflict;
the README names that failure before it happens. A clean starter check establishes readable input, not
completion. Keep the contract baseline and the new lab separate so the verifier can inspect both without
overwriting your work.
Timeline and completion standard
Core reading, authoring, checking and explanation: 60–90 minutes. Allow additional time for setup and
optional stretch.
