Core challenges

Inspect the three working states
Concept
The working tree contains editable files. A commit records a snapshot and its parent history. The index
is the proposed next snapshot, not a synonym for every file in the directory. Staging one file selects its
current content for the next commit; changing that file again can leave one version staged and another
in the working tree. An untracked file has no committed baseline, so its presence in a folder does not
imply version control protects it. This distinction matters when a contract edit and an unrelated note
share a workspace.
For the first snapshot, the baseline contract should enter history while the scratch notes should not.
Inspecting the staged diff and the committed file list gives stronger evidence than a commit command
returning success. The repository root is also part of the boundary: operating from the course checkout
instead of the disposable lab would select the wrong work. Confirm that root before reasoning about
status.
Challenge
Use the prepared inner lab and configure a local training name/email if needed. Confirm its repository
root, inspect git status, and create an untracked notes.txt. Stage only contract.md, inspect git diff
--cached, then make the initial commit. Explain why the note is absent from that snapshot.

Keep the commit hash in evidence.md at the parent attempt root. Remove or ignore the scratch file
before later clean-state checks. Stage an explicit filename rather than the entire attempt, so runtime
files and evidence stay outside this first snapshot.

Phase contents · Reasoning key

Commit an intentional contract change
Concept
A useful commit makes one intention reviewable. A deadline clarification and an escalation rule can
be related business work while still benefiting from separate snapshots: a reviewer can see the delivery
promise and then the response to a missed promise. A commit message describes that intent; the actual
diff proves what changed. Combining unrelated edits makes later diagnosis or reversal harder.
Staging also lets you choose when a change enters history. An accidental extra line in the working file
need not be committed with the deadline, and unstaging differs from discarding content. Inspecting
both ordinary and cached diffs reveals that boundary. The fixture remains ordinary contract text, so the
review should preserve grain and currency while adding a clear time zone rather than silently replacing
the original business assumptions.
Challenge
Change Delivery to daily before 09:00 UTC. Review the working diff, stage that edit, inspect the staged diff
and commit it with a message explaining the deadline clarification. Add Escalation: Training support
in a separate commit.
Save both hashes and their scoped diffs in the parent evidence note. Confirm the original grain, currency
and owner remain. If an unrelated edit appears in the index, unstage it without discarding its working
content. Each commit should let a reviewer assess one contract decision independently.

Phase contents · Reasoning key

Branch and combine compatible work
Concept
A branch names a position in commit history; it is not a separate copy of every file you must manage
manually. Switching branches changes the checked-out snapshot, while merging combines ancestry and
file changes. Compatible edits can be combined without conflict when they touch sufficiently separate
content from a shared baseline. Adjacent edits in a tiny file can still conflict, so compatibility is a property
to observe rather than assume from different branch names.
Use distinct contract facts for this demonstration, such as a nonadjacent delivery refinement and a newly
separated producer note. The goal is to preserve both intentions and explain whether history advanced
directly or recorded a merge. Fast-forward means the target simply reached a descendant commit; a
merge commit records combined parents when histories diverged. Neither outcome alone tells whether
the final text is correct.
Challenge
Create clarify-grain and producer-note from a common main commit. Clarify the existing grain on
the first branch. On the second, append a separate Producer note section with a blank line before it.
Commit each change before switching branches.
Inspect each branch’s diff, merge both into local main and review the complete contract. Record the
common ancestor and whether each merge fast-forwarded or created a merge commit. If the short
file produces unintended overlap, record and repair the separated note layout; reserve the deliberate
ownership conflict for the next task.

Phase contents · Reasoning key

Resolve an ownership conflict
Concept
A conflict means Git cannot choose a combined text automatically. It does not mean either branch is
necessarily wrong or that a valid business decision follows from accepting one side. The conflict markers
show candidate content from two histories; the learner must understand the requirements and produce
one coherent contract. For ownership, the resulting named owner and escalation responsibility must be
compatible rather than two contradictory labels.
The merge remains unfinished until the resolved file is staged and committed. Removing markers without
inspecting surrounding text can still lose the deadline or currency facts. A merge commit’s parents record
which histories were combined, while the resolution diff records the actual decision. That evidence is
useful to a future reviewer who did not watch the editor. The exercise deliberately stops with a nonzero
merge result so the expected failure can be distinguished from tool or identity setup problems.
Challenge
From the same main state, create upstream-owner with Owner: Operations team. On main, set Owner:
Analytics team. Merge upstream-owner and retain the expected conflict state.

Inspect both candidate versions, then resolve to Owner: Analytics team with Escalation: Training
support. Keep the existing deadline, grain and currency. Remove all markers, stage the resolved file,

inspect its staged diff and complete the merge commit. Explain the ownership choice in the parent
evidence note. A removed marker is only part of the repair; the resulting contract must be coherent.

on what state contains the mistake.

establishes that only this new line is unwanted.

git: Phase 2 — advanced practice
Purpose and outcome
Carry a small contract clarification through a collaboration workflow.

This phase extends local Git

into a designated remote repository, an understandable pull request, an actual review response
and synchronization with concurrent upstream work.

The challenge is preserving intent and review

evidence across participants, not merely making a push command succeed. The advanced route has
an independent contract baseline and a supplied review scenario, so you do not need another learner’s
foundation repository.
Dataset and pipeline
The fixture is the same style of holdings contract used in local practice. A delivery-timezone clarification
and escalation responsibility form the proposed change. The review scenario asks for an explanation
and revision, while a separate upstream edit adds input classification. These requirements must coexist
in the final branch. The hosted PR contains the proposal and review state; local history contains your
commits and integrated ancestry. They describe related but distinct collaboration evidence.
Prerequisites and workspace
The instructor designates an authorized private training repository, branch prefix and reviewer. Use the
delivered Git and GitHub CLI tools with the intended training identity. Prepare an independent attempt
through mise, then clone only the designated sandbox into its inner lab directory. Keep the starter
contract and evidence at the attempt root. Confirm remote URLs and repository root before any remote
write; the course repository and production remotes are outside this exercise.
mise run challenge:v2:prepare git phase-two-proficient
cd .local/challenges-v2/git/phase-two-proficient
gh auth status

Account creation, sign-in, reviewer invitation and repository provisioning are arranged preparation, not
automated assessment. If a real reviewer or remote is unavailable, use the supplied scenario locally
with explicit simulated status and leave the corresponding collaboration gate pending. Do not count a
Markdown draft as an actual PR or a self-comment as peer review.
Starter behavior
The contract and review-scenario JSON are readable, benign inputs. There is no real remote state inside
the copied starter. Phase verification requires your actual cloned repository and, for live review checks,
the designated sandbox/PR identifiers. A local reference workflow can demonstrate Git mechanics but
does not satisfy hosted review. The final merge decision follows the instructor’s stated policy; an open PR
may be the honest final state. Never rewrite the route to imply approval just because a check command
exited successfully.
Timeline and completion standard
Core reading, authoring, checking and explanation: 75–110 minutes. Allow additional time for setup and
optional stretch.
• Task: Clone and inspect a collaboration boundary · Minutes: 15–22 · Evidence: Designated private
sandbox, correct clone root, remote and tracking branch
• Task: Push and propose a scoped pull request · Minutes: 15–22 · Evidence: PR URL/head hash and
remote diff contain the intended deadline clarification

Concept

Compare merge and rebase on disposable local history
Concept
Merge and rebase can combine related work while presenting different ancestry. A merge retains the
divergent histories and can record a commit with both parents. Rebase reapplies commits onto another
base, changing their identities even when the resulting contract content is similar. Neither automatically
decides the right business requirement, and rebasing already shared work introduces a coordination
question beyond this local comparison.

comparison should show final content, parent relationships and rewritten hashes rather than declare
one graph universally better. The permitted sandbox review policy still governs the actual advanced
collaboration route. Keeping the experiment separate prevents a history-style exercise from rewriting
someone else’s shared proposal.

Optional contents · Reasoning key

Recover a lost local branch reference through reflog
Concept
A branch is a reference into existing commit history. Moving or deleting a local reference can make a
useful commit less visible without immediately destroying the underlying object. Reflog records recent
reference movements and can help recover the intended local state. Its retention is bounded by repository
behavior and garbage collection, so its bounded reference record cannot replace durable commits and a
separately preserved backup.
The exercise uses only disposable committed work. A reflog entry can identify an earlier commit, but
restoring that pointer does not automatically recover an uncommitted file that was discarded. Keep
those recovery cases distinct. The foundation restore task handled an accidental uncommitted edit; this
optional experiment concerns a committed change whose branch reference moved.
A recovered pointer still needs its committed file content checked.
Challenge
In a new disposable local copy, create recovery-demo, commit a distinctive contract note and record its
hash. With that commit at the branch tip and no uncommitted edits, move only recovery-demo back
one commit using git reset --keep HEAD~1. This intentionally removes the committed note from the
working file; --keep refuses a change that conflicts with uncommitted edits. Inspect git reflog to locate
the saved commit, then use git switch -c recovered-note with that hash to create a recovery branch
at it. Compare recovered file content and history with the saved expected hash. Keep the production/
course repository and actual advanced sandbox untouched, and preserve the original completed attempt
before starting.

Core challenges

Run an image and inspect the lifecycle
Concept
A container’s main process determines its lifetime. A short program that prints and exits can be a
successful container execution; keeping it alive with an unrelated sleep would change the behavior being
inspected. The image is a reusable package, while the container is one process execution with its own
writable layer and recorded state. Removing that container does not automatically delete the image.
The hello command makes this distinction visible before app packaging. Inspecting all containers includes
stopped executions that a default running-only list omits. Logs and exit status answer whether the
process ran as expected, while the image identifier answers which package ran. A familiar tag can point
to a different image later, so retain the actual identifier when comparing runs.
Challenge
Run docker version and docker info, then launch the hello process using your unique container name:
docker run --name "$DC_DOCKER_NAME" python:3.11-slim python -c "print('hello holdings')"

Inspect its logs, state, exit code and actual image identifier. Explain why successful output leaves a
stopped container. Retain those observations, then remove only this named execution. If the engine or
base image is unavailable, resolve that preparation issue before interpreting program behavior. Do not
keep the hello process alive with a sleep: its normal completion is the lifecycle observation.

Explore an interactive shell
Concept
A container writable layer belongs to that execution. Creating a temporary file inside one disposable
container does not place it in the base image or the host application folder. A fresh execution of the
same image starts from its packaged filesystem and a new writable layer. This is why an unmounted
scratch file disappears after the first container is removed.
An interactive shell changes how you inspect the process, not whether it shares the host kernel. The
terminal flags attach input and a pseudo-terminal; a noninteractive command can inspect the same
filesystem facts when the classroom interface lacks a terminal. Keep the image’s OS/runtime observations
distinct from the author’s host environment. A container is not automatically a virtual machine with a
separate kernel.
Challenge

and /etc/os-release. Create /tmp/inside.txt, exit, then launch a fresh container from the same image
and test whether the file exists.

Use a bounded bind mount
Concept
A bind mount exposes a selected host path at a container path. The target can replace what the image
would otherwise show there, so both path and access mode matter. Read-only access lets the supplied
summary read its fixture while protecting that copied input from container writes. Mounting an entire
workspace would broaden the boundary beyond what this task needs.
The app reads its CSV relative to the working directory. A correct mount at one path with execution
in another can still fail, even though the file exists somewhere inside the container. Comparing the
host and mounted input plus the app output distinguishes this path error from a business-data defect.
The deliberate write denial demonstrates the mount promise and should not be repaired by removing
read-only protection.
Challenge

the working directory. Use an absolute host path. Compare the copied input with what the container
reads.

the host copy did not change. Explain the source path, target path and access mode separately. If the
summary cannot find its CSV, inspect the working directory before changing permissions. Keep the mount
limited to the app directory rather than broadening it to the whole workspace.

docker: Phase 2 — advanced practice
Purpose and outcome
Design a bounded multistage image for the supplied summary app. Advanced work separates test and
execution concerns, selects named targets deliberately, runs with a suitable user and diagnoses a real
path assumption. You author Docker configuration and evidence; the app and expected fixture result
remain supplied so the focus stays on runtime boundaries.
Dataset and pipeline
The advanced copy contains the same six-holding app fixture and independent test as foundation practice.
Its expected total is 12,011,626.50. This app dataset is distinct from the assigned Databricks Portfolio
Analytics and CG product sources. A build stage supplies files, a named test target executes the oracle,
and a runtime target includes only the app/input needed for execution. The exact stage graph determines
whether runtime receives a tested artifact and what a target build actually executes.
The app resolves its CSV from the current working directory. A deliberately wrong copy destination
or directory can therefore make a perfectly built image fail at runtime. The named targets and actual
filesystem/user inspections provide evidence that cannot be replaced by reading FROM, USER or COPY
text alone.
Prerequisites and workspace
Prepare an independent advanced attempt through mise from the training project root. Use the delivered
engine and prepared base image, then choose distinct test/runtime tags for your attempt. The advanced
starter includes app/test inputs without requiring your completed foundation Dockerfile. Work from the
copied root so build context and relative source paths are unambiguous.

export DC_DOCKER_RUNTIME_TAG=dc-alex-docker02:runtime

should be tested in a real container; source configuration only states intent. Avoid privileged options,
broad host mounts and global image pruning. Engine access and image pulls belong to preparation
outside the unpiloted task estimate. If unavailable, continue Dockerfile review and the local app oracle
while leaving actual target/user/filesystem checks pending.
Starter behavior
The copied Dockerfile still prints a benign placeholder and has no completed multistage outcome. A
successful starter build is deliberate but cannot pass the finished target checks. Both app and Python
oracle work from their supplied directory. You must author named test/runtime targets, meaningful test
execution, required non-root user and focused runtime contents. The path defect is introduced later in
a disposable version after a working baseline, so an initial missing engine or image is not its intended
failure. Preserve a known working Dockerfile before the drill.

optional stretch.

Core challenges

Separate named build targets
Concept
A multistage file defines a dependency graph of named build stages. Selecting one target chooses the
output image and the stages it depends on; it does not automatically publish every intermediate stage as a
separate tagged image. The test target and runtime target therefore need deliberate build/tag commands
when both are review artifacts.
Named stages also communicate purpose. A runtime target should contain the executable app/input,
while a test target can retain the independent test script and its command. The source file alone cannot
show which target an actual build selected or whether a cached stage was reused. Record command,
target and resulting image identity so a reviewer can connect intended architecture with observed output.
Challenge
Create named base, test and runtime stages in the Dockerfile. The test target runs test_summary.
py; runtime runs summarize.py. State their dependency relationship and how tested app/input reaches

runtime.
Build test with $DC_DOCKER_TEST_TAG and runtime with $DC_DOCKER_RUNTIME_TAG. Inspect both resulting
image IDs and run the targets separately. Keep the selected target explicit in each command so a default
final-stage build cannot stand in for two outputs. Retain the commands and explain which prerequisite
stages each target used. Check that the named stages match the verifier’s expected interface.

Gate the runtime on a tested artifact
Concept
A testing stage is useful when it validates the artifact that runtime receives. An unrelated test command
in an unreachable stage can look reassuring while providing no gate. The stage graph should connect the
tested app/input to the runtime copy path, and a build-time assertion or equivalent explicit workflow
should reject an incorrect artifact before acceptance.
The supplied Python test computes the fixture expectation independently of a hard-coded echo. The tiny
app’s baseline result is fixed, so a controlled copied input or app-path defect should make that assertion
fail. Keeping the test’s purpose visible prevents a Dockerfile from satisfying advanced work merely by
naming a stage test. The runtime output remains a separate observation after the test succeeds.

Run with a bounded runtime user
Concept
A runtime user changes the process’s permission boundary, not the meaning of the app. The image should

broad writable host mounts or privileged flags would change the exercise boundary. An image can build
under root while its final process runs non-root, because build and runtime identities are separate. That
distinction should be visible in the explanation and actual command output.

dbt — Portfolio Analytics
Build a traceable transformation from supplied custodian feeds to a fund/date report on Databricks.
The foundation phase teaches external sources, typed staging, business grain, model references and
independent output checks. The advanced phase supplies that baseline and develops dated enrichment
diagnosis, reconciliation, controlled corrections, history and a reviewable feature. The consumer question
is what each fund’s supplied holdings contribute to GBP exposure on each fixture date, with a carefully
labelled holdings value per synthetic unit measure.

Choose your phase
• Foundation phase: complete the assigned source/staging/report slice and prove its minimum

• Advanced phase: begin from its supplied baseline and demonstrate diagnosis, replay and a useful

Finish the core tasks before choosing optional stretch. These phases use the supplied Portfolio Analytics

Teaching concepts
Trace source declarations to physical owned tables, distinguish source and model dependencies,
preserve composite grain, choose deliberate materializations, and separate native valuation from dated
GBP conversion. Structural tests and independent business calculations protect different failure modes.
The advanced route extends those ideas into controlled Delta replay, snapshot validity, documentation
and the Astro worker boundary. Reasoning keys stay at the end of their owning phase; full runnable
instructor references are supplied separately.
Question-led foundations and further study
Use questions 1–8 alongside the foundation tasks. Questions 9–13 introduce further study.
Foundations
What problem does dbt solve, and where does it fit in a data pipeline?
Custodian feeds arrive as holdings and cash; prices, dated FX and fund metadata explain those positions.
dbt orders SQL transformations and tests. The Databricks warehouse executes SQL and stores views/
Delta tables. Running dbt in a local process does not create a local database. Our consumer output is
a fund/date GBP exposure and a holdings value per synthetic unit, with lineage back to the supplied raw
tables.
What does a dbt project contain, and how do we connect it to our data?
The prepared Portfolio Analytics attempt contains models, eight seeds, tests, macros, profiles and a local
target directory. Read the setup contract before connecting. Profile portfolio_analytics and target local
point to the assigned Databricks warehouse. dev and airflow are also Databricks targets. Record the
project/profile paths and installed versions; reject missing namespace or conflicting aliases rather than
guessing a username.
How does a SQL query become a dbt model?
Author models/staging/stg_holdings.sql. Select fund_cd as fund_id, pos_dt as position_date, isin as
instrument_id, qty as decimal quantity, mkt_val_lc as decimal native value and ccy_cd as local_ccy. Cast
dates and retain extraction time. Its business key is fund/date/instrument. The baseline contains eight
rows: one instrument for each of four funds on each of two dates. A model file becomes an owned view
after execution; its filename is the ref name, while its physical alias includes your prefix.
How do we connect models using source() and ref()?
source(‘custodian’,‘holdings_raw’) reads the prefixed raw seed-backed Delta table.

ref(‘stg_holdings’)

connects transformations and lets dbt establish order. Declare raw source database/schema from the
target and identifier from the ownership prefix. A source declaration does not load data. Run the explicit
eight-seed preparation, then inspect the compiled relation names and graph. Supplementary NAV/fund
seeds alone leave six raw sources missing.

How should we split a large query into understandable, reusable models?
Keep cast/rename in five staging views; dated enrichment belongs in int_holdings_enriched. Join prices
by instrument/date and FX by native currency, GBP and date. Fund metadata joins by fund key. Cash
positions have fund/date/currency grain and remain separate until aggregated correctly. Validate rightside uniqueness before joining: an undated FX join fans eight holdings out across two dates. refdata_raw
is available for a classification extension; it is not a substitute for fund_master_raw.
When should a model be a view or a table?
Views suit the small staging and intermediate transformations. A consumer table persists the report for
repeated reads and a stable tested handoff. Inspect information_schema for the prefixed relation and
its type; do not infer storage from a successful command. Tables on this adapter use Delta. The richer
product has optional optimisation hooks, but the guide omits them to avoid adding managed-permission
assumptions to the core exercise.
How do we know our models produce trustworthy data?
Test non-null keys, composite uniqueness, decimal types, dated join coverage and populations. Missing
FX is an error, not an implicit rate of one. All supplied holdings happen to be GBP; fund PEF-EM-GROWTH
has USD master currency, but this report explicitly values in GBP. Market value is supplied by the custodian
and must not be replaced with quantity times price without an agreed contract. The reference syntheticunit value uses 100 million synthetic units and excludes cash. Compare each of eight fund/date rows
independently with seed_custodian_nav.
How do we make a change confidently and explain the result?
Select the changed model and downstream dependencies, retain compiled SQL and run results, then
query the actual warehouse. For a negative drill remove a dated GBP FX row in a disposable copy.
matched_enrichment must fail; restore, reseed and rebuild before handoff. Documentation must state
grain, units, source meaning and the synthetic-unit measure limitation. A green structural test can miss
a correct-looking wrong business measure.
Further study
Questions 9–13 are separately timed advanced study.
When does Jinja help, and when should we keep the logic in SQL?
A small native_value(value, rate) macro casts the GBP conversion to a declared decimal precision. Inspect
its compiled multiplication and explain the arguments. Keep business joins in readable SQL. Reuse
earns its place when the same expression has the same meaning in both the consumer model and the
correction/replay model; a macro cannot settle currency or grain disagreements.
How can we process less data without producing incorrect results?
In the separately timed advanced phase, the required holdings_replay model uses Delta merge with fund/
date/instrument as its composite key. Read the whole tiny fixture each time so older-date corrections
are included. Copy one holding, add 1,000 GBP to its value, reseed, merge and replay. Query the original
key after each run: corrected value and exactly one row. A maximum-date watermark would miss this
controlled historical correction. This is a labelled variation, not history already present in the source.
How do we preserve history when source records change?
Snapshot a copied fund-master relation before and after one controlled name change using the check
strategy and fund_cd key. Retain validity columns and verify the original closed row plus one current row.
All snapshots remain in the assigned schema with owned aliases. Snapshots record observed states, not
every event between observations. Restoring source CSVs does not delete history; a new attempt/prefix
starts clean.

How does a dbt project move into reliable team delivery?
Review SQL, tests, contract and target routing together. Hand off the exact prepared project to Astro with

missing model, stale data, join fan-out and a currency-definition mistake.

Core challenges

Inspect the project and source grain
Concept
A dbt project describes transformations and dependencies; it does not become a separate database
simply because it lives in a container. The adapter compiles and submits SQL to Databricks, where the
approved catalog, schema and warehouse determine the relations you read and write. Seeds load copied
training inputs. Sources describe that input boundary, while models describe derived relations. Keeping
those roles separate helps diagnose a missing table before changing a transformation.
In this fixture a holding is identified by fund, business date and instrument. The same fund appears
on two dates, so fund alone cannot identify a row. A report with four rows after both dates are loaded
has probably collapsed the date dimension. Inspecting the eight raw rows makes that mistake visible
before SQL is written. Distinguish the position date from the extraction timestamp: one describes the
observation being valued, the other describes ingestion freshness. An old business date can be the correct
teaching input even when its original extraction timestamp is stale. Likewise, a successful connection
says nothing about whether the six raw feeds have actually been loaded.

units. Inspect the project and profile configuration, identifying the adapter, target, approved catalog/

Phase contents · Reasoning key

Declare and use sources
Concept
The source function gives a model a logical dependency on data loaded outside that model. Its first name
identifies the source group and its second identifies the table inside that group. Those logical names
need not equal the physical warehouse relation: the source identifier can add the owned training prefix
while the SQL remains stable. A reference to another model instead declares a derived dependency that
dbt can order and document.
Consider the holdings model reading the custodian holdings source. Databricks ultimately executes a
fully qualified relation in your approved namespace; the source declaration explains why that relation
is an input rather than a generated mart. A raw seed can be present but wrongly mapped to another
learner’s table. Conversely, a perfectly written declaration can resolve to a table that was never seeded.
Compilation and an actual query expose different halves of this boundary. The instrument-reference
input is useful to inspect even though the prepared consumer graph does not depend on it. Do not
invent a lineage edge merely to make every loaded feed appear in the final report.

Phase contents · Reasoning key

Normalize type, unit and key contracts
Concept
Staging gives raw data stable names and types while preserving its declared population. Renaming the
custodian fund code and position date makes their purpose clearer, but it does not justify dropping a
date, replacing a missing key or changing money units. Money stored as native market value must remain
native market value until the dated FX join explicitly converts it. A fund’s master base currency is a
separate attribute, not permission to relabel a holding value.
For example, a holding observed on 20 May and the same instrument observed on 21 May represent
different positions. The composite key preserves both; casting the date into a SQL date type makes
later dated joins less ambiguous. Decimal conversion preserves exact cents within the stated precision,
whereas an uncontrolled floating-point aggregation can introduce comparison noise. Quantity has its own
precision and meaning. The supplied valuation is not necessarily quantity multiplied by the supplementary
price, so reconstructing it that way would silently change the teaching contract. Filtering a zero or negative
amount also changes population semantics unless the contract explicitly requires that rule.

Build a useful mart through ref
Concept
A mart combines modeled inputs into an output a consumer can interpret. Its grain must be declared
before aggregation, because an apparently sensible total can conceal loss of dates or duplication from
joins. Here the consumer result is one row per fund and position date, containing holding count, GBP
exposure and holdings value per synthetic unit. The prepared enrichment provides native market value
and the matching dated FX rate; the report sums converted holding values at that grain.

Add minimum key and relationship proof
Concept
A test is useful when it protects a stated failure mode and its result can be interpreted. A uniqueness test
checks row identity, a not-null test checks required presence, and a relationship test checks membership
in another relation. None independently proves all joins preserve the intended population. A relationship
assertion can ignore nulls, and a reconciliation can compare two outputs that already lost the same fund.
Combining structural checks with independent business values closes different gaps.
The holding grain includes a date, while fund-master membership is checked by fund identifier. A datefree fund uniqueness test would therefore reject valid holdings. Conversely, a report sum could stay
numerically unchanged if an unknown fund’s zero-valued holding were silently filtered out; the population
and relationship assertions should still catch that loss. For missing dated FX, the correct failure is
incomplete conversion coverage, not a guessed one-to-one rate. The teaching drill deliberately changes
a copied input so you can observe the failed assertion, repair its cause and prove the restored output. A
red test is not automatically a successful drill unless it failed for the intended reason.
Challenge
Review the supplied schema and singular tests, then add or repair assertions that match the authored
models: holding composite grain, required fund/date/instrument fields, fund membership, complete
dated enrichment and independent NAV reconciliation. Explain which checks protect population, which
protect type/units and which protect the consumer calculation. Run a clean seed and full selected build
after both authored SQL files are complete.
Create the required relationship negative case in a disposable copy by changing a holdings fund to an
unknown identifier; retain the specific membership failure. Also use the runtime helper to inspect

dbt: Phase 2 — advanced practice
Purpose and outcome
Develop the foundation pipeline into a reviewable data-product change. The core begins with dated-join
diagnosis and repair, then adds a business reconciliation, controlled incremental replay and an explained
feature/history handoff. The starter supplies the supporting models, so a completed foundation attempt
is not required.
Dataset and pipeline
The advanced starter uses the same six raw and two supplementary Portfolio Analytics CSVs as the
foundation phase. Staging and supporting models are supplied; enrichment, its coverage/reconciliation
tests, the reusable value macro, replay model, fund snapshot and final report contain declared unfinished
outcomes. The two May business dates provide a concrete date-join risk. Joining a holding to a price by
instrument alone can match both price dates, increasing the population while appearing to add useful
price information.

Missing dated FX creates a different risk: values become unmatched instead of

duplicated.
The source valuation remains authoritative native market value. GBP conversion uses the corresponding
dated currency rate; the holdings value per synthetic unit denominator stays one hundred million
synthetic units and excludes cash. A controlled correction is a copied input change, not evidence that
the supplied fixture already contained historical corrections. A controlled fund-name change similarly
creates snapshot history for the exercise rather than claiming history already exists.
Prerequisites and workspace
Start in the training project root with the delivered Databricks environment, approved catalog/schema
and an owned prefix different from another active attempt. Use the explicit advanced prepare task, then
run direct dbt commands from the copied directory. The helper copies supporting files and runtime
checks alongside your attempt; no authoring-repository path is needed once prepared. Record the actual
adapter version and inspect the profile’s local/dev/airflow Databricks targets before choosing one.

Core challenges

Diagnose a join fan-out before repair
Concept
A join’s correctness depends on the relationship between its keys and the grain of each input, not on
whether SQL executes. Holdings are at fund/date/instrument grain; prices are at instrument/date grain.
An instrument-only price join can attach both May prices to every holding and duplicate the holding’s
native value. The resulting consumer sum may look plausible because it contains familiar columns and
positive amounts, but it measures a fan-out rather than the intended position population.
Count the holding keys before enrichment and the matching price rows per key afterward. With this
supplied fixture the date-free price join yields sixteen matches from eight holdings; including the position/
price date restores one dated price per holding. An unmatched price or FX observation has a different
symptom: a left join retains the holding with null enrichment, while an inner join can hide it by dropping
the row. A correct pipeline must detect both duplication and loss. The appropriate diagnosis names
which input relationship violated its key contract before choosing a repair. Merely adding distinct to the
final report can hide multiplicity without selecting the right dated observation.

Phase contents · Reasoning key

Repair enrichment at the intended grain
Concept
An intermediate model isolates business relationships that would otherwise be repeated in every
consumer query. Its output contract is more important than its position in a folder: here it retains each
typed holding and attaches a dated price, dated GBP conversion rate and converted value. Left joins
make missing observations visible to a coverage assertion. They do not excuse incomplete data; they
preserve evidence needed to reject it.
A reusable expression is valuable when it states an actual shared rule, such as converting a decimal native
valuation by an explicitly matched rate with an agreed output precision. That macro should compile into
understandable SQL and should not decide the join keys or manufacture a default rate. For example, a
missing May 20 GBP rate must remain null and fail coverage even though GBP-to-GBP is normally one.
The feed’s declared observation is part of the readiness contract. Fund master may describe a USD base
currency while this report remains explicitly GBP. Moving environment routing or relationship selection
into an opaque macro would make the model harder to review and would not add useful abstraction.

Phase contents · Reasoning key

Write reconciliation that detects the negative case
Concept
A business reconciliation compares a consumer result with an independently specified meaning. It should
detect wrong units, key loss, joined duplication and changed values rather than simply compare two sums
built from the same faulty model. The supplied custodian NAV fixture and Decimal CSV reference give
concrete expected results for the unmodified teaching population. Key membership is as important as
numeric closeness: a report missing one date should fail even when another row absorbs its value.
A negative case tests the assertion’s sensitivity. Removing a copied FX observation should fail enrichment
coverage; feeding that incomplete result into a holdings-only NAV report should not produce accepted
output. Another controlled experiment intentionally changes a holding’s value. That makes baseline NAV
comparison fail for a legitimate reason until the variation’s expected output is used. These cases require
different interpretations. A test message without the input variant and failed node cannot tell a reviewer
whether it detected a real defect, an intended correction or an unrelated connection issue. Keep the
assertion’s unit, tolerance, key set and applicable fixture state explicit.

Phase contents · Reasoning key

Prove incremental update and replay behavior
Concept
Incremental materialization changes how a relation is maintained; it does not automatically make
a pipeline correct under late data. A merge needs a stable unique key that identifies the business
observation being replaced. For holdings that key includes fund, date and instrument. Choosing only a
fund would overwrite another date, while appending without key matching would duplicate an existing
observation when the same input is replayed.
This exercise creates a correction to the first copied May holding by increasing its native market value
by one thousand. The selected observation is GBP-denominated, so its independently expected GBP
value changes by the same amount. The date remains the older fixture date. A filter that processes
only dates greater than the current maximum would miss this legitimate correction.

Replaying the

corrected input twice should produce the same eight-key state after both merges, with one changed
value and no duplicate. A second controlled input appends a new holding key: PEF-EM-GROWTH, May 20,
GB00B3M9JJ78, with native and GBP value 500. Its price and FX already exist, so the result must grow
to nine keys with total exposure another 500 higher. Replaying that combined input must retain nine,
proving insertion as well as update. The experiment is bounded to your namespace and copied fixture; it
does not prove a general production late-arrival policy, transaction isolation or concurrent writer behavior.
Those limitations belong in the handoff.

Explain dependency impact and hand over
Concept
An end-to-end feature needs a consumer question, output grain, units, lineage and evidence that
someone can review. Generating another SQL file is insufficient if its result cannot be interpreted. A
small fund-level report can answer how the two supplied dates differ in holdings exposure; it must label
that observation difference without pretending it is investment return. The fixture lacks the flows and
complete unit history needed to establish that stronger measure.
Attribute history is a separate feature. A snapshot can retain successive fund-name versions using
a stable fund key and validity intervals.

second observed version; it is not a correction to the holding value and does not change the reporting
date.

Reasoning keys

Reasoning: Diagnose a join fan-out before repair
Both May price observations share an instrument identifier. The date-free join therefore doubles
matching holdings even though raw keys are valid. Matching the business date repairs that particular
predicate. A missing match remains a separate coverage concern and should not be solved by
dropping the holding. The diagnostic evidence must show input keys, actual multiplicity and the
corrected relation, so the reviewer can understand the cause without trusting a final aggregate.
Return to Diagnose a join fan-out before repair
Reasoning: Repair enrichment at the intended grain
The intermediate output should have the same holding grain as staging. Its left joins preserve
unmatched observations for diagnosis, and the coverage test rejects them before a consumer result
can be accepted. The decimal macro expresses a valuation rule rather than a relationship rule. A
rate-of-one fallback would hide a missing declared feed observation; inferring currency from fund
master would change the report contract. Both mistakes can yield plausible numbers, so inspect
compiled arithmetic and matched keys together.

Reasoning: Write reconciliation that detects the negative case
The useful reconciliation owns its expected keys and units independently of the enrichment. Missing
FX should be rejected as coverage loss; restoration repairs that input cause. The correction exercise
later changes an input value deliberately, so its expected result is recalculated from the copied input
rather than accepted against a stale baseline NAV. A test that merely matches the mart to another
aggregate of the same broken model would miss shared loss or duplication. Record the variant and

Teaching concepts
Schedule interval, business partition and extraction freshness are independent clocks. The tiny dbt build
refreshes the complete fixture, while the receipt selects four fund rows for a named May date. Task
ordering protects evidence after quality, but real run/task identity and independent values establish
execution. Retries must fit their failure category. End-of-phase keys explain cause and recovery; full
runnable DAG references stay instructor-only.

Question-led foundations and further study
Use questions 1–8 alongside the foundation tasks. Questions 9–13 introduce further study.
Foundations
What problem does Airflow solve alongside dbt?
The Portfolio Analytics workflow orders source readiness, transformation/testing and publication evidence.
dbt provides the model graph; Airflow controls when and under what conditions it runs. Databricks
remains the data execution boundary. A final evidence task records a successful checked handoff and
never performs production publication.
What are a DAG, task, operator, run and task instance?
The owned DAG is <prefix>_portfolio_daily. Its named tasks are source_ready, dbt_build, quality and
publication_evidence. The DAG describes dependencies; each scheduled run has a distinct ID, logical
date and instances of those tasks. Record their states from the fresh run rather than presenting an
unrelated green grid. An operator is the implementation used to execute one task.
Which components parse, schedule, execute and record the work?
The terminal prepares files and seeds. Astro mounts data_products into the DAG processor/scheduler/
worker path. The scheduler creates timed runs; workers execute tasks; the metadata database records
orchestration state; Databricks executes dbt SQL. Inspect the actual compose mount and worker
executable. Files visible in your terminal outside that mount are not automatically visible to a worker.
How do we define dependencies and pass information?
Wire source_ready » dbt_build » quality » publication_evidence. Pass only a small partition/run identifier,
never holdings through XCom. Every task checks the explicit May sample partition while preserving the
actual logical date separately. Failure propagates through dependencies, not through a print statement
saying the work is ready.
What do schedules, logical dates, intervals and catchup mean?
The owned classroom DAG has an explicit two-minute timetable, a timezone-aware start date,
catchup=False and one active run. A scheduler-created interval is not the May business date in these
historical CSVs. The fixture_partition parameter selects 2026-05-20 or 2026-05-21 explicitly. Record
both the logical interval and selected partition. Unpause only this owned DAG during rehearsal and
pause it after collecting evidence. A daily production cadence is a separate design choice. Replay the
same business date to demonstrate idempotence rather than assuming each scheduler day creates new
data. The prepared tiny dbt graph refreshes both fixture dates; the receipt selects four fund rows for
the named partition. Do not describe that selection as date-filtered ingestion.
What should happen when a task fails or retries?
Bound retries and retry delay for transient connection failures. A deliberately missing FX rate or qualityfault marker must fail quality and block publication_evidence. Use logging-only callbacks. Keep the old
accepted receipt unchanged on failure and prove that no receipt was created for the failed run. An auth/
config error differs from business-quality failure and should be diagnosed from its first log error.

How do reruns and backfills produce correct results?
Replaying a business date reruns the same owned relations and compares their keys/values. Retain runspecific receipts and show which date they represent. A controlled holding correction exercises Delta
merge in advanced dbt practice; do not claim a second green task proves idempotence. Restore baseline
source data after the drill. Clearing a task is an operational action on a named run, not a repair to its
input contract.
How do we inspect a run and prove completion?
Keep the current Astro graph/grid/log, exact run/task/attempt IDs, dbt run results and independent
warehouse query. The publication receipt binds the contract, fixture partition, source hashes and checked
artifacts. API checks compare scheduler-created identities and task states. Parsing or dag.test() checks
do not establish scheduled worker execution. Use a fresh run to check the scheduler and worker.
Further study
Questions 9–13 are separately timed advanced study.
How do readiness and freshness differ?
Readiness checks that each supplied raw relation exists with the required columns and population.
Freshness checks _extracted_at separately. Historical May timestamps fail a current freshness threshold
until an explicit recorded preparation refreshes only ingestion timestamps. A sensor waiting for presence
cannot prove freshness. Keep freshness separate from business-date selection and avoid inventing new
business rows.
How should Airflow orchestrate dbt, and when does Cosmos help?
The prepared PythonOperator route calls the delivered isolated worker dbt executable with explicit
project/profile/airflow target and artifact paths. The same Portfolio graph runs as on Wednesday. An
optional Cosmos adapter renders that graph using the installed integration, manifest load mode and
task-time token env; its APIs and actual worker behavior must be checked on the measured stack. Do
not replace dbt with a scaffold print or declare import success as execution.
What do Astro Runtime and the CLI add?
Astro supplies the project/image lifecycle around Airflow. Read the delivered Dockerfile and compose
override, then inspect actual mounts and versions. The intended dbt executable is /home/astro/.venv/
cosmos/bin/dbt. Token delivery uses the prepared databricks_default connection at task time; startup,
refresh, expiry and restart are separate checks. A running scheduler does not prove the profile paths or
warehouse permissions.
How do we test and operate a workflow as a team?
Review source/import checks before scheduling, then run success, intended failure, repair and replay
with independent outputs. Keep owned DAG/relation names and cleanup in the handoff. Prove two
simultaneous learner attempts do not contaminate one another and removal of one leaves the other
intact. Resource provisioning, external alert transports and deployment remain optional/reference work.
Can we deliver a workflow and demonstrate recovery?
Present one scheduled success, one intentional quality failure with no premature evidence, and a repaired
replay against the same holdings data. Bind logs, receipt, run results, versions and independent query to
the contract. Explain the business partition and why task success alone is insufficient. Retain a restart/
auth-expiry rehearsal before acceptance; human pacing and UI walkthrough are still required.

Phase contents · Reasoning key

Inspect a controlled task failure
Concept
A task failure is a state with a cause, not merely a red UI tile. A controlled business-quality fault should
fail the quality task after dbt has built its input and prevent downstream evidence. A bad executable
path or expired token is a different failure category and should not be counted as the intended quality
drill. Reading the first useful log error distinguishes these cases and guides the repair.
The supplied fault marker belongs to your owned stage. While it exists, the quality branch raises its
declared teaching failure and the evidence task becomes upstream-failed. The last accepted receipt
should remain available, but this failed run must create no new accepted receipt. Removing the marker
repairs the controlled cause; rerunning without removing it merely repeats the failure. Retries can repeat

airflow: Phase 2 — advanced practice
Purpose and outcome
Develop the four-task Portfolio workflow into a bounded recovery and handoff exercise. The prepared
entry includes the solved dbt product, readiness helper and task scaffold so advanced work can start
without another learner’s foundation answer. You author the missing gate/recovery/evidence behavior
and demonstrate why the repaired result is correct. Check source freshness and worker authentication
while investigating recovery.
Dataset and pipeline
The eight supplied Portfolio CSVs remain the only business inputs. Four funds on each of two May
dates produce eight report keys. Each dbt build refreshes that full teaching graph; the run’s explicit
partition determines four selected fund/date rows in its receipt. Supported partitions are 20 and 21 May
2026. Reject another date instead of silently substituting the latest input. Schedule intervals are current
operational time; business dates and extraction freshness are independent clocks.
Readiness checks population and extraction timestamp; build invokes the actual worker dbt executable;
quality validates the independent report and a controlled teaching fault; evidence writes a run-bound
receipt only after success. A stale input or a missing raw relation fails readiness, while a quality marker
fails the quality gate. A token or path error belongs to another category. The incident note must explain
which category occurred and why the selected repair addresses it.

provisioned Databricks namespace. Prepare an independent advanced copy and choose a unique owned
prefix. Inspect the staged worker paths instead of copying an old terminal directory into an operator.

remain task-time inputs, never saved in receipts or source.

Core challenges

Define bounded replay and input identity
Concept
Replay asks a workflow to repeat work for an identified business input, so correctness depends on more
than the new run’s timestamp. The scheduler interval describes when Airflow created work; the fixture
partition describes which business-date result the receipt presents. The copied graph refreshes both
supplied dates, and its output check must still select the declared partition explicitly. A current run can
therefore describe historical holdings without claiming that old holdings were newly generated.
Readiness has two separate conditions: the declared raw population exists, and extraction timestamps
meet the freshness promise for this rehearsal. A presence sensor alone cannot establish freshness, while
a fresh timestamp alone cannot establish complete rows. The supplied May timestamps intentionally
reveal that distinction. A documented timestamp-only refresh changes ingestion observation time but
keeps fund/date keys and valuations unchanged. The run must reject an unsupported business date
rather than silently attach an empty or latest result. Those explicit contracts prevent a green replay from
referring to the wrong input or a receipt that only relabels yesterday’s evidence.

Phase contents · Reasoning key

Inject failure and observe useful retry behavior
Concept
Retry policies express a belief about which failures might disappear without changing business inputs.
A transient connection interruption can merit a bounded retry; a missing required FX observation or a
deliberate quality marker requires repair. Retrying the latter only repeats the violated contract. The task
log, attempt identity and delay reveal what happened; a final state alone cannot explain whether retry
was useful.
The prepared classroom default uses a bounded retry and a short delay, with logging-only failure callbacks.
Keep those controls within the rehearsal window rather than introducing unlimited waits. The callback
observes a failure; it must not swallow the operator exception or write an accepted publication receipt.
With one active run and a two-minute schedule, an unrepaired fault can affect a later scheduled run as

Write a short incident handoff
Concept
An incident handoff explains impact, cause, action and evidence of recovery so someone else can decide
what to do next. In this classroom pipeline the impact is blocked publication evidence for a named fixture
partition, not a claimed production outage. The cause must be the observed marker, readiness, auth or
path condition; vague statements such as Airflow was broken do not guide a successor.
The handoff also states ownership: which DAG, stage and prefixed warehouse relations belong to this
attempt and how cleanup preserves others. A prepared Cosmos or hosted observability route can be
useful optional depth, but does not become a missing mandatory deployment step. The finite core
demonstrates an understandable data result, intended failure and recovery.

databricks-cli challenges
The Databricks command-line interface (CLI) provides a read-only discovery route into the prepared
training environment. You establish actual profile/identity, distinguish workspace objects from catalog/
schema/table metadata, inspect permitted qualified names, interpret JSON and explain an access
limitation. A visible workspace directory is not a queried table, and a valid identity is not proof of every
grant. This route contributes context for later warehouse work without provisioning resources.
Before you start
Use the delivered CLI and instructor-provided profile, permitted workspace path and approved
namespace/table. Prepare a copied attempt through mise and keep discovery/evidence notes there. Sign
in outside recordings and retain safe names/types rather than tokens. Inspect installed help/version
instead of treating source pins as measured facts. The metadata JSON is a labelled offline example;
its familiar training names do not prove current resources or permissions. No catalog/schema creation,
grant changes or deployment is necessary for this read-only core.
Suggested timeline and tasks
Estimates include reading, practice, checks and explanation. Allow additional time for environment setup
and optional extensions.
• Phase: Foundation · Task: Establish the CLI identity boundary · Minutes: 9–13
• Phase: Foundation · Task: Separate workspace and Unity Catalog names · Minutes: 9–13
• Phase: Foundation · Task: Inspect permitted schema and table metadata · Minutes: 9–13
• Phase: Foundation · Task: Filter JSON and explain a limited result · Minutes: 9–13
• Phase: Foundation · Task: Produce a bounded discovery handoff · Minutes: 9–13
Choose your phase
• Foundation: Foundation core with explicit completion evidence.
• Advanced: Not offered: no tasks or completion gate.
Finish the core tasks before choosing optional stretch.
Teaching concepts
Profile, identity, workspace path, qualified data name and warehouse execution are separate boundaries.
Structured output preserves those distinctions, while empty/missing/denied observations require
different explanations. Metadata discovery does not query row values or execute a dbt model. Use the
end-of-phase reasoning keys after your attempt and record remaining connected probes individually. Full
instructor reference observations belong separately, and no invented advanced assignment is needed to
make this route complete.
Keep a discovery trail that another participant can repeat safely: the exact profile, permitted namespace,
command category and selected metadata fields. When an object is denied or missing, preserve that
limitation with its context instead of replacing it with a more convenient fixture response. This makes
the subsequent connection and source-loading work easier to diagnose without pretending discovery
granted access.

databricks-cli: Phase 1 — foundations
Purpose and outcome
Use the Databricks CLI to discover a prepared training environment without confusing its object types.
You establish identity, distinguish workspace files from Unity Catalog metadata, inspect permitted catalog/
schema/table information, interpret JSON and explain a limited result. The core is read-only. It prepares
you to ask accurate questions about the later dbt warehouse boundary rather than provisioning resources
to make a listing succeed.
Dataset and pipeline
The starter metadata JSON contains a labelled snapshot of one training catalog, schema, table and
workspace directory. It is an example response for offline interpretation, not proof that these objects
currently exist or are accessible. The workspace path is a filesystem-like object; a catalog/schema/table
name identifies governed data metadata. A SQL warehouse is an execution resource rather than another
folder in that hierarchy. The local snapshot deliberately uses familiar training names so you can practice
those distinctions.
The connected route uses the actual approved namespace and object paths provided by the instructor.
Those values may differ from the example. Identity and metadata access remain separate prerequisites:
a valid login can still lack permission to enumerate a particular catalog or workspace directory. The report
must distinguish such a denial from an empty permitted result or missing object.
Prerequisites and workspace
Prepare an independent copied attempt through mise from the training project root. Use the delivered
CLI and identity setup, then inspect the actual installed version/help. Keep your discovery and evidence
files inside the attempt. The instructor supplies the profile, permitted workspace path, approved catalog/
schema and inspected table; do not guess them from the fixture or create replacement objects.
mise run challenge:v2:prepare databricks-cli phase-one-certified
cd .local/challenges-v2/databricks-cli/phase-one-certified
databricks --version
databricks current-user me --profile "$V2_DBX_PROFILE" --output json

Sign-in happens outside recordings. Record safe identity and qualified object names without tokens.
If no cloud access exists here, inspect the labelled fixture and draft the exact probes with their actual
connected observations pending. Source pins are intended versions, not measured installation facts. The
class does not require broad grants, new schemas, infrastructure deployment or production job changes.
Connection variables
Before running connected probes, set V2_DBX_PROFILE to the delivered profile name, V2_WORKSPACE_PATH
to the permitted workspace directory, DBT_CATALOG and DBT_SCHEMA to the approved namespace, and
V2_DBX_TABLE to the fully qualified inspection table supplied by the instructor. These values describe

existing resources; do not create replacements or copy the fixture names into actual-evidence fields.
Record the configured names safely and keep authentication values outside the notes.
Starter behavior
The metadata snapshot parses successfully and there is no deliberate broken resource. Offline verification
checks that example structure and reports supporting evidence only. Completion requires actual readonly environment observations and an explanation of the distinct object types. A denied path may be
a meaningful permitted exercise observation if its boundary is stated; it is not an excuse to label every
unavailable probe successful. Phase two is explicitly not offered and has no tasks or invented timing.

Core challenges

Establish the CLI identity boundary
Concept
A profile selects connection and authentication context; it is not a business namespace or proof of table
permissions. The CLI executable version determines available command groups and output options,
while the active identity determines whose rights those commands use. A copied source configuration
can describe an intended profile/version without establishing the environment currently loaded in the
terminal.
Inspecting current user is a read-only identity probe. It should return a safe account identity in the
prepared environment, but its success does not imply access to every catalog or warehouse. Keep tokens
out of notes and screenshots. When cloud access is absent, the metadata fixture can teach response
interpretation but cannot establish authenticated identity. This distinction prevents a local JSON parse
from becoming a false readiness pass for later dbt work.
Challenge
Inspect databricks --version and the installed current-user help. Select $V2_DBX_PROFILE, supplied
by the instructor, and run the read-only current-user probe. Record the returned account identity, profile
and CLI version in discovery.md without credential values.

Separate workspace and Unity Catalog names
Concept
Workspace objects organize notebooks, directories and other workspace content; Unity Catalog organizes
governed data objects through catalog, schema and table names. A path containing training_dev does
not mean it is the same object as a catalog named training_dev. The CLI uses different command groups
and response fields for those boundaries.
The fixture’s workspace directory under Shared and its qualified holdings table illustrate that naming
similarity. A SQL warehouse supplies execution for queries, while listing a directory or table metadata
does not run model SQL. Misidentifying these objects can send a learner to a filesystem command when
they need governed table metadata, or lead them to infer data access from a visible notebook folder.

Inspect permitted schema and table metadata
Concept
Metadata discovery answers what objects exist or are visible and how they are described. It does not
automatically return their data rows. Catalog/schema/table listings can be filtered by permissions, so a
user may see less than an administrator. A table’s qualified identity and type help connect a later dbt
source declaration to its physical relation.

same table short name can exist in several schemas, and a source profile can resolve one while a manual
CLI command inspects another. Retaining the full qualified name prevents that confusion. Read-only
discovery must not become provisioning: creating schemas, changing grants or deleting a denied object
would change the environment rather than explain the observed access boundary.

CG product-information capstone
Build a product-information data product for a fictional internal Product Information Analyst using

CG product-information business brief
Capital Group is an investment manager. Its public offerings include American Funds mutual funds,
Capital Group ETFs and separately managed account (SMA) strategies. A share class is a particular way
of owning a mutual fund, with its own identifiers and published costs. An exchange-traded fund (ETF)
trades on an exchange. An SMA implements a strategy in a separately managed account arrangement,
often through a sponsor platform. These are different offering types; their costs and published results
are not automatically interchangeable.
Capital Group describes The Capital System™ as an investment approach combining distinct investment
perspectives with a long-term focus.

Today’s assignment concerns published product information:

identities, expenses and performance context.
You are building a product-information data product for an internal analyst who supports sales and
relationship colleagues answering financial-professional enquiries. The role name and requests below
are fictional classroom scenarios, not statements about an actual CG department. The analyst needs
a dependable research view: product identity, stated fund expenses, performance figures with their
calculation method and reporting date, and reasons to seek more information.

Design workshops
The organisational names and reported incidents in these workshop cases are supplied teaching examples.
They do not establish current CG structures, approved definitions, production status or enterprise service
commitments. Use them to practise discovery; confirm any live business assertion with its accountable

Route: optional, separately timed. Purpose: extend consumer interviews, adoption and reviewable design
decisions. Dataset: CG product stakeholder context and your own contract. Prerequisites: Monday design
teaching. Runtime: documents and facilitated conversation. Deliverables: annotated contract, decision
record and communication plan. Projects contents.

Write one from your build
Choose one design decision from the product you built this week. Write only Context, Decision and
Consequences. Use numbers where you have them, name at least one realistic alternative in the Context,
and include one negative consequence with its mitigation. A partner should be able to read the three
sections and implement the same choice without asking what you meant.

Optional activity: stakeholder interviews and a Catalyst contract
This optional extension connects the stakeholder interview with Tuesday’s contract revision. Use it when
adoption or a working-practice concern needs more investigation. Tuesday’s required contract exercise
does not depend on an empathy map.
Optional interview-to-contract extension
DURATION 30–45 minutes outside the core route
OUTPUTS Evidence-labelled empathy map, revised draft and correction log

1. Choose an authorised business example that a participant understands, such as CG product-information
or a product from Monday. In threes, assign consumer and two creator/reviewer roles; use a producer
brief or invite producer validation for source questions.
2. Inspect an example local contract and identify the relevant decision, source and promises. Do not treat
a generated schema or approval as a confirmed fact.
3. Interview the consumer about a real pain point and current workaround. Record observations separately
from interpretations. Map says and does from evidence; mark thinks and feels as hypotheses and ask for
confirmation or correction.
4. Feed the notes and confirmed requirements into Catalyst. Ask it to revise the affected contract sections
and name unsupported decisions with their responsible roles. Use synthetic training inputs when needed,
labelled as synthetic and distinct from source facts.
5. Open the revised file, inspect the changes and compare it with the interview, source and original draft.
Check that an adoption action addresses the stated concern and that no invented permission or approval
appeared.
Check: a requirement is traceable from the consumer statement to the contract; an adoption concern and
a technical/source defect are not confused; source gaps remain visible. The result is a reviewed draft with
outstanding decisions, not a live approval.

When a proposed response makes the concern worse
A response aimed at one concern can worsen another. Repeated assurances that an expert is trustworthy
may increase a consumer’s fear of losing control.

Demonstrating that a calculation is correct may

leave their actual workflow problem unresolved. In this sense, a response can backfire: the intended
improvement produces less willingness to adopt.
Test the interpretation before prescribing a response. Ask which part of the work the person must explain,
control or approve, and what evidence would change their assessment. Conflicting interests may need
negotiated responsibilities or a transition plan rather than more persuasion. If information does not
change behaviour, investigate the remaining concern rather than repeating the same explanation.

Addressing the concern
For the parallel-spreadsheet user, first distinguish a source defect from a need for explanation, control
or training. A volatile asset may be behaving correctly but appear implausible without context; a note
explaining that behaviour can help, while a genuine defect needs a technical correction.
Involve the consumer early in design and review, make progress and decisions visible, and offer a real
channel for feedback. If they need to verify a result, agree a reconciliation view or comparison they can
inspect. Recognition can support adoption when it reflects an actual contribution, but visibility and credit
do not replace access, quality or useful decision rights. Avoid simulated controls that give an impression
of influence without a real effect.

When the quadrants don’t align
Worked example: a salesperson using a portfolio-simulation report. Says: “I recommend this portfolio to
a customer” (though they don’t like the report). Does: observed using the report correctly in a sale, and
the metrics look fine. Thinks/Feels: ambivalent, both frustrated (given a report that doesn’t work the way
they want) and accomplished (they made the sale). A successful sale can coexist with frustration about
the report.
When the quadrants do not align, investigate the difference.

A difference may reflect uncertainty,

context, constraints or reluctance to criticise a tool they still need. Ask for an example and confirm the
interpretation rather than inferring a motive.

Optional activity: interviewing with an empathy map
Optional stakeholder interview
DURATION 45–60 minutes outside the core route
OUTPUTS Interview notes and an evidence-labelled empathy map

Choose a business data product that one participant understands well. In threes, assign consumer, producer
and creator roles. The creator interviews both roles using Monday’s question prompts; the participant closest
to the consumer’s actual work should represent that role.
Before the interview, record what you know about the current workflow, previous changes and existing
difficulties. If a colleague knows the consumer’s context better, ask for it and label it as indirect evidence.
Avoid assuming that a concern is irrational or that a person will react in a particular way.
During the interview, follow “what decisions depend on this data?” with “how are you making those decisions
now?”. Map one pain point into says, does, thinks and feels. Quote observations in the first two quadrants;
label the latter two as hypotheses and ask the consumer to confirm, correct or reject them. If their report and
observed workflow differ, investigate the conditions before attributing a motive.
Produce one requirement, one adoption action and one unresolved question from the map. Check that the
action responds to a stated concern, preserves a real feedback or decision channel, and does not disguise a
technical or contractual defect as a stakeholder problem.
For a pair, use the source brief for producer evidence and record the missing validation. A third observer may
check leading questions and unsupported inferences. Review the interview’s purpose and outputs at the end
so an absorbing conversation still produces a usable handoff.

Case study: Interview findings and product decisions
Cases: consumer decisions and working constraints
• Client analytics. Ingesting client engagement data (website visits, email engagement), grouped by user
role rather than individual users. The interview raised the question of how to define an outlier (compare
to yesterday? to prior periods? to an external baseline?) and clarified that outliers should be reported
on, not removed, because they’re informative. Decision: report informative outliers rather than deleting
them. Reasoning: unusual engagement may be the very signal the consumer needs. Lesson: agree the
comparison baseline and keep the interview focused on a recorded requirement.
• Exposures: security-level exposure informs portfolio rebalancing. Missing data can prevent the decision
and breach detailed contractual commitments. With no equivalent fallback, agree the failure impact,
source dependencies, escalation and consumer update before setting a deadline.
• CG investor data. Data that influences investors’ financial decision-making; if it’s late or worked around,
the risk is the investor goes to a competitor, with frustration and loss of trust in the service. Proposed
focus: real-time delivery. Useful clarification: “real time” here means market close. Always pin down
what real time means to the consumer. Decision and reasoning: Define “real time” using the stated
business event, such as market close. A named event is more usable than an ambiguous latency term.
Verify the event with this consumer.
• Global results: a two-day SLA has a manual fallback for the first six months, followed by stricter
commitments. Consumers want automation but need evidence that it matches their existing result.
Agree a parallel comparison, transition criteria and the later service promise; upstream checks alone do
not establish adoption.
• HR promotion pipeline. Data integrated across several stages of the HR process, with different data
needed at different points; combines internal data (employees) with external data (competitor pay ranges).
Empathy finding: risk and anxiety around promotions. Decision and reasoning: Identify which stage uses
each field and who may access it. Different stages and external pay sources create distinct meaning and
sensitivity questions. Validate the staged workflow with its owner.
• Company data. The reference data representing companies, foundational for the entire enterprise, critical
to compliance, ESG, stock trading, and many other functions. Decision and reasoning: Declare the

reference identity and accountable source before designing consumers’ views. Multiple downstream
compliance, ESG and trading uses raise change impact. Trace each consumer dependency.
• Legal invoices: budgeting external-counsel spend depends on vendor cooperation and the ability to
