missing tool, source or agreement with its owner.

Case study: Interview findings and product decisions
Cases: definitions, responsibility and trust
• Salesforce data (external source). An initial problem is assigning the roles. Who is actually the consumer
and who the producer? Issues were data duplication and getting data in a timely manner, ultimately leaving
the consumer feeling they couldn’t do their job, with concern about explaining the result to others (which
makes esteem relevant). Decision and reasoning: Resolve producer and consumer responsibilities before
specifying freshness and deduplication. A source label does not identify who can promise delivery. Name
the accountable contact.
• Investor detail and content data (combined product, broken down by region). Delays in refreshing the
published pages. A useful finding: the issues persist mainly through lack of prioritisation, and answering
why it was never prioritised is what stops you falling into the same trap again.
• Capital market assumptions (received annually; drives forecasting). Impacts of delayed data collection
and errors: reputational risk. That risk has actually been realised: a consumer of the documents came
back and said “your numbers are wrong” before the team caught it themselves.
• Marketing publication: “real time” means the moment a document becomes legally effective. An hourly
job may miss that business trigger. Agree the effective event, producer notification, permitted publication
time and handling of a delayed notification.
• Sales data. Technical participants need a business representative to validate the consumer perspective.
There’s a voice of the business, of the consumer, of the producer, and of the technical team, and balancing
them is hard. Decision and reasoning: Have a business representative validate the interpretation before
treating a technical discussion as consumer evidence. Multiple voices serve different responsibilities.
Mark any missing validation in the handoff.
• Monthly data feed with missing or inconsistent data. The consuming team applies a band-aid fix: when
data is missing, they reuse the last reported data for their calculations. The frustration is that this happens
monthly; the provider is not proactive about following the contract or even communicating when data is
missing, and SLAs are violated. The expectation is a fix within an hour or so, and it sometimes takes over
a day. Decision and reasoning: Agree how missing values, temporary reuse of prior values and correction
delays are communicated. A silent carried-forward value changes the meaning of the result. Label the
fallback and ask the consumer whether it is acceptable.
• Factsheet publication. At a high level, agreeing SLAs is easy; the pain is in the details, e.g. week-ofAfrican-market data missing at the time of publication when the contract requires interest data available
without gaps by a certain time. Upstream may only commit to “available by second business day” when
the downstream deadline is earlier. Pin these things down at the start of the contract. The timelines
are contractual first (multiple parties sit between producer and end consumer), with some regulatory
obligations layered on top. Decision and reasoning: Reconcile upstream second-business-day availability
with the earlier downstream publication deadline. A promise cannot ignore a producer dependency.
Record the mismatch and its owner before agreeing the contract.
• Dependency ownership: a downstream team may bear the impact of a third-party failure without
controlling its cause. Record the dependency owner, escalation route and consumer communication.
Investigate frustration through the workflow rather than assigning a motive to the affected team.

• AFSG semantic layer: a lakehouse names an implementation, while the consumer needs reports or
discoverable service data for analysis. State the business decision, supported vocabulary and output

• Product reference data for portfolio simulation. Wholesalers build hypothetical portfolios for advisors
and need product reference data behind a search bar. Value discussion: fast search is a non-functional
requirement; the real value is improved decision-making for sales conversations. Hardest question: who
is the consumer, the internal salesperson or the end advisor? Lots of products have this ambiguity. The
missing SLA is a design gap to resolve with the consumer and producer. Decision and reasoning: Identify
the salesperson and advisor roles separately, then distinguish search speed from the sales decision
enabled. Performance is one requirement; consumer value is another. Add the missing service promise.
• Holdings data. A flattened holdings/asset-reference record with multiple consumer categories: regulatory
reporters (“keep us out of litigation”), shareholders, research analysts, sales. Value and ROI require further
evidence. Holdings are scattered today, so the product is a consolidation view, and the value is abstracting
complexity away from downstream consumers. Design implication: option value (creating the ability for
other systems to develop around something) is intuitively valuable but the hardest kind of value to justify,
and often where the most value lies. Decision and reasoning: List the different consumer decisions and
what complexity the consolidation removes for each. Option value may matter even without a current
monetary estimate. Record the assumptions rather than claiming a measured return.
• Capital market assumptions (CSG). Parts of the product already exist, but they always need a few extra
data points from external vendors, and each request is a slow procurement process, so the value is a
data product that includes everything they need. Legal and compliance questions include whether vendor
terms permit use by an AI workflow. Check the actual contract and renewal terms; a technical capability
does not establish permitted use. Decision and reasoning: Include procurement delay and permitted
vendor use in feasibility and cost. Extra external fields can change both timing and rights. Ask the
authorised owner to confirm the current terms.

Learning Review
Retrieve the distinction between an observation, an inferred motivation and a product requirement. Apply it to
a consumer who reproduces a report in Excel: what would you ask before concluding that the problem is trust?
Check that the proposed response addresses the actual workflow, names the producer/approver dependency
and retains evidence for the chosen decision. Return to the interview when those facts are missing.

Optional activity: planning stakeholder communication
Optional adoption planning
OUTPUTS A communication plan and decision-rights register

In groups, choose an existing data product in your organisation. Who are its stakeholders? Is it successful,
meaning used by its consumers and meeting its SLAs?
Now suppose you want to build a version 2. Who would block it, and why? Who would it affect negatively?
Positively? Who should be involved in each design decision, who can represent a role, and why? Who should
be kept informed but not involved? Finally, suppose you do all this analysis and it still fails. Why? What did
you miss? Choose a product with a real change in responsibilities or working practice.

Case study: Adoption decisions and consequences
Client and party master data. A heavily used enterprise product has late nightly completion and merge/unmerge
problems in unique client profiles. A proposed second version adds critical-event updates during the day and
improves integration. Decision: use an architect or engineering manager to represent feasibility during initial
discovery, then involve the implementation engineers at a declared scope checkpoint. Reasoning: discovery
needs time to define the desired outcome, while delivery needs technical challenge before promises are fixed.
Lesson: document which decisions require engineering input and share the context; “we will involve them
later” is not a decision rule.

Secure-lending application. A vendor product replaces an internal interface, leaving the old application as a
back-end feed. Users outside the main group must learn a new interface; the maintaining team loses some
control and institutional influence. Decision: agree the changed operational responsibilities, vendor SLA and
transition support before migration. Reasoning: responsibility may shift to the vendor, but internal consumers
still need a clear accountable contact. Lesson: a marginal user may value simplicity while a power user values
specialist capabilities. Evaluate both workflows and preserve critical requirements rather than treating all
resistance as unwillingness to change.
Disclosure system. A dynamic, text-based disclosure replaces static tags. Existing users know the tag system,
and an incorrect disclosure has serious business consequences. Decision: investigate reliability objections,
confirm approval criteria with the accountable role, and compare the systems in parallel for a defined transition
period. Reasoning: validated calculations alone do not address uncertainty about a new workflow or lost review
control. Lesson: distinguish a real reliability defect from an adoption concern through evidence and interview
questions; avoid dismissing a concern because the new system appears technically sound.
Web analytics migration. An old internal system requires increasing support, while the migration has substantial
cost and limited immediate reporting benefit. Decision: involve the budget owner with a clear explanation of
support risk, maintainability and service promises. Reasoning: uncertain benefits should remain uncertain
rather than being given invented metrics. Lesson: use a measurable commitment when evidence supports
it, and explain qualitative benefits in plain language when it does not. “Available every day except a stated
maintenance allowance” can be easier to review than a percentage with no assumptions attached.

kafka: Phase 1 — foundations
Purpose and outcome
Explore how a dataset-arrived event can trigger a prepared processing workflow without making the
event the dataset itself. This is an optional event clinic. You inspect a contract, use a supplied broker/
consumer bridge, follow event identity into an actual run/output and reason about replay. The bridge and
processing baseline are prepared so learners do not need to build Kafka infrastructure, author a complete
consumer and repeat dbt/Airflow labs in one phase.
Dataset and pipeline
The event contains event identifier, type, dataset identifier/version, controlled fixture location and arrival
timestamp. The small immutable holdings fixture produces exposure A 150, B 100 and C zero. This
retained event fixture is intentionally separate from the assigned eight-seed Portfolio Analytics pipeline.
Its prepared local Airflow/DuckDB chain demonstrates event identity and offset semantics; it cannot
establish Databricks/Astro completion for the assigned guides.
Kafka retains records in an ordered partition log, and a consumer group tracks progress through offsets.
The supplied bridge validates allowed input identity/location, triggers the prepared DAG and records
partition/offset/run evidence.

Start the prepared local broker and inspect a topic
Concept
A Kafka topic contains partition logs: ordered lanes of retained records. Each record has an offset,
its position in that lane. A consumer group maintains its own progress. Two groups can consume
retained records independently, but two learners accidentally using the same group can affect each
other’s observed offset progression. Topic/group ownership is therefore part of the classroom setup
rather than an optional naming preference.
A broker metadata response establishes that the intended topic/partition is reachable. It does not mean
an event was produced or a workflow completed. The prepared local runtime keeps infrastructure work
outside this short clinic. A port collision or missing container engine is a setup condition; it should not
be repaired by deleting unrelated services. The learner’s task is to inspect the actual allocated boundary

Produce and follow a uniquely identified event
Concept
Producer acknowledgement means the broker accepted a record at a partition/offset. It does not mean
a consumer processed it or a downstream data job succeeded. The supplied bridge reads the event,
validates its input contract and triggers the prepared Airflow run with a deterministic identity. Its evidence
records broker position and the corresponding run so those boundaries can be traced.
Consumer offset progress also has a policy: acknowledging or committing a consumed record can occur
before downstream success, depending on the bridge contract. The learner must inspect that behavior
rather than call every committed offset completed data. A uniquely identified event avoids confusing a
current trace with a prior record already retained in the topic. Actual task states and receipts provide
later execution evidence.

Phase contents · Reasoning key

Replay and explain duplicate policy
Concept
Replay policy defines how retained records are interpreted when the same event is seen again. The
supplied bridge can reuse an identical completed run when its receipt matches the event payload. A
record with the same event identity but changed payload is a conflict, not a new legitimate input under
that policy. The broker can assign a later offset while the bridge reuses the prior run.
This is a bounded teaching strategy based on a matching completed receipt, not a general exactly-once
guarantee. An existing run without a matching completed receipt needs explicit recovery inspection, and
concurrent events or a broader deduplication store introduce additional design questions. The learner
should explain those limits rather than claiming that a successful replay solved all distributed failure
modes. Business output stability and run reuse are separate checks.
Challenge

replay.

conflicting-payload rejection and its offset behavior.

SQL readiness check: five patterns
Knowledge check: Read the SQL meaning
Before running a query, can you name its grain, join relationship and treatment of unmatched or null records?
Which small fixture would distinguish two plausible interpretations?

Predict the grain, join behaviour and returned rows for each query before running it. Then vary one
condition: use a left join, add a grouping column, stack another CTE, introduce a cast, or change the
filter.
1. A staging rename.
select id as customer_id, name as customer_name from customers

Same rows, two renamed columns, which is what a staging model does.
2. A two-table join.
select o.order_id, c.customer_name
from orders o
join customers c on o.customer_id = c.customer_id

With unique customer keys, one row per order that has a matching customer; orders without a match
disappear. That disappearance is the difference between join and left join, and it matters in the
intermediate models.
3. A GROUP BY with a filter.
select customer_id, count(*) as order_count
from orders
where status = 'complete'
group by customer_id

One row per customer: grouping changes the grain from orders to customers. The filter runs first, then
the grouping collapses orders into customers.
4. One CTE.
with completed as (
select * from orders where status = 'complete'
)
select customer_id, count(*) as order_count
from completed
group by customer_id

Identical output to snippet 3: a CTE is a named sub-query, and the intermediate models are built out of
them.
5. The negative amount.
select order_id, amount from payments where amount < 0

If negative payments violate the contract, this query returns the offending rows. It returns no rows when
that rule holds. A dbt data test uses the same pattern.
Explain each result before using the pattern in your project. If a prediction surprises you, try a small
input with an unmatched key, a null or a duplicate and compare the result.

Appendix A — Readiness

Appendix A — Readiness
Use this appendix to prepare for the course. Read the business explanation before the design exercises,
or go straight to the practical instructions to open the workspace, check your setup, or find a definition.

Investment and organisational context
Understanding the business comes before choosing a transformation. A SQL query can run correctly and
still answer the wrong question if it treats a client’s account as a fund, a trade as new money entering
the account, or a transaction fee as an advisor’s income. The sections below explain the distinctions you
will use when designing the course’s data products. If you need to prepare your computer first, follow
Open the correct project and Setup and readiness, then return here before the design exercises.

Capital Group and the Capital System
Capital Group describes the Capital System as an investment approach in which several portfolio
managers contribute to one portfolio.

They share research and ideas while making their own

investment decisions. The published explanation also describes investment groups that make decisions
independently. The Capital System.
This helps explain why “portfolio” can mean different things in different conversations. It can mean the
whole collection of investments, or a particular manager’s part of that collection. A manager’s part is
often called a portion or sleeve. When you work with a real CG dataset, ask its owner which level the
portfolio identifier represents. Do not assume that a field called portfolio_id always identifies the same
kind of thing.
An account answers a different question: which investments are recorded for this investor? A fund brings
investors’ money together to invest under a shared objective. The investor owns shares in the fund, while
the fund holds the underlying investments. A client-facing advisor helps serve the investor’s relationship
and needs. The portfolio manager decides how to invest within the authority they have been given. These
roles and levels are related, but they are not interchangeable.
Perspective

What it describes

Investor and account

An investor has an account with recorded positions. Those positions may include
shares in funds.

Investment management

A fund or investment mandate has a portfolio of investments. Managers may be
responsible for different portions of it.

Client relationship

An advisor serves clients and uses reports about their accounts. The advisor is not
necessarily the manager choosing a fund’s investments.

These are ways of understanding the business, rather than a diagram of CG’s databases. The exact
relationships and names depend on the service and dataset you are working with.
A share class is a particular class of shares in a fund. Classes can have different charges and arrangements
for paying financial professionals, even when they belong to the same fund. Capital Group’s shareclass explanation gives examples of these differences. The CG capstone selects Class F-3 offerings and
published fund expense ratios; these figures do not describe every investor cost.
A model portfolio describes a proposed mix of investments. A target allocation says how much is intended
to be invested in each part. Actual holdings describe what is held on a particular date. A mandate sets
the investment objective, authority and restrictions. A list of securities and percentages could appear in
any of these, so ask what the percentages mean before using them.

Appendix A — Readiness

Ownership, look-through and double counting
Suppose a client account owns fund shares worth 1,000 GBP. A look-through report explains that
investment as 600 GBP of equity exposure and 400 GBP of bond exposure. The client still has 1,000 GBP
invested in the fund. Adding the fund shares and the two underlying exposures would count the same
money twice and produce 2,000 GBP. Use the underlying exposures to explain the investment, not to
add another layer of owned assets. The same problem occurs if you add a whole portfolio’s value to the
values of the manager portions that make it up.
Two accounts and several funds can all hold the same security. Finding that shared security does not
show that either account owns shares in those funds. To establish fund ownership, you need a record
of the account’s fund shares or another clearly defined ownership relationship. A join on a common
instrument can repeat one trade across several funds and inflate a total. Being able to join two tables is
not enough to show that the result makes business sense.

People, products and accountable roles
Investors provide the money being invested. Financial advisors support client relationships. Portfolio
managers make investment decisions, and analysts contribute research.

Building a data product

introduces another set of responsibilities: someone supplies the source data, someone builds the
product, someone agrees its business meaning, someone uses it, and someone supports the platform
on which it runs.
For example, a trading-operations team might supply executions in CSV files. That team is the producer;
the CSV is how the data is delivered. A creator checks the input and builds an activity report. The business
owner agrees what the report’s fees and totals mean. An advisor or reporting analyst consumes the result,
while a platform operator keeps the scheduled job running. This example illustrates the responsibilities;
it is not an organisational chart for CG.
One person may carry out several of these jobs, but you should still be able to say who answers each
question. Who can explain or correct the source? Who agrees the product’s meaning? Who approves its
use? Who responds when it fails? The person funding a project may be different from its data owner,
and the person approving a release may be different from its consumer. Titles such as DPM or steward
help only when their responsibilities have been explained for the product.

Events, states and financial measures
A trade execution records a completed purchase or sale of an instrument. A fund subscription means
buying participation in a fund, and a redemption means selling that participation back. A contribution
or withdrawal moves money into or out of an account. Selling an investment inside an account usually
replaces the investment with cash; it does not necessarily mean the client has withdrawn money.
A position describes how much is held at a particular time. To calculate a complete closing position, start
with the opening position, add purchases, subtract sales and include other changes such as transfers or
share splits. If you only have a list of trades, you can calculate the change represented by those trades.
You cannot know the complete closing balance without knowing what was held beforehand and whether
anything else changed. A negative result could represent a short position, but it could also arise because
the opening holding or another event is missing.
An execution price is the price paid or received in a trade. A valuation price is the price chosen to value
a holding at a particular time. An independent daily price feed can provide a valuation price even when
the account has not traded that day. The latest execution price can be a useful classroom substitute,
but it may be old and is not necessarily the market’s closing price. Check the price’s date, currency and
units before multiplying it by quantity. A bond quote per 100 of face value needs different handling from
a price per share.
379

+44 (0)20 3583 0972 | info@decoded.com | decoded.com

DECODED

Appendix A — Readiness

Market value estimates what a position is worth using an appropriate price. Assets under management,
or AUM, describes the value of assets managed within a stated collection of accounts or investments.
You must explain what is included, when it is valued and which currency is used. Net asset value, or
NAV, is assets less liabilities. NAV per share divides that amount by the number of outstanding shares.
Averaging underlying security prices does not calculate either measure. Investor.gov’s NAV definition.
Cost basis is the acquisition cost assigned to an investment under the relevant accounting rules. When
part of a holding is sold, those rules determine which acquisition costs belong to the sale and which
remain.

Realised gain concerns sold investments; unrealised gain concerns investments still held.

Purchases less sales do not automatically give you the remaining holding’s cost basis. Calculating an
investment return also requires a method for handling valuations, income, time and money entering or
leaving the account. Trading activity and transaction fees alone cannot give you that return.
Transaction fees are charges connected with executions. Management fees pay for management services
under a separate arrangement. A fee paid by a client account does not tell you who received it. Keep
these meanings separate in the report.
For every financial total, explain which records it includes, the date or period, the currency, the units and
how missing values are handled. Adding USD and JPY numbers produces a number, but not a comparable
measure of wealth. Checks must also protect the final report: valid trades can still be duplicated by a
join, assigned to the wrong advisor or omitted from an aggregate.

The two supplied business cases
Portfolio Analytics is the fund-reporting case used on Wednesday and Thursday. It contains historical
holdings with supplied market values. Preserve those values rather than replacing them with quantity
multiplied by a quoted price. Dated exchange rates convert the values to GBP, and cash is supplied
separately. The report divides holdings-only GBP value by 100 million synthetic units to demonstrate a
calculation. That result is a teaching value per unit, not an official fund or share-class NAV.
Friday uses the CG product-information brief. The source snapshot describes ETFs, Class F-3 mutualfund offerings and SMA strategies. It contains product identities, expense components, published returns
and provenance. The direct internal consumer is a fictional Product Information Analyst.

From source to consumer, and from code to execution
A data product often starts with operational events and reference data. The creator checks those inputs,
gives them useful business definitions and prepares an output for a consumer. “Source-aligned” means
organised around an originating source; “domain-aligned” means organised around reusable business
meaning; “consumer-aligned” means designed for a particular use. These names describe the product’s
purpose. Staging, intermediate and curated describe processing stages. A single product can use several
processing stages, and bronze/silver/gold is another set of names for those stages.
Use the project instructions and naming conventions provided for your exercise.

Other teams may

use different repositories or deployment arrangements. The development container, Airflow workers,
Databricks warehouse and deployment pipeline each have their own jobs and permissions. Running a
local check is not the same as running the product on the warehouse, and passing a quality check is not
the same as obtaining approval to publish it. For real work, ask the responsible team which procedures
and approvals apply.

Why the course uses a dev container
VS Code is the editor: it shows project files, previews Markdown and opens terminals. A workspace is the
project folder you have opened. The training dev container is the prepared Linux environment connected
to that workspace. Its configuration supplies compatible tools, certificate settings and setup tasks so the
class can run the same commands without installing every dependency separately on each computer.
Keep track of the execution location. A terminal opened in the connected VS Code window runs inside the
dev container. A terminal you open from your computer’s desktop runs on the host. Docker also launches
a separate Airflow runtime, and connected dbt work sends SQL to a remote Databricks warehouse. The
assigned v2 route uses copied projects with dbt-databricks. Offline file checks and CSV calculations
support the work but do not establish warehouse execution.

Product alignment is a separate question. Calling a product source-aligned, domain-aligned or consumeraligned says whose needs it serves. Layer terms say how far a model has been processed, and one aligned
product may contain several layers.
So which of Wednesday’s two vocabularies do you use? When you document or talk about a product,
to consumers, to non-technical colleagues or in the marketplace listing, call it source-, domain- or
consumer-aligned. When you build, follow the supplied project’s folders and prefixes, including stg_ and
int_ where provided. Do not assume every Catalyst version or team uses identical naming. If a repository

uses bronze/silver/gold, explain those processing labels separately from product alignment. A layer label
such as “gold” does not explain whose decision the table supports.

Glossary
Further background is available in The Capital System, Capital Group’s share-class explanation and

Term

Meaning and course use

Fund

A pooled investment vehicle that invests for its shareholders.

Fund share

An investor’s unit of ownership in a fund. Owning the share is different from directly
owning the fund’s underlying securities.

Share class

A class of shares in a fund with its own charges and arrangements.

Account

A record of investments associated with an investor.

Mandate

The investment objective, authority and restrictions governing a management

Portfolio

A collection of investments. It can describe a whole investment portfolio or a

A separately managed part of an investment portfolio.

Model portfolio

A proposed mix of investments, rather than a record of what is actually owned.

The intended proportion invested in each part of a portfolio.

An investment quantity held by a stated owner on a stated date. Portfolio Analytics

An investment object such as a share, bond or ETF, identified by its own key.

The person or organisation whose investment relationship is represented.

A person who makes investment decisions within assigned authority.

A person who researches investments and contributes information to investment

Book

An advisor’s defined set of clients or accounts.

The quantity held at a time.

A completed purchase or sale.

An investor’s purchase of participation in a fund.

An investor’s sale of participation back to a fund.

A movement of cash. External contributions differ from trade settlement.

The price paid or received in a trade.

Valuation price

The price chosen to value a holding at a time.

Market value

A position’s value using an appropriate price and units. Portfolio Analytics preserves
supplied values.

Assets under management. Explain which assets are included, their valuation date
and currency.

Dimension

This example uses an imaginary account-holdings table to explain a three-table join. It is not a Morningstar
or CG schema. Each holdings row carries an account ID and instrument ID; the other two tables add the
client, advisor and instrument descriptions:
select
h.as_of_date, h.portfolio_id,
p.client_id, p.advisor_id,
h.instrument_id, i.ticker, i.asset_class,
h.weight, h.market_value
from example_account_holdings h
join portfolios p using (portfolio_id)
join instruments i using (instrument_id);

The holdings table supplies weight and market_value, while the dimensions explain who and what the
row concerns. Before summing market value, check that the rows share a currency or join an FX rate.
Before summing weight, check whether the intended total is per portfolio, date, asset class, or the whole
result set.

Window functions
Extra
A group by collapses many rows to one row per group. A window function keeps each row and computes over
related rows selected by over (...). Ranking uses an ordered window; rolling measures add a frame.
Function

Tie behaviour for values 100, 90, 90, 80

row_number()

1, 2, 3, 4: every row differs; the order inside a tie needs a second sort key.

rank()

1, 2, 2, 4: ties share rank and leave a gap.

dense_rank()

1, 2, 2, 3: ties share rank and the next distinct value follows without a gap.

Appendix A — Readiness

For an illustrative expense ranking, equal published expense ratios can share a dense rank. This orders a stated
measure; it does not establish suitability or all-in cost. Exclude unknown values from the numeric ranking
while retaining them in the enquiry’s follow-up output.
select
product_id,
net_expense_ratio_bps,
dense_rank() over (order by net_expense_ratio_bps) as expense_rank
from product_cost_example
where net_expense_ratio_bps is not null;

product_cost_example is an illustrative relation; use your capstone’s actual output and field names.

For a rolling measure, partition by asset_class gives each class its own history, order by trade_date
defines sequence, and rows between 6 preceding and current row includes the current row plus six earlier
rows. It’s a seven-row window. That’s seven calendar days only when each class has a row for every date.
with daily as (
select
t.trade_date,
i.asset_class,
sum(t.gross_value) as traded_value,
sum(t.fee) as fees,
count(*) as trades
from dom_trading__trade t
join dom_instrument__instrument i using (instrument_id)
group by t.trade_date, i.asset_class
)
select
trade_date,
asset_class,
traded_value,
fees,
trades,
sum(traded_value) over (
partition by asset_class
order by trade_date
rows between 6 preceding and current row
) as rolling_7d_value
from daily;

The CTE builds one row per asset class per trading date first. The outer query then adds up those daily totals,
so each row in the window is one day for one asset class.

Appendix B — Data contracts and decision records, worked
Recording decisions: the RFD
A migration plan records what will change; a decision record explains why. For example, a team choosing
a lakehouse should record why Delta Lake and a star schema fit its constraints, and which alternatives
it rejected. A future reviewer can then assess the decision without reconstructing its rationale.

ADR and RFD vocabulary
An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) captures a design choice and its rationale. The supplied course
materials use a Request for Discussion (RFD), with repository and review conventions illustrated below.
Confirm the current internal process with the product’s architecture owner before applying it to live work.
The reasoning begins with three sections:
Section

What goes in it

Context

Measured technical, business, compliance, organisational and cost constraints, stated
without arguing for one option

Decision

One choice in active voice, specific enough for an engineer to implement

Consequences

Positive, negative and neutral effects, including mitigations for accepted risks

One RFD records one decision. If two independent choices have appeared in the Decision section, split
them so that either can later be replaced without rewriting the history of the other.

The Capital Group wrapper
The supplied RFD example numbers decisions with four digits and stores each one at rfd/NNNN/README.
md. Work happens on a matching rfd/NNNN branch. Review comments and alternative proposals stay on

the pull request, so the whole discussion stays attached to the merged RFD.
The lifecycle is a five-stage flow with two possible outcomes at the final stage:
Stage

State

Form the question

ideation

Open a draft PR

prediscussion

Invite review, revise on the PR and get approval before

discussion

Phase 4
Merge the agreed record

published

Record the outcome

committed when acted on, or abandoned when the

published decision is dropped

Numbers are not reused. When a committed decision is superseded, the old RFD stays in the repository
and links to the replacement, because deleting it would remove the constraints the next team needs to
understand.

When the RFD gate applies
In the supplied governance case, the paved path is an approved-pattern registry maintained by the Data
Architect community. These gate criteria are training-case rules; confirm the current internal registry,
classification thresholds and authorised reviewers before applying them to a live product. A design that
cites an approved pattern can proceed without formal architecture review. An off-pattern design triggers
398

DECODED

Appendix B — Data contracts and decision records, worked

a Phase 3 Data Architect review and uses the RFD to describe the deviation, alternatives and trade-offs. A
separate Phase 3 InfoSec gate applies to products classified Restricted or above, or to products covered
by named regulatory requirements. Some designs trigger both gates, with each reviewer signing the part
they own.

Measure before you optimise
Expert
Start an optimisation record from a measurement. “The query feels slow” isn’t one. Take a 14.2-million-row
holdings table with 3,847 files and a 4.1 MB median file size, where the p95 account query took 12.3 seconds
against a 5-second target. The query plan showed a full scan. Those numbers are what justify comparing
compaction, Z-ordering, liquid clustering, pruning and data skipping, and Appendix C has the full table. Put
the baseline in the RFD Context. In Consequences, say how you’ll re-measure after the change and what the
chosen technique costs you.

The following illustrative SQL returns offending rows; it is a review example, not an additional classroom
execution task. Its null handling is deliberate because a SQL comparison with null is unknown.
select *
from exposure_candidate
where portfolio_id is null or as_of_date is null
or exposure_type is null or updated_at is null
or quality_status is null
or quality_status not in ('CURRENT', 'STALE', 'MISSING', 'QUARANTINED')
or (quality_status in ('CURRENT', 'STALE') and
(exposure_value is null or source_file_date is null
or exposure_value < 0 or exposure_value > 1))
or (quality_status in ('MISSING', 'QUARANTINED') and
(exposure_value is not null or source_file_date is not null));

Separately compare accepted publication times with the requested date’s agreed deadline in America/
New_York: CURRENT must be on time and STALE late. Verify source_file_date against the accepted

provider file and its documented business-date mapping; do not assume file date equals as_of_date.
These checks need delivery provenance and a business calendar beyond the row-shape SQL. Also group
by the three key columns and reject any count greater than one. Schema, key, duplicate or status-rule
failures block the entire candidate at Critical severity; keep the previous accepted release and escalate.
A missing expected source produces a High-severity MISSING row. An out-of-range observation produces
a Medium-severity quarantine record and QUARANTINED status while unaffected accepted observations
may publish. Late accepted observations produce Medium-severity STALE output. These actions use the
existing response and resolution times; status publication records a miss rather than erasing it.

security

§6 Change

Removal, narrower precision, required-field addition and changed meaning are breaking.
Nullable additions and clearer descriptions are compatible. Use major/minor/patch
semantic versions and support the current plus one prior version during migration.

§7 Consumers

The registry below names each consumer, its access route, a contact role and the
onboarding date.

§8 Approvals

The DPM signs scope and version. The Data Steward signs schema, classification and
quality. Security or privacy reviewers sign when their review is triggered. Each consumer
signs the SLA and access route. Real names and dates replace the role labels before
launch.

Quarantine row

An accuracy or range failure may be an error or a real Pólya-type tail event, where a
few rare, large observations hold much of the information. Oil futures going negative
in 2020 was one. Quarantine lets a person correct the error or release the event
without silently trusting or deleting it.

Appendix D — dbt and tooling reference
For assigned Portfolio Analytics workspaces, tasks and checks, use the dbt project. This appendix provides
command and concept reference. Historical code examples require version-specific adaptation; use a

Slowly changing dimensions with dbt snapshot
Say the portfolio-manager coverage table has four columns, fund_id, manager_id, manager_name and
updated_at, and it’s updated in place. When a fund changes manager, the old name is overwritten. You

know who runs the fund now, but you’ve lost who ran it last quarter, and attribution needs that.
A dbt snapshot compares the current source rows with the copy it stored last time and keeps the history:
{% snapshot pm_coverage_snapshot %}
{{
config(
target_schema='snapshots',
unique_key='fund_id',
strategy='timestamp',
updated_at='updated_at'
)
}}
select fund_id, manager_id, manager_name, updated_at
from {{ source('reference', 'pm_coverage') }}

{% endsnapshot %}

unique_key sets the tracked grain. The timestamp strategy versions a row when updated_at advances;
check compares named values when the source has no reliable timestamp.

Run dbt snapshot on an Airflow schedule and each version gains dbt_valid_from and dbt_valid_to; the
current row has a null end. A quarter-end query selects the row whose validity range contains 30 June.
SCD type

Storage rule

Choose it for

1

Overwrite

Current state only; no lookback.

2

Add a date-ranged row

Full point-in-time history.

3

Keep a previous-value column

Current and one prior value.

Delta MERGE closes the old type-2 row and inserts the new one. A dbt snapshot or a compatible configured
loading strategy writes the required SQL; inspect the actual implementation and warehouse behavior.
For facts, dimensions and a worked Morningstar join, see Organisational context.
A bitemporal load tracks two perspectives: business time, when the value was true, and system time,
when it was recorded. A correction adds a version while preserving the earlier observation. dbt has no
bitemporal mode as such. A configured snapshot tracks changes through validity intervals; an incremental
update alone does not preserve every overwritten version. Define both time perspectives explicitly when
the consumer requires them. bitemporal_load_v2 is the supplied Capital Group packaged example;
inspect its actual audit fields below and the dbt snapshot behavior.
The maintained local v2 audit map uses dl_business_start_date, dl_business_end_date, dl_
system_start_timestamp, dl_system_end_timestamp and dl_current_indicator. Older examples use
*_from_date/*_to_date names. Match the model to the assigned macro rather than assuming those

naming families are interchangeable.
An as-of join reproducing historical knowledge must filter both the business interval and the system
interval. Define the meaning of a current flag before testing its cardinality:

Case study: A toolchain error is not a model defect
Situation. A dbt command fails before the model executes because the selected shell cannot find the expected
profile or dependency environment. Rebuilding model SQL would not address that failure.
Decision and reasoning. Identify the executable, profile, target and actual error before changing code. Inspect
one configuration boundary at a time, then rerun the same bounded command. Configuration and dependency
interactions make a multi-tool environment harder to diagnose than one SQL query.
Lesson. Classify setup/identity errors separately from model behavior, and retain the operation that failed. Use
the current environment appendix for recovery.

• SQL-based transformations: a model query is materialized as a configured relation or inlined as an
ephemeral model.
• Model selection: --select names the resources to run or inspect; check dependency scope before
execution.
• Adapter boundary: connection and adapter settings select compute. SQL dialects and platformspecific behavior may need changes when porting a model; reuse does not guarantee portability.
• Tests: a data test returns failing records. Schema tests and purpose-built SQL checks protect
different parts of the declared contract.
• Test packages: inspect the installed package and version for its available tests. Package availability
does not replace a requirement-specific acceptance example.
• ref and source: configured relations and model references produce a dependency graph ordered
for execution. A topological ordering respects those edges; it does not establish correct joins or
population.
• YAML configuration: profiles, project settings, tests, descriptions and tags have distinct purposes.
Read the effective configuration before interpreting a result.
• Documentation: dbt docs generate produces resource descriptions and lineage artifacts. The
generated graph helps review dependencies, while a human reviews whether descriptions and rules
are correct.
Learning Review
Retrieve materialization, selection and dependency resolution. Apply them to a model with two parents and
one failed test: which selected build can proceed? Check the effective configuration, dependency scope,
failing records and the consumer rule before explaining the result. This reference self-check supplements the
day-ending review.

Appendix D — dbt and tooling reference

What Airflow is: orchestration
Airflow schedules tasks, evaluates dependencies and tracks execution and failure. DAGs are defined
in Python; tasks can invoke shell commands, Python functions or remote systems. In this course, dbt
defines transformations, Databricks executes their SQL, and Airflow coordinates the scheduled workflow.

DAGs (directed acyclic graphs)
A directed acyclic graph (DAG) defines task dependencies without a directed cycle. Independent branches
can run concurrently when resources permit. A run can retry a task, and later runs can repeat the graph.
A successful task can make downstream work eligible; a failed task can block it. Failure callbacks report
or record incidents separately from those dependency rules. In Airflow, the DAG object also carries
scheduling configuration. dbt’s DAG records model dependencies instead: keep data-flow, task-order
and organisational SLA relationships distinct.

The four key terms: DAG, task, operator and scheduler
• DAG: the workflow definition and its scheduling configuration.
• Task: a unit of executable work, such as a Python function or CLI command.
• Operator: the template for a task, such as BashOperator or an operator supplied by a provider
library.
• Scheduler: evaluates scheduling rules and dependencies, then makes eligible tasks available to the
runtime.
Cosmos supplies the dbt integration described below.

Reading a DAG file
This historical Airflow 2-style example checks two inputs before staging, integration, calculation,
publication and notification.

Use the assigned Airflow guide for supported imports, scheduling

arguments and the current starter.
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.bash import BashOperator

default_args = {
"owner": "positions-team",
"retries": 2,
"retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=10),
}
with DAG(
dag_id="positions_daily",
description="Integrated positions table, ready by midnight",
start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
schedule="0 22 * * *",
# 10 PM daily, after both feeds land
catchup=False,
default_args=default_args,
tags=["positions", "training"],
) as dag:

check_imap = BashOperator(
task_id="check_imap_landed",
bash_command="python checks/imap_landed.py",
)
check_reference = BashOperator(
task_id="check_reference_landed",
bash_command="python checks/reference_landed.py",
)
stage = BashOperator(

419

+44 (0)20 3583 0972 | info@decoded.com | decoded.com

DECODED

Appendix D — dbt and tooling reference

task_id="stage_positions",
bash_command="dbt run --select staging",
)
integrate = BashOperator(
task_id="integrate_positions",
bash_command="dbt run --select integration",
)
calculate = BashOperator(
task_id="run_trade_calculations",
bash_command="dbt run --select calculations",
)
publish = BashOperator(
task_id="publish_to_caspian",
bash_command="python publish/broadcast_file.py",
)
notify = BashOperator(
task_id="notify_consumers",
bash_command="python notify/distribution_list.py",
)
[check_imap, check_reference] >> stage >> integrate >> calculate >> publish >> notify

Read the definition in order:
• The imports. Ordinary Python. DAG is the container object and BashOperator is one kind of task.
datetime and timedelta are there because scheduling is all about time arithmetic.

• default_args. Settings applied to every task in the DAG unless a task overrides them. retries=2
with retry_delay=timedelta(minutes=10) means a failed task is attempted up to two more times,
ten minutes apart, before Airflow declares it failed. Your SLA, in code explains why those two lines
matter for the SLA.
• The schedule line. "0 22 * * *" uses five cron fields: minute, hour, day-of-month, month and
day-of-week. It schedules 22:00 daily, after the example’s input arrivals. @daily corresponds to
midnight ("0 0 * * *"), which would leave no processing buffer before the example’s midnight
deadline.
• start_date and catchup. The date from which schedules exist, and whether missed ones are
replayed. The weekend outage covers both.
• The operators. Each task is an operator instance, and a BashOperator is the simplest adaptor. The
system it talks to is the shell, so it’s simply a terminal command to run. The task_id is the name you
will see in the UI. Three of the seven commands here are Wednesday’s dbt project being run layer
by layer with --select; the pipeline’s middle is the dbt project. Whether you author or generate a
DAG, review its task IDs, commands, dependencies and failure behavior; syntax you cannot explain
needs further inspection.
• The dependency line. [check_imap, check_reference] >> stage >> integrate >> calculate
>> publish >> notify. The two input checks can run in parallel; staging waits for both. Each

remaining task waits for its predecessor.
Scheduling warning
When the promise is tied to local time, use a timezone-aware start date such as pendulum.datetime(2026,
4, 7, tz="America/New_York"). Timezone and scheduling has the scheduling patterns and works out how

much retry time you have.

The arrow has more than one spelling, and generated DAGs and the Airflow documentation use all of
them. They all have the same effect:
t1 >> [t2, t3]
[t2, t3] << t1
t1.set_downstream(t2)
↪
same as t2 << t1
t1 >> t2 >> t3

# a list fans out: t2 and t3 both wait for t1
# the same edges, written from the right
# is the same as t2.set_upstream(t1) is the same as t1 >> t2 is the
# chaining: a straight line of three

>> and << express dependency direction; the methods record the same edges. A list creates fan-out or

fan-in dependencies, allowing concurrent execution when other requirements are met. Once the file is
loaded, the web interface is where you act on it: from there you can manually trigger a DAG, inspect a
task’s logs, and monitor task status. The Airflow UI tour goes through each one.
Start a business review with the schedule, source checks, transformation commands, publication and
notification. Explain which contract promise each step serves before inspecting its implementation. A
reviewer can challenge a missing dependency or unrealistic deadline without first becoming the DAG
author.

Your SLA, in code
Translate the contract’s timing and failure promises into retry settings, failure callbacks and deadline
checks.
When

What happens

22:00

The scheduled start, in the business timezone you declared.

First run fails

Wait 10 minutes and retry.

Retry 1 fails

Wait 10 minutes and retry again.

After retry 2

Check the delivery deadline. If the run is complete, the promise is met. If it’s late or failed,
a Datadog event goes out and is routed to a person by priority.

retries and retry_delay. Some failures are transient: a connection drops, a file arrives ninety seconds

after the check ran. Two retries ten minutes apart can absorb a temporary failure while retaining its
attempts in the run record. They also consume deadline buffer; account for runtime and retries along
the whole critical path. In the positions-product example, critical failures require an on-call response;
the retry settings establish how many attempts occur before escalation. Choose retries against the SLA:
too few can escalate transient faults, while too many can delay intervention.

on_failure_callback. Monday’s RICE example ranked three SLAs: timing, quality and the duty to explain.

In Airflow, the duty to explain starts with a function:
def post_to_team_channel(context):
ti = context["task_instance"]
send_message(
channel="#positions-pipeline",
text=f"{ti.dag_id}.{ti.task_id} failed for {context['ds']}. "
f"Logs: {ti.log_url}",
)

default_args = {
"retries": 2,
"retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=10),
"on_failure_callback": post_to_team_channel,
}

Airflow calls the function when a task has used up its retries and failed. It passes a context dictionary
with the task, the run date and the log link. send_message stands in for whatever the team posts with,
and on the paved path that’s a Datadog event. Configure a tested notification route for missing or late
data rather than relying on manual discovery.

sla and sla_miss_callback. Failure callbacks fire when something breaks. But a pipeline can miss its

deadline without failing at all. Every task succeeds, slowly, and the 7:30 delivery from the RICE example
lands at 9. Airflow 2 handles this with an sla on the task plus an sla_miss_callback on the DAG:
with DAG(
...,
sla_miss_callback=post_late_delivery_notice,
) as dag:

publish = BashOperator(
task_id="publish_to_caspian",
bash_command="python publish/broadcast_file.py",
sla=timedelta(hours=9, minutes=30),
)

In this Airflow 2 example, a 07:30 promise after a 22:00 scheduled start allows nine and a half hours.
Airflow 3 removed sla; Airflow 3.1 introduces deadline alerts. Check the supplied version’s syntax before
adapting the example.

Runbook and incident log
Workflow
Keep a runbook beside the DAG and change it in the same pull request as the code. It has seven sections:
• Service overview: purpose, owner, schedule and SLA.
• Architecture: the path from source to consumer, and its dependencies.
• Access: Airflow, Databricks, logs and dashboards.
• Common alerts: symptom, diagnosis and fix for each one.
• Escalation: who’s on call, in what order, and how fast they respond.
• Manual procedures: backfill, retry, rollback and how to check the result.
• Contacts: team roles, channels and xMatters schedules.
For the Morningstar exposures pipeline, two alert rows look like this.

At resolution, log what happened and the runbook step used. No matching step means a new failure mode, so
add an entry before closing the follow-up.
• dbt full refresh: rebuild bad incremental state from source.
• Delta time travel: RESTORE TABLE ... TO VERSION AS OF ... for a known good table version.
• Airflow task clear: after fixing the cause, rerun the failed task and its downstream chain.
Operations has the full runbook template, a four-row alert table and the incident-log schema. The incident
drill applies it to a failure.

Backfill, catchup, and idempotency: the weekend outage
Suppose an expired certificate prevents the weekend runs and is repaired on Monday. Decide which
missed business dates require replay.
• catchup is the setting that decides automatically. catchup=True allows scheduled runs for missed
intervals; catchup=False does not automatically create that full backlog. The example DAG sets it
to False, because for this pipeline consumers want tonight’s positions, and rebuilding Saturday’s
file on Monday serves nobody. A pipeline producing daily history files would choose the opposite.
Either can be right. What goes wrong is leaving it to the default, which is why “is catchup set?” is
on the closing challenge’s checklist.
• Backfill is the manual form of the same replay, for when you want specific dates: airflow dags
backfill positions_daily -s 2026-08-22 -e 2026-08-24 re-runs the DAG for that date range,

whatever catchup says. That’s the Airflow 2 command. In Airflow 3, which the challenge runs, it’s
airflow backfill create --dag-id positions_daily --from-date 2026-08-22 --to-date 202608-24.

• Idempotency is the property that makes either replay safe: running a task twice for the same date
must leave the same state as running it once. The counter-example is a task that appends. Replay
the weekend and Saturday’s rows land twice. A table rebuilt from fixed inputs can reproduce its
result; an incremental model needs a key and update policy that prevent duplicate replay. Volatile
expressions such as current_timestamp() can change values between runs. When you audit a
generated DAG, “can every task run twice safely?” is the question behind both the catchup setting
and the clear-to-rerun button in the UI.

Astronomer
The supplied stack combines Airflow, Astronomer and Cosmos. Astronomer provides tooling for local
development and managed Airflow hosting:
1. Local, automatic running of Airflow jobs in containers on your own system, which is what makes
Airflow pipelines reproducible and is how the dev-container challenges run Airflow on this course.
2. Managed Airflow hosting. The supplied platform routes deployment through Harness. Learner
practice uses local Astro services; deployment is a separate authorised operation.
Questions for choosing a managed runtime:
• Where does dbt run? The assigned route runs dbt on an Astro worker and sends SQL to Databricks.
Databricks also offers scheduling; choose the orchestrator according to the supported execution
and dependency requirements.
• Vendor dependence: assess platform-specific configuration, operating costs and migration effort.
In the supplied scenario, per-team Airflow instances reduce the coupling created by one shared
instance.

Cosmos: one Airflow task per dbt model
Something has to run Wednesday’s dbt project inside Airflow, and the blunt option is the one already
visible in the walkthrough DAG, a BashOperator per layer, or even a single one for the whole project:
run_dbt = BashOperator(
task_id="run_dbt",
bash_command="dbt build --project-dir /usr/local/airflow/dbt/positions",
)

Figure 139: The same dbt project at two Airflow resolutions: one BashOperator task, or the model-andtest graph rendered by Cosmos.
A single BashOperator provides task-level logs and retries for the entire dbt command. Airflow cannot
separately retry a model within that task, though the dbt log identifies the failed resource.

Cosmos renders the dbt dependency graph as Airflow tasks, with model-level logs and retries. Its test
configuration determines how tests appear and gate downstream work. The following sketch shows the
project configuration; a runnable DAG also needs the appropriate profile and execution settings:
from cosmos import DbtDag, ProjectConfig

positions_dbt = DbtDag(
dag_id="positions_dbt",
project_config=ProjectConfig("/usr/local/airflow/dbt/positions"),
schedule="0 22 * * *",
start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
)

DbtTaskGroup embeds the rendered dbt tasks within a larger DAG, so input checks, publication and

notification can surround the transformation graph:
from cosmos import DbtTaskGroup, ProjectConfig, ProfileConfig
with DAG(dag_id="positions_daily", schedule="0 22 * * *", ...) as dag:

# check_imap, check_reference, publish and notify as in the walkthrough
positions_models = DbtTaskGroup(
group_id="positions_dbt",
project_config=ProjectConfig("/usr/local/airflow/dbt/positions"),
profile_config=ProfileConfig(profile_name="positions", target_name="dev"),
)
[check_imap, check_reference] >> positions_models >> publish >> notify

The transformation logic stays in dbt. The three layer-level BashOperators become a group of model-level
tasks; the surrounding checks, publication and notification remain ordinary Airflow tasks. Use DbtDag for
a dbt-only workflow and DbtTaskGroup when dbt sits within a larger workflow.
Expert
A production deployment also supplies a profile configuration pointing at the connection details created by
Wednesday’s .env setup. The paved path chooses this over the bash one-liner because each model becomes
independently retryable and observable, at the cost of a dependency on the Cosmos library.

Data mesh and localised development
Data mesh places data-product ownership and development in the relevant business domains rather than
one central delivery team. Shared platform tools support self-service while domains remain responsible
for meaning, consumers and service promises.
Self-service does not remove coordination needs. Teams still need contracts, access rules, dependency
responsibilities and clear ownership. Per-team Airflow instances can reduce runtime coupling, but folder
or instance boundaries alone do not establish a governed product.

Problems seen in the client dev container
If authentication fails, don’t fix it by installing packages into some other environment. Check which
executable you’re running and which target it points at.
Common failure boundaries in the prepared client environment:
• If you start Astro before the setup exports the warehouse HTTP path, its runtime variables can be
empty. Fix the dev-shell setup, then restart the Astro stack so its processes pick up the new values.
• Logging in again with OAuth in your own shell doesn’t refresh a worker’s cached connection. Refresh
the token or connection through the repository’s own setup, then look at the run you selected.
• Windows profile links and corporate path expansion can point at host folders the container can’t
see. Find out which process reads the path before you change it.
• A dbt selector can pick up tests on models that are still stubs. Select only your own model while
you’re working, then run the full selector before you finish.
• The current v2 preparation/reset interface creates a new attempt and refuses an existing destination.
Preserve the previous workspace and choose a fresh --workspace path; verify that same path
explicitly.
• Some retained legacy verifiers resolve dependencies or restore lock files. Current v2 checks use a
temporary copy and hash the supplied workspace. Inspect the command’s boundary and the diff
before accepting evidence.
• Before rebuilding an image, identify the failing executable, target and error.

Stakeholder roles, influence and adoption
Stakeholder roles
Identify the sponsor (commissions or champions work), approver (authorises a decision), consumer (uses
the output), blocker (can prevent progress) and influencer (affects others’ decisions). Check these roles
against actual responsibilities and decisions, as well as interview answers.
The supplied course uses the operating roles below. These are a different dimension from sponsor,
approver, consumer and influencer; they are not one-to-one replacements. A data owner may sponsor
one decision and consume another product. Record who approves access, business meaning and release
separately, using the current product’s responsibility matrix rather than inferring authority from a title.
• Data owner — accountable for the data and may sponsor or approve related work.
• Data product manager — owns product priorities and represents consumer needs.
• Data steward — maintains SLAs, standards, quality and rules.

Identify the named person;

stewardship may be a responsibility rather than a job title.
• Data product creator — designs, builds and checks the product.

Stakeholder mapping, and finding your leaders
Map stakeholders by influence and interest, then add their responsibilities for the specific decision.
Influence / interest

Communication and involvement

High / high

Review critical decisions with the approver or champion; address a blocker’s concerns
directly.

Low / high

Consult users and specialists where their knowledge is needed. Align at the start and end
of a phase, and provide progress summaries.

High / low

Provide concise updates on strategic decisions and request approval when required.

Low / low

Share a relevant release brief and monitor for changed involvement.

Recheck the map: a trusted specialist may influence an approver without formal authority. Interest
suggests how often to communicate; responsibility and influence identify which decisions need someone’s
involvement. Avoid replacing a required approval with repeated discussion among interested colleagues.
Agree communication responsibilities with the product manager. As a creator, identify the decisions you
own, evidence you supply and approvals you need.

7
Esteem concerns respect and recognition within a relevant group. Public embarrassment, unclear accountability and losing a
valued contribution can obstruct adoption. Credit useful work and provide meaningful involvement; an award cannot compensate
for inaccurate or inaccessible data.

Case study: A decision with the wrong participants
Situation. A creator repeatedly discusses a proposed product with interested colleagues, but the access or
delivery decision remains blocked. The person with formal responsibility has not reviewed the evidence.
Decision. Identify the required approver, the people affected and the domain reviewer who can test the proposal.
Send the relevant evidence to each role and record a decision point instead of adding another broad meeting.
Reasoning. Interest helps explain needs and adoption, while formal responsibility determines who can approve
the particular change. Neither is a reason to dismiss a valid concern. Match the discussion to the decision and
retain the affected consumer’s requirements.
Lesson. Use the stakeholder map to arrange a review, then verify the assumptions behind the roles. Update it
when responsibility or the product scope changes.

Match each review to the person’s responsibility and evidence needs. An informed sceptic may expose a
valid defect; use evidence and explicit decision criteria rather than dismissing the concern because of a
label.

Stakeholder attitudes and influence
The diagram separates how much formal influence someone has from how ready they are to support the
change. An influential sceptic may know things about the domain that you need, and an enthusiastic
colleague with little authority may make the best early tester. For each person on the map, write down
one thing you’ll ask of them, such as reviewing a valuation rule, letting you watch their current workflow
or sponsoring an access decision.

Why good data products stall
A technically sound product can stall because it lacks priority, access, discovery, training or a fit with the
consumer’s workflow. Check those practical objections before interpreting resistance as a question of
esteem, power or control.
• Esteem: recognise useful contributions and provide meaningful involvement.

Appendix G — AI reference

Appendix G — AI reference
For a generated diagram or source-to-target mapping, substantiate each edge with supplied keys and
each measure with its definition. In the CG product brief, a shared product ID alone does not make
two return observations comparable: check basis, kind, period and reporting date. Mark unsupported
relationships and assumptions explicitly.
Use this reference alongside Tuesday’s product-to-Catalyst workflow to understand model training, review
risks and AI costs. The supplied Catalyst version is 1.13.0.

Model training and post-training
Pre-training learns patterns from data to predict or generate text. The learned parameters are not a
recoverable archive of training documents, and an answer is not necessarily a lookup of an existing
passage.
Instruction fine-tuning uses examples of responses to requests. Preference training uses comparisons
or ratings to shape preferred outputs. These activities can improve usefulness while leaving factual
errors and incomplete instruction-following.

The InstructGPT paper describes one combination of

demonstrations and human comparisons; training methods vary by model.
A request to “write a data contract” leaves many product facts unspecified. A fluent draft can use
the wrong consumer, invented columns or an unsupported delivery promise. Supply the actual product
evidence and inspect the result. The GPT-3 paper illustrates why performance should be assessed for
the particular task.

Generated claims and the word “hallucination”
Unsupported output can read as confidently as a correct answer.

A claim about a table, approval

or successful command needs evidence: check the cited source or relevant tool result.

The term

“hallucination” describes an output problem, rather than an intention to deceive. Correct the authoritative
artefact so later work does not inherit the error.

Imitation and simulation as teaching analogies
Recognising a familiar pattern differs from validating the process you need. A proposed schema may
look plausible while missing correction behaviour or unusual macro arguments. Ask what was tested:
inspect generated SQL, compile it in the supported environment and compare executed output with an
independently specified example. Parsing validates structure; it does not validate the business rule.
Prompt and context improvements should be evaluated on the task they serve. Repeat the relevant
checks when grain, data type, correction policy or consumer changes.

Repeated actions, correlated mistakes and responsibility
Expert
If independent actions each have a 1% failure probability and any failure makes the run unsuccessful, the
chance of at least one failure in 100 actions is 1 - 0.99^100, about 63.4%. This example is not a measured
Catalyst rate: real errors can be correlated, repaired and different in consequence.

Appendix G — AI reference

Distinguish error frequency from impact. Many correct fields cannot compensate for a wrong currency
basis, missing regulatory field or unapproved access rule. Rare, high-impact errors can dominate the cost
of a process; measure both their likelihood and consequence.
Shared prompts, skills and glossaries can create correlated mistakes. Ten contracts using one incorrect
glossary are not ten independent confirmations. Check against independent evidence and correct the
authoritative glossary, template or skill.
“De-responsibilisation” describes reduced personal responsibility when a system appears to decide. The
creator remains accountable for the reviewed artefact and its use. An agent transcript records a proposal;
it does not grant approval.
Choose review points according to the cost of a wrong assumption. Verify facts before they become
implementation inputs and verify executed results before treating an implementation as successful.
Separate observed tool results from the model’s summary.

The economics of AI: a dated framework
Compare the cost of producing an accepted result, including infrastructure, integration and review. The
following framework distinguishes cost categories; it is not a current price list or forecast.

Broad training as an investment
Training requires data, compute, engineering and evaluation. Its up-front cost differs from the cost of
another request and from your team’s implementation and support costs. Open-weight releases can
widen access to a capability; running them still requires resources, rights and governance.

Instruction and preference data
Reviewed examples can capture useful organisational knowledge: consumer questions, faithful contracts
and tested corrections. A team can maintain these examples in prompts, templates and skills without
retraining a model. Fine-tuning changes the trained model; editing a prompt changes its supplied context.
Select an approach according to the problem and evaluate the result.
Use the organisation’s approved service and data-handling rules. Check the applicable agreement for
retention and training rights rather than assuming that providers or account types handle information
identically.

Inference, reasoning and repeated requests
Inference consumes resources during use. A conversation or agent workflow can involve several model
requests and tool operations, with additional computation in some systems. Measure the whole task’s
latency, recurring resource use and review effort against the accepted result. A subscription allowance
or editor credit multiplier is not a direct measure of the provider’s underlying cost.
Compare approved models and effort levels on the same representative task, using correctness,
completeness, duration and inspection effort. Record the configuration and version; price alone does
not establish suitability.

Agent workflows and specialised organisational value
Agent workflows coordinate operations using context, tools and review. Catalyst supplies organisationspecific instructions and artefact structures; assess whether those help someone perform a real
responsibility reliably.
The “flooring effect” describes a possible consequence of widely available baseline capabilities: additional
value may come from specialised data meaning, integration, useful interfaces and trusted decisions. Test

Appendix G — AI reference

that hypothesis for your workflow. A team-specific skill needs maintenance and a check that it transfers
to another product or department.

Models, harnesses and applications
A model supplies generation; a harness provides tools and context; an application connects them to a
workflow and user. Costs and value can arise at each layer. A faster draft may shift effort into review
and correction, so compare time to an accepted artefact rather than the number of pages generated.

Model choice, resource budgets and deployment options
Check the current approved models, allowances and reasoning controls in your environment. Evaluate
them with a representative task. Hosted APIs, managed cloud services and self-hosted stacks have
different data-handling and operational boundaries; local hosting also requires hardware, maintenance
and governance.
A project-facts file can reduce repeated context questions. Keep it accurate, exclude secrets and retain
the required approvals and output review.

Appendix I — Historical data and bitemporal loading

Appendix I — Historical data and bitemporal loading
A financial report depends on more than the values available today. It may need the values that applied
on a particular business date, the values that were available when the report was produced, or today’s
corrected understanding of that earlier date. These are different questions. A reliable historical model
records enough information to answer the question the consumer actually intends.
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to distinguish business time from system time, design a
temporal grain for reference and balance data, explain a retrospective correction, choose an appropriate
incoming-file policy, and test historical queries and repeated loads.

Three kinds of history
Suppose a portfolio changes manager. An ordinary update replaces the old manager’s name with the new
one. This is useful for a current directory, but it loses the information needed to attribute last quarter’s
performance to the right manager.
A slowly changing dimension of type 2 keeps separate versions and associates each version with a validity
interval. A query can then select the manager whose interval contains the reporting date. A type-1
dimension overwrites the old value, while a type-3 design retains a limited previous-value attribute. The
choice depends on the consumer’s need for history.
There is a further complication. The manager change may take effect on October 1 but reach the platform
on October 8. A report produced on October 5 could reasonably contain the old manager because the
new information had not arrived. Reproducing that report and producing a corrected report are both
legitimate operations, but they should return different answers.
A bitemporal model records two clocks:
Clock

Question

Meaning of the interval

Business-valid

When did this fact apply?

The period during which an attribute or relationship is true in

time

the business domain

System-record

When did the platform know

The period during which this version was part of the

time

this version?

platform’s recorded understanding

A business change and a data correction can have the same arrival date but different effective dates.
Using the arrival timestamp as the business start date collapses the two meanings and prevents accurate
reconstruction.
Table-version history is a third concept.

Delta’s transaction history supports storage-level recovery

and inspection of table states. Its availability depends on retained logs and data files. It does not
automatically encode the effective dates supplied by a business source or provide a durable businesshistory interface. Retained table versions, type-2 dimensions, and bitemporal records solve related but
different problems.

Define time and grain before writing the merge
The grain tells us what one business observation represents. A master/reference record might identify
an instrument. A positions record might identify a portfolio, instrument, account, currency, and business
date. Temporal versions add another layer of identity: the same business observation may have several
recorded versions.
For reference data, define the natural key and the attributes being versioned. For balances, include the
as-of date in the observation grain. A portfolio’s balance on October 4 is a different observation from its
446

+44 (0)20 3583 0972 | info@decoded.com | decoded.com

DECODED

Appendix I — Historical data and bitemporal loading

balance on October 5, even if the amount is unchanged. A correction to the October 4 balance is a new
system version of that same observation.
Choose the time types deliberately.

A business-valid date may have day precision, while a system

timestamp needs sufficient precision to order multiple arrivals on one day. Define the time zone for
timestamps and the convention for simultaneous events. The database column type and the source’s
effective-date meaning must agree.
This chapter uses half-open intervals:
start <= requested_time < end

The start is included and the end is excluded. A version ending at midnight on October 8 and another
starting at that instant do not overlap. When a source supplies an inclusive end date, normalize it carefully
into the chosen representation rather than mixing interval conventions.
An open interval may use a null end or a distant-future sentinel such as 9999-12-31. A low businessdate sentinel such as 1900-01-01 means an unspecified or conventionally unbounded start; it does not
establish that the entity existed in 1900. Query predicates must match the representation chosen by the
product.

A reference-data correction across both clocks
Consider instrument I1. The platform receives its reference record on October 4. The source says that
the instrument has been named Orion Holdings since September 1. On October 8, the source supplies a
correction: the name should be Orion Asset Management from October 1.

The first result reproduces earlier knowledge. The second uses the correction for the same business
