For this example, the two temporal predicates can be written as follows. The parameters identify the
requested business date and knowledge timestamp; they are supplied by the report or application.
select instrument_id, instrument_name
from instrument_history
where business_from <= :business_date
and (business_to is null or :business_date < business_to)
and system_from <= :knowledge_timestamp
and (system_to is null or :knowledge_timestamp < system_to)

The query uses both clocks. Filtering only on a current flag cannot reproduce all three answers. Filtering
only on business time could return the old and corrected names together because both are valid
representations of different knowledge states.
A product’s loading macro may store the history differently, but the observable query behavior must
satisfy its contract. Define expected results from concrete histories before selecting an implementation.

Late-arriving dimensions
A position can arrive before the descriptive record for its instrument. The position is a fact; the instrument
description is a dimension. This is a late-arriving dimension problem.
Suppose a position dated October 1 arrives that day, but its instrument definition arrives on October 5.
A business-date join made with today’s knowledge may enrich the earlier position successfully. A report
reproducing knowledge on October 2 must reflect the absence of that definition at that time.
Choose how the product handles the gap. It may retain the fact with an explicit unknown classification,
hold publication until the reference record arrives, or expose a separately documented incomplete state.
An inner join that silently drops the position makes the problem harder to detect. The intended policy
should be visible in tests, reconciliation, and consumer documentation.
There are two different quality questions: whether every required reference record is available now,
and whether the historical report accurately reflects what was available then. A reconstruction can be
historically accurate while containing an unknown value. A current corrected view can resolve that value
without pretending it was known earlier.

A historically known balance query selects the business as-of date and the system interval:
select portfolio_id, instrument_id, market_value
from position_history

and system_from <= :knowledge_timestamp
and (system_to is null or :knowledge_timestamp < system_to)

A reference/master strategy and a balance strategy therefore use different business semantics. Applying
the reference strategy to daily observations can accidentally stretch one day’s balance across several
days. Applying a balance strategy to continuously valid reference attributes can force consumers to
manufacture daily snapshots they do not need.
The unique key must include all columns needed to distinguish the actual observation. Portfolio and date
alone are insufficient when the portfolio contains several instruments or accounts. A generated surrogate
key is useful for joins and storage, but it does not repair an incorrectly defined business grain.

Source delivery policy and loading policy
Before temporal merging, decide which arrivals should be processed. A pipeline may normally receive
one file per day and then find several files waiting after an outage.

Latest-file processing is safe only when the newer delivery really supersedes the older ones for the same
scope. If each file contains different incremental additions, taking the latest loses data. If consumers
need to reproduce every arrival, discarding intermediate full snapshots may also violate the history
requirement.
Combining batches requires a duplicate and overlap policy. UNION ALL preserves every incoming row;
UNION removes identical rows. Neither decides which of two different corrections to the same business

observation should win. Establish batch identity, source sequence, effective dates, and tie-breaking
before merging.
These choices are separate from three other decisions:

• dbt materialization: how a model is persisted and updated.
• Temporal strategy: how business and system versions are maintained.
• Publication policy: when validated results become visible to consumers.
An incremental source delivery may feed an incremental dbt model using a balance strategy, with
publication held until quality checks pass.

The repeated word “incremental” does not make these

decisions interchangeable.

Prepared models and custom loading macros
In Caspian-style prepared models, the custom bitemporal_load_v2 strategy works within dbt’s
incremental materialization. Configuration selects the load type and business-key metadata. Balance
loads also identify the business as-of column.
A prepared balance model has the following configuration shape:
{{ config(
materialized='incremental',
incremental_strategy='bitemporal_load_v2',
load_type='balance',
as_of_col='position_date',
detect_change_flag='Y',
file_format='delta',
unique_key='dl_row_uid',
meta={
'surrogate_key_cols': [
'portfolio_id', 'instrument_id', 'position_date'
]
}
) }}

This example assumes those columns are the observation grain and that the project’s macro supplies
the matching row identifier and audit fields. The complete model must produce the business values,
checksum or change-detection inputs, keys, and audit columns expected by that macro. Configuration
alone does not implement the load.
Temporal column names are part of the project interface. The maintained local get_bitemporal_column_
names('v2') map uses dl_business_start_date, dl_business_end_date, dl_system_start_timestamp,
dl_system_end_timestamp and dl_current_indicator; its checksum name is dl_checksum_value. Older

examples use *_from_date and *_to_date names. Do not substitute one family into a model expecting
the other. Inspect the assigned macro, its expected audit-column list and its boundary behavior together.
The course’s maintained local strategy delegates through get_incremental_bitemporal_load_v2_sql to
the shared strategy generator. It distinguishes incremental, full, balance and balance_full branches.
The source-delivery catch-up policy is a separate configuration: the supplied curation enum calls its
alternatives latest, chronological and combined. These names establish the configuration boundary;
they do not prove that every late correction or recovery requirement has been implemented. Acceptance
histories must verify that behavior in the assigned environment.
The interval tables in this chapter define a consumer requirement, rather than promise that every
packaged macro produces exactly this physical representation. Before adopting a macro, compare its
compiled statements and observed results with the expected histories. A loading strategy that cannot
split a retrospective business interval needs adaptation or a different documented product interface.
A current indicator also needs a precise definition. It may represent the current business state, the latest
known system version, or a specific combination. In a fully reconstructed business timeline, several
historical business intervals can be part of the latest system understanding at once. “One current row
per key” is meaningful only after defining which kind of current the flag denotes.

Appendix I — Historical data and bitemporal loading

dbt snapshots provide type-2 history with dbt_valid_from and dbt_valid_to. They can be appropriate
when that validity history meets the requirement. A single snapshot interval does not automatically
provide independent business and system clocks. Similarly, an ordinary incremental MERGE that overwrites
a match does not preserve the previous recorded value merely because it runs incrementally.

Corrections, replacements, and deletions
A full snapshot, an incremental change stream, and a bounded replacement have different meanings
when a key is absent.
In a full snapshot, absence may mean that an entity is no longer present. In an incremental file, absence
usually means that the batch says nothing about that entity. A bounded replacement may supersede only
a declared portfolio, date range, or other block. Deleting everything not present in a partial delivery can
remove valid data outside that block.
Explicit deletion indicators require equally clear semantics. A source may withdraw an incorrect return
calculation or remove an entity. Decide whether consumers should see a tombstone, an ended validity
interval, an excluded current result, or a physical removal under an agreed retention policy. A logical
withdrawal and erasure of all historical evidence are different operations.
Corrections can arrive out of order. A later received message may have an earlier effective date than
a previously processed message. The product must reconstruct the intended business intervals rather
than assume that arrival order is business order.

Checkpoints, replay, and retained history
A checkpoint records which inputs a load has successfully processed. Advancing it before the output is
durable can skip data after a failure. Failing to advance it after success can trigger duplicate processing.
Design the checkpoint and output commit behavior together, and test the interruption points between
them.
A replay of the same identified input should not create another business observation or an unjustified
historical version. This is idempotency: repetition should preserve the correct final state. System-time
history may record genuine new observations or source corrections, but a retry of the same batch should
not masquerade as a new correction.
A full refresh deserves special attention. Rebuilding only from a current-state source cannot recover
versions that existed solely in the historical target. Before rebuilding, establish which retained inputs
can reconstruct the required history. A valid recovery plan identifies the source batches, transformation
version, temporal rules, and historical output to restore.
Storage maintenance must respect this plan. Removing obsolete physical files affects table-version
recovery, while deleting logical historical rows affects the consumer’s business-history interface. Define
the retention period for each and assess the impact on audit, reproducibility, and recovery.

Verify behavior with small histories
Temporal tests should exercise a sequence, not just a final row count. Start with a small set of keys and
record the expected answer after each arrival.
Case

Expected property

First arrival

The business observation is available from the correct knowledge time

Unchanged retry

No duplicate observation or false correction is introduced

Genuine effective-date change

Business intervals change at the specified boundary

Retrospective correction

Historical and current-knowledge queries return their different intended
answers

Late reference arrival

Enrichment follows the documented incomplete-data policy

Several waiting files

All required changes are processed in the correct scope and sequence

Explicit withdrawal

Current consumption and historical reconstruction follow the deletion
policy

Failed load and recovery

Output and checkpoint remain consistent

Check that a query at a business/knowledge pair returns the expected cardinality. Non-overlap means
that contradictory versions should not both cover the same business point and system point for the
same key. Business intervals can legitimately overlap across different system-history versions; the old
and corrected understandings in the reference-data correction above demonstrate why.
Review questions:
1. Why does selecting only the maximum load timestamp fail to reconstruct some historical reports?
2. In the Orion example, which rows answer a business date of October 2 with knowledge dates of
October 6 and October 9?
3. Why is the business date part of a balance grain?
4. When does selecting only the latest source file lose valid information?
5. What does your current indicator mean, and which query cannot be expressed with it alone?
6. What evidence shows that a retry neither skipped an input nor created a false version?
Use the dbt and tooling reference for the snapshot example and the dbt project for assigned practice. The
separately timed temporal-history clinic applies these principles to frozen arrivals, retries and recovery
without changing a live platform.

Appendix J — Astro operations and runtime ownership

Appendix J — Astro operations and runtime ownership
A managed orchestration service reduces the infrastructure work required to run Airflow. Reliable data
products still require explicit ownership of workflows, dependencies, credentials and delivery outcomes.
The platform team establishes common infrastructure and access conventions; the product team
maintains the applications running within that boundary.
This optional reference extends the orchestration material with operational decisions for a hosted
deployment.

The assigned classroom project uses local Astro orchestration and remote Databricks

computation. Its successful execution establishes evidence about that prepared environment; hosted
access, resilience and support arrangements need separate validation.

Federation and the service hierarchy
A central Airflow installation couples teams to one dependency environment, scheduler, release process
and upgrade timetable. Federation gives a team a deployment whose products can follow a common
maintenance lifecycle. It reduces some shared failure modes while placing responsibility for that lifecycle
with an identifiable owner.
Choose deployment boundaries around compatible operating needs. Products sharing dependencies,
availability requirements and an upgrade owner can reasonably share a deployment.

A separate

deployment for each small task increases administration and resource consumption without necessarily
improving delivery.
Component

Operational meaning

Organization

Top-level service administration and organizational access boundary

Workspace

Logical grouping of deployments and user access

Deployment

Configured Airflow environment receiving released code and execution settings

Cluster

Hosting infrastructure associated with deployments in the applicable platform
arrangement

Astro Runtime

Packaged runtime defining Airflow and supporting software

A workspace groups access; it does not execute SQL. A deployment schedules work, maintains execution
state and provides the relevant worker and UI/API services.

The warehouse or remote job service

may perform most data processing. Establish the actual execution mode, executor and infrastructure
arrangement before assigning responsibilities.
Environment names also need evidence. For each development, SQA and production deployment, record
its catalog/schema targets, credential identity, network route and intended consumer population. Two
deployments named differently can still write to the same database. Isolation requires distinct, correctly
configured boundaries.

Provisioning and configuration authority
Provisioning establishes a reproducible environment before regular application releases begin. A vended
repository can provide runtime definitions, dependency files, DAG layout, delivery templates and
environment configuration. Managed groups supply access through the approved onboarding route.
The platform IAC reference describes Terraform Enterprise state, environment-specific values, AWS roles
and secrets, and monitoring integration. It sits outside assigned learner practice. Platform owners
supply environment values and review infrastructure plans; ordinary DAG development uses the resulting
environment.

Decide which configuration system owns each setting. A maintained Terraform value and an emergency
UI adjustment can disagree. A later infrastructure apply may restore the declared value, unexpectedly
undoing the incident response. Record exceptional changes, their reason and their expiry, then reconcile
the maintained configuration before the next application of that state.
A release record should identify the application commit, dependency image, deployment and configuration
revision. A successful pipeline proves that its steps completed for those inputs. Inspect the target
environment to confirm the expected code and settings arrived, then obtain scheduled-run and output
evidence separately.
Access controls follow boundaries.

Deployment inspection, production administration, warehouse

queries, secrets retrieval and consumer table access are different permissions.

When a task fails,

establish which identity crossed which boundary instead of requesting broad access to every layer.

Connections across hosted and classroom environments
In an AWS Secrets Manager-backed hosted pattern, the configured backend supplies approved Airflow
connection and variable values. The deployment identity needs the corresponding retrieval permission.
Adopt one maintained source for each value and avoid conflicting copies in the Airflow metadata database,
environment variables and external backend. The actual lookup configuration determines which value
execution receives. Astronomer’s secrets backend guide describes the supported integration routes.
Plain variables, JSON-valued variables and connections have different uses.

Supported operator

template fields can retrieve configuration through expressions such as var.value.product_setting,
var.json.product_settings.target_name and conn.product_api.host.

Only designated fields are

rendered; arbitrary strings do not become templates automatically. Hooks and task code can retrieve
values through the runtime APIs appropriate to their execution path.
The classroom follows its delivered OAuth and worker connection route. The Portfolio setup requires
terminal sign-in through mise run setup:databricks, then worker refresh through mise run databricks:
oauth-refresh after starting Astro. Scheduled tasks resolve host and token from databricks_default at

execution time. A newly authenticated terminal does not automatically refresh that worker connection.
Check the running worker’s executable, versions, mounted project, writable artifact directories and
selected catalog/schema/warehouse. Reconcile its namespace with the terminal’s seeded relations. A
terminal build can succeed while a worker lacks the executable; both can authenticate while selecting
different schemas. The setup’s owned prefixes and staging metadata make these differences diagnosable
without overwriting another learner’s attempt.
Record host, connection name and target identity where appropriate, with credentials redacted. Keep
tokens, passwords and local environment files out of evidence and source control. Rehearse expiry,
refresh and restart, then demonstrate a fresh scheduled task with the intended identity. Authentication
is a maintained execution dependency.

Runtime inventory and upgrade evidence
Maintain an inventory connecting each deployment to its runtime image, Airflow version, executor,
providers, dbt adapter, Cosmos integration and customized shared templates. Include the owning team,
upgrade decision date and applicable support policy. Check current release notes and maintenance
milestones when planning an upgrade; a runtime tag copied from a training example is not a long-term
production policy.
An image that builds successfully may still change graph generation, connection resolution or operator
behavior. Use a non-production environment with representative inputs and comparable configuration.

Active-run handling follows the documented deployment strategy

For Portfolio, use the controlled quality failure, repair and replay sequence as a small regression workload.
Preserve the historical business partition explicitly; the scheduler’s logical date does not create newer
holdings. The final classroom evidence task records checks and delivery evidence rather than granting
consumers access.
Separate the code release decision from the runtime upgrade decision when that makes failures easier
to isolate. Keep the previous validated artifact and a recovery procedure, while recognizing that restoring
an image does not undo database changes or external notifications.

Vulnerability ownership and shared templates
A managed service maintains its service boundary.

Teams remain responsible for their application

dependencies, configured integrations and adopted template copies. Record who fixes each vulnerability
and how the update reaches the deployed product. A centrally maintained template provides value only
when its consuming repositories have an effective update path.
When a security gate blocks promotion, identify the affected package, installed version and available
remediation. Evaluate compatibility, rebuild the artifact and run the relevant regression checks. Removing
a gate without resolving the risk does not establish a maintained deployment. If remediation requires a
temporary exception, use the organization’s existing risk process and record its owner and expiry.
An inventory also prevents indefinite postponement.

Agree maintenance capacity before a support

deadline forces an urgent upgrade alongside business changes.

Security remediation and runtime

compatibility need evidence from the actual execution environment.

Releases while work is active
A release changes the software available to execute; an Airflow run performs work using that software.
Daily processing can use the same release repeatedly. The release record and the product delivery record
answer different questions.
DAG-only changes and image changes have different deployment paths. Dependency, plugin or runtime
changes require image validation even when the visible DAG change is small. Deploy the complete
intended DAG set for the selected deployment boundary, including unchanged workflows. A partial
artifact can unintentionally remove definitions used by other products.

Astronomer’s deployment

overview describes the supported deployment options.
Establish how the installed runtime, executor and bundle configuration associate code with active runs.
Do running tasks retain old code? Which code do later tasks and retries receive? Are dependencies and

shared files versioned with the DAG? A claim about one deployment mode does not establish another

Suppose a NAV run has already produced a candidate using one column name when a release renames
the downstream task’s expected column. Later tasks must consume a compatible interface or remain
bound to the validated version. One strategy is to stop new admission, allow active work to finish, deploy
and validate, then resume scheduling. Pausing a schedule alone does not prove that active tasks have
drained.
Another strategy preserves compatibility across the transition, such as supporting both representations
until all earlier work finishes. Rehearse that strategy, including retries. Preserve the business date,
immutable input selection, candidate identity and release identity throughout; a task retry must not
silently pick up a different supplier file or verify a replacement candidate under earlier evidence.

Capacity, remote compute and cost
Scheduler capacity supports parsing and timely scheduling. Worker capacity supports task execution
within memory, CPU and concurrency limits. Remote Databricks compute supports the query or job itself.
Increasing resources at one boundary cannot repair an unrelated constraint at another.
Observed symptom

Investigation before changing capacity

Slow definition loading or scheduling

Parse duration, scheduler utilization and DAG complexity

Tasks waiting to execute

Queue delay, worker availability, pools and concurrency limits

Worker termination

Peak memory, resource errors and task-local processing

Remote query taking longer

Warehouse/job metrics, contention and query plan

Submission rejected

Credentials, permissions, request limits and target availability

For example, a worker that submits a large warehouse query may use little CPU while waiting. A longer
warehouse execution time does not alone justify a larger worker. Conversely, a task that loads results into
memory may need worker capacity even when the remote query is fast. Gather representative periods
and peak behavior; average utilization can conceal a memory limit.
Use supported queues or routing where task classes need different resources. Form a hypothesis, change
the relevant setting and compare scheduling delay, task duration and delivery time. Include cost alongside
those results. Consumer deadlines and isolation requirements matter more than maximizing utilization
of every component.
Hibernation can reduce non-production resource use outside required periods. Verify what scheduling,
queued work and service startup do in the configured arrangement.

Rehearse credential recovery,

dependency availability and readiness after waking. Include a responsible owner for restarting before
planned tests; dormant development infrastructure cannot supply evidence until it is ready again.

Availability, disaster recovery and support
High availability keeps service functioning through failures within an operating environment. Disaster
recovery establishes how service resumes after a broader disruption.

A deployment’s availability

arrangement does not automatically recover source data, warehouse state, credentials or delivery
evidence.
Define recovery objectives from the product agreement, then identify the state needed to achieve them:
code and configuration, execution metadata, input identities, durable candidates, published relations and
receipts. Exercise restoration and replay. Verify the recovered product independently before reopening
its consumer interface.

Appendix J — Astro operations and runtime ownership

Operational monitoring must connect infrastructure health with business delivery. Logs and metrics
help locate a failing boundary; freshness, completeness and publication evidence establish whether the
consumer received the agreed product. Ensure the owning team can access monitoring and incident
systems before an incident.
Route support by the failing boundary.

Product owners diagnose logic, quality and delivery impact.

Internal platform teams address onboarding, shared configuration and managed patterns. Managedservice support addresses service issues through the applicable agreement. Keep current escalation
contacts and internal coverage accessible, select severity from business impact and send a concise
packet: environment, deployment, runtime, release, run/task identities, redacted error and affected
delivery.
An upstream readiness event supplies a producer milestone. The consumer still needs evidence of its own
transformation, checks and publication. Carry dataset identity, business date and release or candidate
identity across the dependency. Restoration of orchestration alone does not establish restored delivery.

Review questions
1. Which runtime, application and delivery responsibilities belong to the product team, platform team
and managed service?
2. How would you detect that two apparently separate environments write to the same warehouse
relations?
3. Why can terminal OAuth sign-in succeed while a fresh scheduled worker task fails?
4. Which regression evidence would you require before changing the runtime and dbt adapter together?
5. A NAV run is active during a column rename. How would you preserve compatible execution, input
identity and candidate evidence?
6. Which observations distinguish scheduler delay, worker saturation and remote warehouse
contention?
7. What state and checks must be restored before declaring recovery of a published product?
